sections.methods:
This study is part of a broader research project on brain imaging in migraine (MIG_N2Treat). It followed a prospective, longitudinal, within-subject design, and consisted of a comprehensive neuroimaging protocol encompassing arterial spin labelling MRI, diffusion MRI and task-fMRI as well as resting-state fMRI. In this report we focus specifically on the pain imagery task and resting-state fMRI data, while the methods and results of other parts of the protocol are described elsewhere (Domingos et al. ; Esteves et al. ; Fouto et al. , ; Guadilla et al. ; Matoso et al. ; Ruiz-Tagle et al. ). The research protocol and statistical analysis were not preregistered. The study was approved by the Hospital da Luz Ethics Committee and all participants provided written informed consent in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki 7th revision.

People with migraine were recruited by a neurologist during routine consultations at the headache outpatient clinics of Hospital da Luz, Lisbon, Portugal. Healthy female controls were recruited through social media advertisements targeting the general population and university campuses, ensuring they matched the patient group in gender, age, contraceptive use, and menstrual phase at the time of scanning. We did not conduct a statistical power analysis prior to starting the study. Notwithstanding, we aimed to have a sample size of 15 people with migraine, aligning with previous MRI cohort studies that detected group differences during spontaneous migraine attacks with sample sizes of N = 13 (Coppola et al. , ) or N = 17 (Amin et al. ). The inclusion criteria were: being between 18 and 55 years; having at least 9 years of education; speaking Portuguese as their first language; being generally healthy (excluding migraine, for the patients), with no diagnosed condition significantly impacting active and productive life or causing life expectancy to be below 5 years. Additionally, patients were required to suffer from episodic menstrually related migraine without aura, diagnosed according to the criteria of the 3rd edition of the International Classification of Headache Disorders (ICHD-3), Appendix A1.1.2 (International Headache Society ). The menstrual relationship of the migraine attacks was established by a clinical interview conducted by the neurologist responsible for the recruitment of people with migraine. The exclusion criteria were: history or presence of a neurologic condition (excluding migraine, for the patients); history or presence of a psychiatric disorder and/or severe anxiety and/or depressive symptoms as assessed through questionnaires; history or presence of vascular disease; receiving treatment with psychoactive drugs (including anxiolytics, antidepressants, anti-epileptics, and any migraine prophylactics); being pregnant or trying to get pregnant, breastfeeding, being post-menopausal, or using contraception precluding cyclic menses; contraindications for MRI.

We aimed to assess patients during the ictal (M-ict) and interictal (M-inter) phases. For the interictal session, participants were required to be free from pain for at least 48 h before, with confirmation of the absence of a migraine attack obtained 72 h post-scan. Healthy controls were assessed in two phases of the menstrual cycle to match the peri-ictal and interictal phases of the patients, yielding respectively the perimenstrual phase (HC-pm) and the post-ovulation phase (HC-postov).

Resting-state (RS) fMRI data were collected (7 min, eyes-open) both for M-inter/HC-postov and M-ict/HC-pm. Participants were instructed to keep their eyes open, looking at a black screen, and to not think about anything in particular. For the pain imagery (PI) task, patients (M-inter) performed attack imagery, recollecting the experience of their most severe migraine attack episode, while controls (HC-postov) had to recall their most severe episode of internal head pain (e.g. tooth pain). The task consisted of eight 20-s periods of pain imagery alternated with eight 20-s pain relief imagery (~ 5min30s), with eyes-closed following verbal instructions. The experimental protocol is schematically represented in Fig. .

Additionally, we collected detailed clinical history information from people with migraine, including disease duration, typical attack characteristics (e.g., pain intensity, frequency, and duration), and related clinical features. Demographic variables (e.g., age and years of education) were obtained for both groups. All participants completed the State–Trait Anxiety Inventory (STAI; State and Trait subscales)(Silva and Campos ; Spielberger et al. ) and the Positive and Negative Affect Schedule (PANAS)(Watson et al. ) to assess anxiety and affective state. The STAI-Trait was administered once to capture stable anxiety disposition, whereas the STAI-State and PANAS were administered at the beginning of each experimental session to assess session-specific anxiety and affective states prior to task performance. People with migraine additionally completed the Headache Impact Test (HIT-6)(Kosinski et al., ), a measure of headache-related functional impact, and the Mig-SCog questionnaire (Gil-Gouveia et al. ), which assesses migraine-related subjective cognitive complaints. These measures were used to characterize the sample and to explore potential associations between clinical features and neuroimaging metrics.

The MRI data was collected using a 3T Siemens Vida system, with a 64-channel radio frequency (RF) coil. Functional images were acquired with a T2*-weighted gradient-echo Echo Planar Imaging (EPI) with the following parameters: TR/TE = 1260/30ms, flip angle = 70º, in-plane generalized autocalibrating partially parallel acquisition (GRAPPA) acceleration factor = 2, simultaneous multi-slice (SMS) factor = 3, 60 slices, 2.2 mm isotropic voxel resolution. T1-weighted structural images were obtained with a magnetization-prepared rapid gradient echo (MPRAGE) sequence, with TR = 2300 ms, TE = 2.98 ms, inversion time (TI) = 900 ms, and 1 mm isotropic voxel resolution. Fieldmap magnitude and phase images were obtained using a double-echo gradient echo sequence (TR = 400.0 ms, TE = 4.92/7.38 ms, voxel size: 3.4 × 3.4 × 3.0 mm 3 , flip angle = 60º). We acquired 262 and 333 fMRI volumes for the pain imagery task and resting state, respectively. Earplugs were provided to reduce acoustic noise exposure, and small cushions were placed around the head to minimize movement.

The FMRIB Software Library (FSL)’s tools (Jenkinson et al. ) were used to preprocess the MRI data. For the structural images this included non-brain tissue removal using Brain Extraction Tool (BET) and bias field correction using FMRIB’s Automated Segmentation Tool (FAST). Each structural image was registered to the subject’s functional space (reference volume) as well as the standard MNI space using FMRIB’s Linear Image Registration Tool (FLIRT) and FMRIB’s Non-Linear Image Registration Tool (FNIRT), respectively. fMRI data preprocessing consisted of: EPI distortion correction using FMRIB’s Utility for Geometrically Unwarping EPIs (FUGUE) based on the acquired fieldmap; volume realignment with respect to the middle volume (reference) using FLIRT, yielding 6 rigid-body motion parameters; and high-pass temporal filtering with a cut-off frequency of 0.01 Hz to remove slow drift fluctuations. Finally, spatial smoothing was performed using SUSAN tool (FSL’s SUSAN), employing a Gaussian kernel with a full-width half maximum of 3.3 mm. The preprocessing pipeline can be found here: https://github.com/martaxavier/fMRI-Preprocessing .

For dFC computation and characterization of the temporal dynamics of the SN, we employed the leading eigenvector dynamic analysis (LEiDA) framework (Cabral et al. ), previously used to study conditions such as major depressive disorder (Figueroa et al. ) and schizophrenia (Farinha et al. ). The code for the LEiDA toolbox was publicly available ( https://github.com/PSYMARKER/leida-matlab ) and was used with MATLAB software version R2023b. The pipeline is illustrated in Fig. .

The dynamic functional connectivity eigenvectors were extracted from preprocessed parcellated fMRI data (Fig. a). fMRI data was parcellated by computing region average time courses using Schaefer atlas (Schaefer et al. ) with 100 parcels, directly corresponding to the 7 canonical intrinsic functional networks defined by Yeo et al. (): fronto-parietal network (FPN), default mode network (DMN), dorsal attention network (DAN), limbic network (LN), salience network (SN), somatomotor network (SMN) and visual network (VN). The time series of each region were demeaned and bandpass-filtered from 0.01 to 0.1 Hz using a 5th order Butterworth filter.

We estimated the individual instantaneous phase of each region ( ) for each timepoint by applying the Hilbert Transform to each region time-course. The phase coherence ( PhCoh ) between regions n and p for each timepoint was then estimated as:

PhCoh values vary between − 1 and 1, where − 1 indicates that areas n and are anti-phase at time t and 1 means they are synchronized. For all subjects, we computed it for all pairwise combinations of brain areas ( n,p ), with at each timepoint t , with for the PI task or for the RS. The first and last timepoints for each scan were excluded since they could suffer distortions induced by the Hilbert transform.

Following the LEiDA approach, which concentrates on the principal patterns of PhCoh matrices by analysing their leading eigenvector, we computed the leading eigenvector for each time point, , a vector (reflecting the parcellation into 100 regions) that indicates the main direction of phase alignment across all brain regions, dividing brain regions into two communities based on the sign of its elements. If all elements of share the same sign, it reflects a global phase coherence, meaning all regions are grouped into one community. However, if contains both positive and negative elements, brain regions are divided into two communities according to their phase coherence. The absolute value of each element of indicates how strongly each brain region contributes to its assigned community. By convention, we set up so that most of its elements are negative (multiplying by -1 in case this is not true), noting that both and are valid leading eigenvectors. This approach allows us to select a distinct functional network comprising brain regions with positive elements, representing regions that deviate from the global coherence mode. By employing the LEiDA methodology, we achieve significant dimensionality reduction while preserving over 50% of the variance in phase coherence across all scans and time points.

After calculating from the PhCoh matrix for each time point, we identified recurring dFC states observed over time (Fig. b). To do this, we combined the leading eigenvectors from all scans, including data from both groups and all three conditions, into a single dataset. We then used k-means clustering to group the leading eigenvectors into clusters, exploring a range of 3 to 10 clusters ( K=3:10 ). Clustering was conducted by minimizing the cosine distance between eigenvectors within each cluster. The algorithm was run 1,000 times, with a maximum of 500 iterations per run, to minimize the chance of settling on a local rather than a global solution. For each value of K , the process yielded K clusters. Each cluster was represented by a centroid ( ), a vector of dimension , corresponding to a recurrent dFC state. The centroid was calculated as the average of the leading eigenvectors assigned to that cluster.

After determining the possible clustering solutions, we identified the centroid that most closely resembled the SN for each number of clusters K , i.e., the one with the largest spatial overlap (Fig. c). To achieve this, we created a vector, , representing the SN, where each element was calculated as the proportion of voxels in each region of Schaefer’s functional parcellation (with direct matching to Yeo’s intrinsic functional networks) corresponding to the SN, relative to the total number of voxels in that region. We then computed the Pearson correlation between and each cluster centroid vector, . Following the standard LEiDA convention, all negative values of were first set to zero, such that the correlation was computed using only the positive centroid elements, which define the regions participating in the functional network of interest, whereas negative values represent regions with an opposite phase relative to the dominant pattern. For each number of clusters, K, the centroid with the highest significant correlation with was designated as representing the SN, .

For each clustering solution, we derived a binary time course for the salience network (SN) state for each subject (Fig. d). This binary time course indicated whether the SN was in the background (when the assigned centroid did not correspond to the SN) or dominant (for time points assigned to the SN centroid). To characterize the SN dynamics, we calculated two parameters: fractional occupancy and dwell time. Fractional occupancy represents the probability of the SN state occurring, defined as the percentage of time points assigned to the SN state. Dwell time refers to the average duration of the SN state, calculated as the mean number of consecutive time points assigned to the SN state across all occurrences. This calculation excludes instances where the state occurs at the very beginning or end of the scan, since it may have already started or may have not finished yet and the duration would not be correctly estimated.

Between-group differences in age were assessed using the Wilcoxon rank-sum test. Statistically significant differences between groups during pain imagery and resting state for both sessions were evaluated using a permutation-based t-test as implemented in the LEiDA toolbox This non-parametric test evaluates group differences by permuting group labels to generate the null distribution, rather than relying on standard parametric distributions. The null distribution was computed separately for each population, and a t-test was performed for each of the 5,000 permutations to compare between-group (two-sample) and within-group (one-sample, performed only for the resting state). For each parameter, we then applied multiple comparisons False Discovery Rate (FDR) correction with the Benjamini-Hochberg method (Benjamini and Hochberg ; Martínez-Cagigal ). FDR correction was applied separately for the between-group and within-group analyses, accounting for the number of clustering solutions (K = 3–10) and the number of comparisons in each analysis (between-group: M-inter vs. HC-postov RS; M-inter vs. HC-postov PI; M-ict vs. HC-pm RS; within-group: HC-postov vs. HC-pm RS; M-inter vs. M-ict RS). The effect size was evaluated using Hedges’ g, to accommodate the small sample size (Hedges and Olkin ). To assess the potential influence of age on the primary findings, post hoc robustness analyses were conducted using linear regression models including group and age as predictors.

To examine the potential clinical relevance of salience network (SN) dynamic functional connectivity (dFC) metrics, we performed correlation analyses using Spearman correlation between temporal features showing significant differences between M and HC and a subset of clinically relevant variables. These included three measures linked to usual attack severity and impact (attack pain intensity, HIT-6, and Mig-SCog), as well as three measures reflecting session-specific affect and anxiety (PANAS positive affect, PANAS negative affect, and STAI-State). Associations were evaluated using two-tailed Spearman’s rank correlation coefficient, given the sample size. These analyses were considered exploratory and were not included in the multiple-comparisons correction applied to the primary group-level permutation tests.
sections.results:
The flowchart of the recruitment and participant selection is presented in Fig. .

An initial pool of 29 people with migraine and 60 healthy controls were approached out of which 18 and 16 were included in the study, respectively. Of the 18 people with migraine, one was excluded due to an incidental finding and only 11 people with migraine completed the 2 sessions and were included in the analysis. From the 16 healthy controls, one subject was excluded due to incidental findings, leading to a final sample of 15 healthy controls. Due to technical issues, data acquisition was truncated for two participants. However, given the nature of the analysis and the small sample size, their data were still included. Specifically, for one participant during M-inter PI, 235 out of 262 volumes were acquired, and for another participant during HC-pm RS, 222 out of 333 volumes were acquired. From the 3 conditions of the final groups of 11 people with migraine and 15 healthy controls, we obtained a total of 78 scans to define the SN states. Table presents the demographic and clinical variables for both groups. Age did not differ significantly between groups (Wilcoxon rank-sum test, p = 0.113).

For each clustering solution, we identified the centroid exhibiting the strongest significant correlation with the SN. Further details regarding this procedure are provided in the Supplementary Material (Tables S1-S2 and Figure ). The spatial patterns of the selected centroids are shown in Fig. . Across the clustering solutions, the correlation of the centroid with the SN was statistically significant (FDR-corrected p-values below 0.05, as presented in Table ) and ranged between 0.62 and 0.75, with maximal values obtained for . From the distribution of the positive elements of the centroid vector, represented with red bars, we may observe that most of these elements correspond to regions within the SN. Additionally, the centroid vector highlights the contributions of brain regions from each of the other six canonical intrinsic functional networks defined by Yeo et al. (), with other contributions coming mostly from the DAN and SMN. Notably, the clustering solutions were consistent across different values of K , reinforcing the robustness of the observed patterns.

In Fig. , we make a link with anatomical regions that constitute the SN for each clustering solution, by showing the contribution to the centroid attributed to the SN state. For instance, the ACC and the insula play a key role in the salience network and have been linked to migraine pathophysiology. For K=6 up to K=10 , the ACC is represented bilaterally, whereas for other K s only the right side shows a contribution. Regarding the insula, it presents a bilateral contribution for all K s, being the strongest. In general, the represented regions and the values of their contributions are consistent across K s.

The fractional occupancy and dwell time for all sessions and tasks across K s are represented in Fig. . No significant between-group differences in fractional occupancy were observed for any session or task. A significant between-group difference in SN dwell time was observed during the PI task, with M-inter exhibiting significantly lower SN dwell time compared to HC-postov, for . Large Hedges’ g effect sizes were observed for these clustering solutions ( K= 7 , g = 1.19; K = 8 , g = 1.33; K = 9 , g = 1.36). The remaining clustering solutions showed a similar trend, consistent with their analogous state configurations, although these differences did not survive the significance threshold after correction. While the effect size was small for K = 3 (g = 0.46), it exceeded 0.9 for the other clustering solutions even when statistical significance was not retained following FDR correction. To facilitate the interpretation of the dwell time findings, complementary analyses of the SN state temporal metrics are provided in the Supplementary Material (Table S3).

No significant between-group differences in SN dwell time were detected in the present sample during RS for any clustering solution, either comparing M-inter with HC-postov or M-ict with HC-pm. Moreover, no significant differences were found within-group for RS, as shown in Figure S2 (Supplementary Material). Therefore, the present study did not detect changes associated with the migraine attack or the menstrual cycle under these resting-state conditions.

As a robustness analysis to assess the potential influence of age, linear regression models were fitted for the significant dwell time comparisons (K = 7-9) , with dwell time as the dependent variable and group and age as predictors. The results were consistent with the primary permutation analysis, with the group effect remaining statistically significant across all three clustering solutions after adjustment for age, whereas age was not a significant predictor in any model (Table S4, Supplementary Material). As a further robustness analysis, the primary LEiDA permutation analysis was repeated after excluding the participant with the truncated pain imagery scan. Although the between-group comparisons no longer survived FDR correction, the pattern of results remained consistent, with similar effect sizes and uncorrected permutation p-values across the clustering solutions that were significant in the primary analysis (K = 7-9) , suggesting that the findings were not solely driven by the truncated acquisition (Table S5, Supplementary Material).

Regarding the association between the significant results and the clinical variables, there were no significant correlations, as shown in Figure S3 (Supplementary Material).

Figure depicts the time-course of the SN for all participants, sessions and tasks, for K=7 , the first clustering solution for which there are significant differences regarding the dwell time. Consistently with the significantly shorter dwell time, it can be observed that the SN events during the PI task tend to be shorter for M-inter compared with HC-postov, as indicated by the statistical analysis.
sections.discussion:
We found a significant between-group difference in SN dynamics during the pain imagery task, in which people with migraine recalled a previous migraine attack and healthy controls recalled non-migraine head pain, with people with migraine exhibiting shorter SN dwell time. In contrast, no between-group differences were detected in the present sample during resting state either in the interictal phase or during spontaneous migraine attacks (ictal phase). dFC analysis revealed that the SN state in patients remained dominant for shorter periods than in controls, indicating reduced temporal persistence of the SN state (see Supplementary Material for complementary analyses of fractional occupancy and entry count). Importantly, this between-group difference was observed during the pain imagery task, suggesting that this paradigm may be particularly sensitive to group differences in SN dynamics related to the cognitive and emotional processing of pain-related representations rather than reflecting a generalized disruption. However, because the recalled experiences differed between groups, it remains to be determined whether these differences are migraine-specific or are influenced by characteristics of the recalled experiences.

Our finding of shorter mean duration of SN occurrences indicates increased temporal instability of SN dynamics during pain imagery, which is not fully aligned with the work by Veréb et al. () reporting greater SN temporal instability in people with migraine with aura during the interictal phase. In contrast to Veréb et al. (), we found SN instability in patients without aura and only while they were engaged in the imagery of an attack. It is possible that, during the resting state, only people with migraine with aura, who likely exhibit higher cortical excitability, show altered sensory processing that leads to changes in SN dynamics, whereas our use of a pain imagery task enabled us to detect these effects in patients without aura. This interpretation is also consistent with the heterogeneous resting-state fMRI literature in migraine with aura, in which findings have often been difficult to reproduce across studies (Hougaard et al. , ). One possible explanation is that resting-state activity may be inherently more variable than task-related brain activity, whereas a standardized pain imagery paradigm may provide a more controlled context for detecting group differences in network dynamics. In line with Veréb et al. (), a resting-state electroencephalography (EEG) study reporting that a microstate linked to the SN exhibited a shorter mean duration for patients during the interictal phase compared to healthy controls (Li et al. ). Indeed, EEG microstates are thought to reflect the spatiotemporal dynamics of brain networks showing quasi-stable spatial configurations, akin to the fMRI dFC states in our analysis (Abreu et al. ; Allen et al. ; Bréchet et al. ; Qiu et al. ). In contrast with these previous studies, we did not detect alterations in SN dynamics during rest but only during the pain imagery task. This may reflect the fact that the task explicitly engages cognitive and emotional processes related to pain, such as memory retrieval, anticipation, and evaluative appraisal, which strongly recruit the SN. Under these conditions, subtle alterations in salience processing may become more detectable than during unconstrained resting-state activity.

This is the first study to employ a pain imagery fMRI paradigm to assess SN connectivity in people with migraine. We have previously investigated brain activation using our proposed pain imagery fMRI paradigm by employing a whole-brain voxel-wise approach (Perdigão et al. ). We found that, compared to healthy controls, people with migraine exhibited significantly greater deactivation of the ACC, among other pain-processing regions, indicating a dysregulation of pain inhibition. The ACC is involved in the emotional aspect of pain processing, becoming active when we observe others in pain and when we experience our own pain-related distress. It also helps regulate perceived pain intensity, contributing to the ability to adapt to discomfort and manage suffering in pain responses (Fuchs et al. ; Xiao and Zhang ). These findings suggest that alterations in these regions may emerge even in the absence of direct nociceptive input, when patients engage with pain-related mental representations. The current study further supports it through its involvement in the abnormal dynamics of the SN.

A few fMRI studies have previously analysed brain activation during pain imagery or similar protocols (Derbyshire et al. ; Gu and Han ; Ogino et al. ; Raij et al. , ), reporting the involvement of areas belonging to the SN, such as the ACC, insula, cerebellum, dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and secondary somatosensory cortex. To our knowledge, only Eck et al. () employed a pain imagery paradigm in people with migraine, whereby participants had to create mental images (compared to counting the number of vowels) based on pain-related and non-pain related adjectives. During imagination of pain-related words, patients showed stronger activation in affective pain-related brain regions compared to controls. Interestingly, although the words used in the paradigm were not migraine-specific, five people with migraine and one control referred having imagined a headache as an example of a pain-related word. Despite some similarity with our imagery conditions, the SN connectivity and temporal dynamics were not analysed and therefore the results cannot be directly compared with our current study.

The ACC and the insula are two crucial regions within the SN that contributed to the identification of the SN dFC state in our study. Since pain is a multidimensional experience (Lee et al. ), the pain imagery task is expected to preferentially engage the affective and cognitive components of pain rather than its sensory-discriminative aspects, which aligns with the known roles of the ACC and insula. In fact, observing a noxious stimulus being administered to someone else, or viewing a cue that signals its impending delivery, does not directly activate nociceptors, but it carries a high degree of salience (Iannetti and Mouraux ).

Furthermore, the insula has been linked to autonomic and somatosensory alterations in migraine, as it is involved in autonomic regulation, interoception and emotion (Menon and Uddin ; Moayedi ). The anterior insula is connected to the middle and inferior temporal gyri, the anterior cingulate cortex, and various limbic regions, all of which contribute to its role in emotional regulation. In contrast, the posterior insula is linked to premotor, sensorimotor, supplementary motor areas, and the middle-posterior cingulate cortex, supporting its involvement in sensorimotor integration. The insula has been associated not only with nociception but also with the affective dimension of pain, particularly the unpleasantness of a painful experience (Lee et al. ). It is also involved in empathizing with others’ pain (Jackson et al. ) and remains active during noxious stimulation even in individuals with congenital insensitivity to pain (Salomons et al. ). This aligns with our findings that alterations occur even without painful stimuli; simply imagining a painful and unpleasant experience can lead to observable differences in the SN of people with migraine.

Since we did not detect between-group differences in SN dynamics during spontaneous migraine attacks (ictal phase), either comparing to healthy controls or to the interictal phase of people with migraine, our findings suggest that different processes may dominate large-scale brain dynamics during the ongoing experience of an attack compared to the cognitive reconstruction of an attack through imagery. These mechanisms might either obscure the contribution of the SN or fundamentally alter its behaviour, by affecting oxygenation, metabolism, and neuronal excitability. For instance, during the ictal phase, heightened cortical excitability or other network-level adaptations (Messina et al. ; Peng and May ) could dominate sensory processing, potentially obscuring subtler alterations in SN dynamics that may be more easily observed during engagement in a pain-related cognitive task. This shift in network dynamics indicates that the migraine attack involves complex overlapping processes that differ from those present during periods without an attack.

Another possible explanation for not finding SN disruption in the ictal phase is that sensory processing abnormalities fluctuate throughout the migraine cycle, intensifying in the preictal phase but generally diminishing during the attack (de Tommaso et al. ). This suggests that an adaptive or protective mechanism may be active during the interictal phase, leading to an amplification of certain sensory processing components during this period.

Importantly, pain imagery may engage predictive and memory-based aspects of pain processing that are not fully active during resting-state ictal scans, when the experience of an attack is actually occurring and not being retrieved. In people with migraine, repeated headache experiences could strengthen associations between pain cues and anticipatory or evaluative processes, transiently destabilizing SN dynamics during imagery. This mechanism highlights how cognitive and emotional representations of pain can selectively recruit the SN, revealing alterations that may be masked when ongoing nociceptive input dominates network activity.

Although the proposed attack imagery task does not exactly mimic the experience of a migraine attack, it successfully elicited SN dynamics that were distinct from healthy controls undergoing a pain imagery task. However, because the recalled experiences differed between groups, it remains unclear whether these differences reflect migraine-specific mechanisms or characteristics of the retrieved memories. Nevertheless, the findings suggest that this paradigm may provide a valuable approach for studying the cognitive and emotional aspects of recalled pain experiences in people with migraine. When applied during the interictal phase, this attack imagery paradigm may help disentangle these processes from the sensory and physiological changes accompanying an ongoing migraine attack, although future studies using more closely matched imagery conditions and behavioural assessments will be important to clarify the underlying mechanisms.

Regarding the pain imagery task, all participants were informed about it before entering the MR scanner and were given the opportunity to select their pain experiences and practice beforehand. However, it was only performed during the interictal session for people with migraine and the post-ovulation for healthy controls, not allowing for a within-group comparison. Moreover, due to its subjective nature, the content of their imagery may have varied significantly, possibly leading to less consistent or less specific mental representations among healthy controls. Our protocol did not include post-task ratings of the imagery experience, which could have provided insight into these variations by assessing variables such as imagery vividness, recalled pain intensity, emotional valence, and cognitive effort. These measures would also have enabled a quantitative comparison of the recalled experiences between groups. Future studies could incorporate established imagery questionnaires, such as the Vividness of Visual Imagery Questionnaire (Marks ) or the Plymouth Sensory Imagery Questionnaire (Andrade et al. ), together with visual analogue scales for task-specific ratings. Moreover, because people with migraine recalled previous migraine attacks whereas healthy controls recalled non-migraine head pain, the observed SN differences may reflect characteristics of the recalled experiences (e.g., emotional salience, self-relevance, vividness, or affective content) rather than migraine-specific neural mechanisms. Future studies using more closely matched imagery conditions are needed to disentangle these possibilities.

Furthermore, we did not observe significant associations between the neuroimaging findings and clinical measures indexing typical attack severity (pain intensity), headache-related impact (HIT-6), migraine-related cognitive complaints (Mig-SCog), or session-level affective and anxiety states assessed prior to scanning. However, these measures were collected outside the task context and may not adequately capture momentary subjective experience during imagery. Additionally, the potential influence of having eyes open during resting state versus closed during the pain imagery task cannot be entirely ruled out, and further data is needed to clarify these effects.

The relatively small sample size of the study is an obvious limitation of our study, as it limits the statistical power to detect more subtle between-group differences and may not fully capture the diversity of migraine attack experiences and FC patterns. The sample size was constrained by two main factors: our choice of a very specific cohort of people with migraine (menstrually related episodic migraine without aura), and the longitudinal design requiring each patient to be studied over multiple sessions. Although the choice of a specific cohort reduces variability between patients, thus eliminating potential confounds, it not only limits the sample size but also restricts the generalizability of our findings to other migraine subtypes. On the other hand, the relatively homogeneous cohort also reduced potential sources of biological and clinical variability that are often present in broader migraine cohorts.

Moreover, the data were not always collected within the same migraine cycle for each participant. This may have introduced additional variability due to differences between attacks in the same patient, including pain intensity during the ictal phase.

Regarding the LEiDA analysis, clustering was performed using all fMRI time points across participants, and the k-means algorithm was run with multiple replicates to reduce the influence of convergence to local minima. Importantly, the reported differences in the LEiDA temporal metrics were consistently observed across adjacent clustering solutions (K = 7-9) , supporting the stability of these metrics and of the identified salience network state across different levels of clustering granularity. Nevertheless, replication in larger, independent cohorts is needed to establish the reproducibility and generalizability of these LEiDA temporal metrics and the associated findings.

Another limitation is the use of hormonal contraception by some participants, introducing a potential confound, since hormones influence FC (Dubol et al. ) and migraine pathophysiology (Ahmad and Rosendale ; Krause et al. ). Unfortunately, restricting the use of hormonal contraception would have further reduced the sample size. Additionally, we did not measure hormonal levels, which renders uncertainty in the definition of the menstrual cycle in women with natural menstrual cycles.

We employed a case-control longitudinal design to study patients with menstrually related migraine without aura during ictal and interictal phases, along with healthy controls matched for menstrual cycle phase. Resting-state and interictal pain imagery fMRI data were analyzed using time-varying functional connectivity to characterize SN dynamics. Compared to healthy controls, people with migraine exhibited shorter SN dwell times specifically during the pain imagery task, whereas no between-group differences were detected during interictal or ictal resting states. These findings suggest that pain imagery may provide a valuable paradigm for investigating SN dynamics in people with migraine by engaging the cognitive and emotional processing of recalled pain. Future studies using more closely matched imagery conditions are needed to determine whether the observed between-group differences reflect migraine-specific mechanisms or differences in the recalled experiences between groups.

title: Postmarketing pharmacovigilance study of levothyroxine based on FDA adverse event reporting system (FAERS) and Mendelian randomization.
abstract: This study utilizes adverse event records for levothyroxine from the FAERS database to explore and evaluate its post-marketing adverse events. Using levothyroxine adverse event records from the FAERS database, four methods-report ratio odds ratio (ROR), proportional reporting ratio (PRR), Bayesian confidence propagation neural network (BCPNN), and multivariable gamma-Poisson shrinkage model (MGPS)-were applied to assess pharmacovigilance signals for levothyroxine adverse reactions. Causality between levothyroxine and adverse events was assessed via two-sample Mendelian randomization (MR) analysis. This study identified multiple adverse events not listed in levothyroxine prescribing information, including dizziness, depression, myalgia, migraine, celiac disease, lactose intolerance, autoimmune thyroiditis, and nail disorders. Mendelian randomization analysis indicated a causal relationship between levothyroxine and myalgia, migraine, celiac disease, lactose intolerance, and autoimmune thyroiditis. These findings provide valuable reference information for reducing clinical risks associated with levothyroxine use. Clinicians should be vigilant for these adverse reactions when prescribing levothyroxine.

title: New-onset alopecia areata during calcitonin gene-related peptide inhibitor therapy: first reported case.
abstract: Dear Editor, Calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) is a neuropeptide with potent vasodilatory effects and a key role in trigeminovascular signaling, underlying the pathogenesis of migraine. Consequently, the inhibition of CGRP activity has been demonstrated to reduce the incidence of acute migraine attacks. Based on this evidence, monoclonal antibodies against CGRP or its receptor have been approved by the European Medicines Agency for prevention of both episodic and chronic migraine. Among CGRP inhibitors, galcanezumab has also been authorized for the treatment of episodic cluster headache. Since the advent of CGRP inhibitors, several cases of drug-induced telogen effluvium have been reported, with incidence rates ranging from 1.10% to 7.23%. However, to the best of our knowledge, alopecia areata (AA) associated with CGRP inhibition remains undescribed in the literature. [...].

title: Pediatric migraine.
abstract: Migraine headaches are common in children and adolescents, with a wide spectrum of clinical forms. The most frequent pattern in children is migraine without aura, characterized by attacks of frontal, pounding, nauseating headache lasting 1 to 72 hours. The spectrum of migraine with aura includes migraine with typical aura, hemiplegic migraine, and basilar-type migraine, all of which may manifest during early childhood and pose challenging diagnostic dilemmas. The periodic syndromes are a fascinating subset of migraine peculiar to extremely young children, which are viewed as "precursors" to more typical migraine and can be associated with frightening focal neurologic disturbances. Migraine treatment philosophy now embraces a balanced approach with biobehavioral interventions and acute and preventative pharmacologic measures. A growing body of controlled pediatric data is beginning to emerge regarding migraine treatment in children, lessening our dependence on extrapolated adult data.

title: Prophylactic effect of riboflavin on pediatric migraine: a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial.
abstract: BACKGROUND AND AIM: Riboflavin may have an acceptable effect on migraine among children. This study was carried out to determine the prophylactic effect of riboflavin on migraine in children. METHODS: This randomized clinical trial study was performed at Shahid Beheshti Hospital in Kashan, Iran from December 2012 to February 2015. Ninety children with migraine were allocated randomly into 3 groups (placebo, low-dose and high-dose riboflavin). The outcomes (frequency, intensity and duration of headaches) were measured at baseline and 12 weeks of medication in each group, and the decrease of them were compared. SPSS software version 16 was used for analysis of the data. Descriptive statistics, Chi-square, Fisher's exact and t-test were used for statistical analyses. RESULTS: There was a significant decrease of migraine frequency (p=0.000) and mean duration (p=0.000) in the high-dose group compared with the placebo group. No significant reduction of frequency and mean duration of attacks were reported in the low-dose group compared to the placebo group (p=0.49 and p=0.69 respectively). There was no significant reduction of migraine intensity in the low-dose and high-dose groups compared to the placebo group (p=0.71 and p=0.74 respectively). CONCLUSION: High-dose riboflavin is a safe, well tolerated, cost-effective method of prophylaxis for children with migraine. TRIAL REGISTRATION: The trial was registered at the Iranian Clinical Trial Registry with number IRCT2013020412361N1. FUNDING: The study was supported by the Deputy of Research, Kashan University of Medical Sciences (grant number 91073).

sections.methods:
This double-blind, randomized clinical trial study was conducted on 5 to 13-year-old children with migraine, from December 2012 to February 2015 in the neurology clinic of Shahid Beheshti Hospital, Kashan, Iran. All cases were diagnosed and examined by a pediatric neurologist. After obtaining the informed consent from parents, questionnaires were filled. The questions covered different areas including age, sex, migraine with and without aura, months passed since onset of migraine, family history of migraine and mean intensity, frequency and duration of headache in the last month preceding our trial. Diagnoses were made based on diagnostic criteria for migraine with or without aura and tension headaches present in the International Classification of Headache Disorders, 2 nd edition (ICHD-II) (). Inclusion criteria were 5 to 13-year-old children with or without aura who had at least two moderate to severe intensity attacks per month. Exclusion criteria were: 1- severe neurologic disorders or epilepsy 2- liver, kidney, gastrointestinal, cardiovascular or metabolic disorders 3- prophylactic drug use during the month prior to the trial 4- less than two attacks per month 5- tension headache 6- mild intensity headache 7- uncooperative parents and children.

Sample size was estimated according to a study by Condo et al., in which a significant decrease of mean headache frequency in phase 2 compared to baseline (21.7±13.7 vs. 13.2±11.8) in riboflavin group, α =0.05 and power equaled 0.8 (). Sample size was estimated as 90 for all groups (30 patients in each group). Data were entered into SPSS software version 16 (SPSS, Inc. Chicago, Illinois, USA). Statistical analysis was performed based on intension-to-treat (ITT) method. Continuous data were measured by mean and standard deviation (SD) and categorical data were shown by frequency and percentage. Comparison of riboflavin effect between groups on attack frequency and intensity was evaluated by Chi-square and Fisher’s exact tests, and the effect on duration of headaches was conducted by independent-samples t-test. The riboflavin effect on three headache items in each group was determined by paired-samples t-test. All statistical tests were considered significant at p<0.05.
sections.results:
Migraine is a common disorder among children and adolescents, with prevalence of about 3% in early childhood and up to 23% in adolescents (). Occasionally, frequency and severity of migraine become overwhelming which cause disturbance of life quality and can lead to high rates of absenteeism from school and many social problems. In such circumstances, prophylactic therapy is recommended to reduce excessive drug usage and improve the quality of life (, ). The safety of many prophylactic drugs in adults with migraine has not been tested completely on children, so symptomatic therapies are preferred for them (, , ). Despite the use of topiramate as a prophylactic agent for migraine, some studies have indicated marked side effects on cognition (, ). Cinnarizine is a calcium channel blocker that has been documented as an effective prophylactic agent for migraine (). Nevertheless, in spite of various drugs, no Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved medication is recommended for prophylaxis of migraine in children (). Riboflavin is involved in the mitochondrial electron transport chain and has been used in some patients with mitochondrial disorders (–). Riboflavin is a known co-factor of mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation and is a precursor of flavin which is needed for transport of electrons in respiratory process of the mitochondria and some investigations have shown a mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation dysfunction in adults with migraine. So, supraphysiological doses of riboflavin could be beneficial for this impairment ().There are some studies that suggest the efficacy of high-dose riboflavin (400 mg/day) for migraine prevention in adults (–), and doses of 100–400 mg/day of riboflavin in children are concordant with adult studies (, ). There is limited evidence for riboflavin use among children (). A randomized, placebo-controlled trial showed no effect of high-dose riboflavin on migraine prophylaxis in children (, ). Another study on 8 to 18-year-old children in Italy indicated decrease of migraine frequency and intensity by riboflavin (). The side-effects of riboflavin have been shown as minimal, including diarrhea and polyuria (1 out of 43 adults). The most common harmless adverse effect of riboflavin is yellow to orange color change of the urine (). Due to substantial controversy about the effectiveness of riboflavin in children with migraine and a few side effects of it, we decided to perform a study to determine the effect of low dose and high dose riboflavin on intensity, duration and frequency of migraine

Following a one-month baseline period, patients were randomized to either receive a capsule of placebo, 100 mg riboflavin (low-dose) or 200 mg riboflavin (high-dose) daily for 12 weeks. No other prophylactic drugs were used during the study and only analgesics were prescribed if needed. Double-blinding was implemented in this trial. Researchers and participants were not aware of group allocation. A pharmacologist supervised the randomization process. For assessment of blinding, the parents were asked which medication their children were receiving (they did not know anything about it). At first, between numbers 1–90, 30 random numbers were chosen from a random number table and allocated to the placebo group and then another 30 random numbers allocated to the low dose group and finally the remaining 30 numbers were allocated to the high dose group (simple random sampling). They were written in a check list which was unseen by researchers and patients. The drugs were numbered from 1 to 90 by a pharmacologist, and the pharmacology staff gave them to patients respectively without any awareness about them. The pharmacologist had the check list and after filling it at the end of the study, the results were analyzed. Patients were instructed to take the capsules at breakfast. The capsules were manufactured by a pharmaceutical company with supervision of a pharmacologist. The drugs were similar according to their shape and taste. Both riboflavin and carotene make yellow/orange urine discoloration. So, to assure a double-blind study was taking place, 100mg carotene was used in placebo capsules. The patients were instructed to improve their sleep quality and increase its duration, stop caffeine intake and decrease the time of computer activity or television watching to a maximum of two hours daily. The parents and children received data concerning childhood migraine () and the patients consumed acetaminophen or ibuprofen orally during attacks.

Severity (intensity) of attacks was evaluated according to the following Likert scale: 1- for mild headaches during which the patient performs the usual activity, 2- for moderate headaches that slow down patient activity without halting it and 3- for severe headaches that stop patient activity (). Mean duration, intensity and number (frequency) of attacks were assessed two times, the first at the month before starting of riboflavin (baseline or week 0) and the second at the last month of riboflavin prophylaxis (week 8 to 12 or in other word week 12). Duration of attacks was defined as hours and frequency of attacks was based on the number of headache attacks per month (). The patients’ parents were asked to fill a headache diary in two stages (baseline period and the last month of riboflavin prophylaxis) of study including date, intensity and duration of any headache attack. Furthermore, the side-effects of the drugs were noted by the parents. Response was evaluated in the last month of consuming prophylactic medication in each group according to outcome variables. Primary and secondary outcomes were defined as follows: at least 50% drop in the number of headaches (frequency), one degree decrement in intensity and/or lessening of mean headache duration in last month of prophylaxis (last 4 weeks of treatment) regarding to the month before prophylaxis (4 weeks baseline or week 0) ().

The study was approved by the ethics committee of Kashan University of Medical Sciences with number 29/5/1/4410. All parents and some patients filled the informed consent and the nature of the study was explained to them. The information of participants was kept confidential. No charge was obtained from the patients. They were informed about the side-effects of the drugs and that they could contact the corresponding author regarding them. If any cases at any time decided to exclude themselves from the study, they were free to do so without any recompense. The Iranian Clinical Trial Registry number was IRCT2013020412361N1.

In total, 130 patients were enrolled and 40 children were excluded due to not meeting inclusion criteria, presence of exclusion criteria or declined to participate in the study (). The 90 remaining children were randomly and equally allocated in each group (placebo, low-dose riboflavin and high-dose riboflavin). Because the study had incorporated an ITT design, after allocation of the patients to the three groups, the lost follow up patients were not excluded from the study and their outcome variable data were reported equally at baseline and the last month of investigation (). The baseline characteristics of the three study groups are shown in and no confounding factors exist among them. shows the mean (SD) frequency, duration and intensity of migraine attacks at baseline and the end of riboflavin prophylaxis and mean decrease of them (baseline - end) in each group. The outcome variables were assessed at the end of the last month of medications. No significant difference was found between placebo and low-dose groups regarding 50% or more reduction of frequency attacks (p=0.49), but there was significant decrease of migraine frequency in the high-dose group compared with the placebo group (p=0.000). Four (13.3%), 6 (20%) and 24 (80%) patients had 50% or more decrease in migraine frequency in the placebo, low dose and high dose groups respectively (p=0.000). There was no significant diminution of migraine intensity in low-dose and high-dose groups in comparison to the placebo group (p=0.71 and p=0.74 in order). No significant difference was found in decline of mean duration of headache attacks in the last month of prophylaxis between the placebo and low-dose riboflavin groups (0.30±1.12 vs. 0.17±1.49) (p=0.69). Meanwhile, there was a dramatic shortening of mean duration of migraine attacks among the high-dose group individuals compared to those in the placebo group (4±3.49 vs. 0.30±1.12) (p=0.000). Also, there was a marked decline in mean duration of migraine attacks in the high-dose group compared with the low-dose group (4±3.49 vs. 0.17±1.49) (p=0.000). A significant decrease in frequency of attacks was reported in the high-dose group in comparison with the low-dose group (p=0.000). No significant reduction of migraine intensity was seen among the high-dose group compared to the low- dose group (p=0.47). Out of the three groups, 21 (70%), 20 (66.7%) and 7 (23.3%) of placebo, low dose and high dose group patients required analgesic drugs respectively (p=0.000). No noticeable side-effects of the treatment were reported during the study.

The present study showed that riboflavin prophylaxis significantly reduces migraine duration and frequency, but not the intensity. These data are in line with Condo et al. regarding frequency, not intensity (). The probable cause of frequency reduction may be due to high-dose riboflavin use in both studies. During an investigation on 48 Australian children, 200 mg/day riboflavin was not effective on frequency and severity of migraine attacks () which is inconsistent with our study, concerning the frequency response. This discrepancy may be due to genetic variation causing differences between distinct populations. On another note, the duration of therapy was three months in the Australian survey (), whereas in the Condo et al. investigation, the proper duration was proposed to be 4 months (). This is incongruent with our research, because we used riboflavin for three months. During a trial in the Netherlands on 6 to 13-year-old children, 50 mg/day riboflavin was prescribed for four months and no significant difference in mean duration, frequency and intensity between riboflavin and placebo groups was found (). These findings are in contrast with our results. The observed difference may be due to the fact that no upper limit () for migraine frequency (15 or more attacks per month is indicative of riboflavin resistance) was chosen as exclusion criterion and also, low-dose riboflavin was used (). The upper limit of eight headache attacks per month was used as an exclusion criterion in a MacLennan et al. study (). It must be mentioned that we did not determine any upper limit for headache frequency in our study. Condo et al. showed that riboflavin prophylaxis reduced migraine intensity and frequency, and this is compatible with our study according to headache frequency but not intensity (). Notably, they found a significant reduction of migraine frequency among children less than 12 years of age and a substantial decrease of migraine intensity in males (). It seems that age and sex may have influence on riboflavin’s effect, probably due to various riboflavin serum levels and pharmacokinetics (). These findings are incompatible with our data that indicate no relationship between age and sex and effect of riboflavin treatment on migraine intensity and frequency. Some adult studies have suggested that riboflavin prophylaxis diminishes migraine frequency but not migraine intensity, and this is congruent with our results (, ). Because of a probable high metabolic rate among children, Condo et al. treated patients with 200 mg or 400 mg/day riboflavin, however, no significant differences were detected in intensity and frequency responder rates between the two doses (), so we decided to choose 200 mg as the high-dose therapy. In a trial by Bruijn et al., cross-over design was performed for placebo and riboflavin (50 mg daily) groups. Nevertheless, no effect was reported on frequency and duration of migraine (). Probably due to use of low- dose riboflavin, their results were not in line with our research. Based on a recent pharmacogenetic study among adults with migraine, patients with non-haplogroup H human mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) respond better than those with haplogroup H mtDNA to riboflavin therapy (). In the present study, no riboflavin side-effects were reported which was consistent with other investigations (, ). Half-life of riboflavin is about 1 to 2 hours and its absorption has been indicated to reach saturation rate at 30–50 mg (). So, riboflavin dose between 100 to 400 mg daily in children with migraine seems to be safe for several months ().

The present study has some strong points: 1- The sample size is larger than some surveys (, , ). 2- A placebo-controlled, double-blind, randomized study was conducted. 3- Drop-out cases during the study were negligible. 4- Two appropriate doses of riboflavin were compared with the placebo group. To be noted, riboflavin is a low-cost drug without side-effects, so its use could be recommended to parents of children with migraine who have financial restrictions. Some limitations of our investigation include the following: 1- Duration of riboflavin prophylaxis was 3 months, whereas the minimum duration is usually recommended to be about 4 months (). 2- Upper limit for migraine frequency as an exclusion criterion was not ascertained. 3- Cross-over design was not performed for groups.

The present study indicates that high-dose riboflavin decreases the frequency and duration of migraine attacks in children, with no side effects. The practical importance issue is that it can be used instead of other medications. It is recommended that high dose riboflavin be used for migraine prophylaxis among children. Further studies with larger sample sizes and longer duration of riboflavin treatment with cross-over design will be helpful in the future.

title: Daytime Hypersomnolence in Migraine : Prevalence , Clinical Correlates and Independent Predictors in Malaysia
abstract: Abstract Background and objectives Sleep disturbances, including daytime hypersomnolence, are increasingly recognized as clinically significant comorbidities of migraine that adversely affect quality of life. However, data on the prevalence and determinants of daytime hypersomnolence among migraine patients in Malaysia and the broader Southeast Asian region remain limited. This study aimed to determine the prevalence of daytime hypersomnolence and to identify the clinical and sociodemographic factors associated with excessive daytime sleepiness in adult patients with migraine. Methods A single-center, cross-sectional study was conducted between April 2024 and April 2026 at the Neurology Clinic, Hospital Canselor Tuanku Muhriz (HCTM), Universiti Kebangsaan Malaysia (UKM). Eligible participants were adults aged 18 years and above with an established diagnosis of migraine for at least one year, confirmed by a neurologist according to the International Classification of Headache Disorders, Third Edition (ICHD-3) criteria. Baseline sociodemographic and clinical migraine data were systematically collected. Daytime hypersomnolence was assessed using the validated Epworth Sleepiness Scale (ESS), with a score exceeding 10 defining the outcome. Migraine-related disability was assessed using the Migraine Disability Assessment (MIDAS) questionnaire. Data were analyzed using IBM SPSS Statistics Version 29, with binary logistic regression performed to identify independent predictors. Results A total of 278 participants were recruited (mean age 46.4 ± 15.75 years; 85.6% female ). Twenty-five participants (9.0%) met the ESS threshold for daytime hypersomnolence. On univariate analysis, factors significantly associated with daytime hypersomnolence included coffee consumption, higher MIDAS score, comorbid gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), higher migraine attack frequency, greater pain severity, multiple migraine-associated symptoms, and use of sumatriptan, topiramate, and propranolol (all p Conclusion Daytime hypersomnolence affects approximately one in ten adult migraine patients attending a tertiary neurology clinic in Malaysia. Higher migraine-related disability, sumatriptan use, higher educational attainment, and earlier age of migraine onset are independent predictors. Routine screening for daytime hypersomnolence using ESS is practical, non-invasive, and clinically warranted as part of the holistic assessment and management of patients with migraine.

title: Insights into Pathophysiological Pathways in ME/CFS Through Genetic Correlation and Mendelian Randomization
abstract: Abstract Myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS) and post-acute infection syndromes (PAIS) are multisystem disorders involving immune, vascular, neuroinflammatory, and metabolic abnormalities, yet the causal relevance of these processes remains unclear. Using genome-wide summary statistics from DecodeME (15,579 cases), we performed genetic correlation, pleiotropic heritability, and Mendelian randomization analyses. Across 22 auxiliary traits spanning five mechanistic domains, cellular energetics, neurovascular regulation, and barrier–microbiome function showed the strongest genetic overlap with ME/CFS, with migraine and irritable bowel syndrome contributing most to shared pleiotropy. Immunothrombotic related and inflammatory traits showed smaller but measurable genetic correlations. Energetics-related traits, including type 2 diabetes and blood lactate, displayed consistent genetic correlation but relatively low shared pleiotropy, suggesting that metabolic dysfunction may act through broader physiological networks. Mendelian randomization identified three biomarkers with evidence for causal effects on ME/CFS risk: higher mitochondrial DNA copy number was protective, whereas increased glycoprotein acetyls and mean platelet volume increased risk. Together, these findings indicate that ME/CFS susceptibility reflects interacting pathways involving barrier–microbiome dysfunction, neurovascular instability, inflammation, platelet activation, and impaired cellular energetics Main Text

title: Conventional and genetic association between migraine and stroke with druggable genome-wide Mendelian randomization.
abstract: The genetic relationship between migraine and stroke remains underexplored, particularly in the context of druggable targets. Previous studies have been limited by small sample sizes and a lack of focus on genetic-targeted therapies for these conditions. We analyzed the association and causality between migraine and stroke using multivariable logistic regression in the UK Biobank cohort and Mendelian randomization (MR) analyses based on genome-wide association study (GWAS) data. Integrating expression quantitative trait loci (eQTLs) data from blood and brain regions, we explored the phenotypic and genetic links between migraine medications, drug target, and stroke. Additionally, we explored novel druggable genes for migraine and evaluated their effects on migraine signaling molecules and stroke risk. Migraine was significantly associated with stroke, particularly ischemic stroke (IS) and intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH), with MR analysis confirming a causal link to ICH. HTR1A emerged as a potential link between antidepressants (preventive medications for migraine) and stroke. We identified 17 migraine-related druggable genes, with 5 genes (HMGCR, TGFB1, TGFB3, KCNK5, IMPDH2) associated with nine existing drugs. Further MR analysis identified correlation of CELSR3 and IMPDH2 with cGMP pathway marker PRKG1, and identified KCNK5, PLXNB1, and MDK as novel migraine-associated druggable genes significantly linked to the stroke risks. These findings established the phenotypic and genetic link between migraine, its medication and stroke, identifying potential targets for single and dual-purpose therapies for migraine and stoke, and emphasized the need for further research to validate these associations.

title: Effects and side effects of migraine prophylaxis in children.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Migraine is the primary cause of headache in children. Most patients can be treated with lifestyle changes and acute attack prophylaxis. Prophylaxis should be considered when symptoms cause frequent school absenteeism, poor quality of life, recurring emergency room visits, and frequent analgesic use. We aimed to compare the efficacy and side effects of drugs used in migraine prophylaxis, chosen according to the clinical and/or demographic characteristics of the patients. METHODS: One hundred eighty-six patients aged 6-18 years were evaluated and who were diagnosed with migraine according to The International Classification of Headache Disorders, 3rd edition beta version (ICH-3β). Propranolol, topiramate, flunarizine, and cyproheptadine were given as prophylactic treatment. The Pediatric Migraine Disability Assessment Score (PedMIDAS) score, severity, duration, and frequency of the headache attacks were evaluated from the medical records and pre- and post-treatment values were compared. RESULTS: The median age of the patients was 14 years (range, 6-18 years) and the mean duration of headache was 29.6 ± 21.02 months. The mean PedMIDAS score was 29.9 ± 21.2 before and 14.9 ± 12.5 after treatment. Most reduction in the frequency of attacks was observed in the topiramate group. All four drugs significantly reduced the PedMIDAS score. The most common side effect was palpitations. CONCLUSIONS: Significant improvement was found in PedMIDAS scores in all drug groups. Topiramate was found to be the most effective drug in reducing the frequency of attacks. All four drugs in this study may be utilized for migraine prophylaxis in terms of effectiveness and safety.

title: Stress, Anxiety, Depression, and Pain Catastrophizing in Migraine: Associations with Disability and Quality of Life.
abstract: Migraine is a chronic neurological condition that significantly impairs daily functioning and quality of life. This study investigated how psychological factors, including anxiety, depression, perceived stress, and pain catastrophizing, influence migraine symptom severity and quality of life among 128 patients attending outpatient clinics in SADAT City, Egypt. Participants completed validated Arabic versions of the Migraine Disability Assessment, Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale, Pain Catastrophizing Scale, Migraine-Specific Quality of Life Questionnaire, and Perceived Stress Scale. Findings revealed high levels of psychological distress, with over two-thirds of participants reporting elevated anxiety and depression symptoms. Correlation and regression analyses demonstrated that depression and perceived stress were strong predictors of migraine severity and diminished quality of life, while anxiety and catastrophizing also contributed significantly. Female participants exhibited higher anxiety symptoms, depressive symptoms, and catastrophizing levels compared to males. These results highlight the central role of psychological distress in exacerbating migraine burden and reducing overall well-being. The findings emphasize the necessity of integrating psychological assessment and interventions, such as cognitive-behavioral therapy and stress management, into migraine treatment plans. This study contributes to the literature by simultaneously examining multiple psychological predictors of migraine disability and migraine-specific quality of life within an underrepresented clinical population in Egypt, providing further evidence for the biopsychosocial understanding of migraine. Addressing emotional and cognitive factors may enhance clinical outcomes and improve patients' functional and emotional quality of life.

title: Cost-Utility Analysis of Acupuncture for the Prevention of Episodic Migraine from a Lifetime Canadian Health System and Societal Perspective.
abstract: ObjectiveTo assess the lifetime cost-effectiveness of acupuncture in the prevention of episodic migraine from both a Canadian public health care payer and societal perspective.BackgroundAcupuncture has been used for pain relief for thousands of years in China and could be an alternative to drugs in managing pain. Nevertheless, there is limited evidence to determine if acupuncture is cost-effective in migraine prevention in the Canadian setting.MethodsA cost-utility analysis with a decision-analytic Markov model was constructed to compare acupuncture with drug prophylaxis and no active treatment among adult patients with episodic migraine over their lifetime. The efficacy inputs (migraine days) were based on a Cochrane systematic literature review. Quality-adjusted life years (QALYs) were the modeled health outcome. Direct and indirect medical costs were derived from a Canadian burden of illness study on patients with migraine. All costs were inflated and reported as the present value of lifetime costs in 2021 Canadian dollars (CAD), discounting at 1.5%.ResultsFrom a health system perspective, acupuncture was cost-effective when compared with no active treatment (CAD 35,060/QALY) and drug prophylaxis (CAD 47,128/QALY) at a willingness-to-pay threshold of CAD 50,000/QALY gained. Acupuncture was dominant compared with no active treatment and drug prophylaxis from a societal perspective. Cost savings were driven by reduced productivity loss from fewer migraine days with acupuncture treatment.ConclusionAcupuncture could be a cost-effective option for patients with episodic migraine. Future studies are encouraged to inform decisions regarding the use of acupuncture in the management of episodic migraine.

title: Enhancement of the endocannabinoid system through monoacylglycerol lipase inhibition relieves migraine-associated pain in mice.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Migraine affects over 1 billion people worldwide and is a leading cause of disability. Targeting the cannabinoid system offers a promising approach for pain and migraine relief. This study evaluated a novel monoacylglycerol lipase (MAGL) inhibitor to prolong endocannabinoid action in acute and chronic mouse models of migraine. It also examined MAGL and cannabinoid receptor 1 (CB1) mRNA expression in key head pain-processing regions. METHODS: C57BL6/J male and female mice received the human migraine trigger nitroglycerin (NTG) acutely or every other day for 9 days. Allodynia was assessed by von Frey hair stimulation of the periorbital area. A single dose of MAGL inhibitor (ABD-1970) was tested in acute and chronic NTG models. Additionally, ABD-1970 was given daily for 5 days to assess tolerance. In situ hybridization measured transcript expression of MAGL, CB1, and neuronal marker Rbfox3 in trigeminal ganglia (TG) and trigeminal nucleus caudalis (TNC). RESULTS: A single injection of ABD-1970 blocked cephalic allodynia induced by acute NTG. ABD-1970 also blocked chronic allodynia established by chronic intermittent NTG. Repeated administration did not induce tolerance, and ABD-1970 continued to block NTG-induced allodynia after 5 days of administration. There was high expression of MAGL and CB1 in the TG and TNC, present in Rbfox3 positive and negative cells. CONCLUSION: MAGL inhibitor effectively blocked acute and chronic migraine-associated pain, likely through prolonged endocannabinoid action. This effect may be mediated through action at peripheral or central sites considering the high MAGL and CB1 expression in the TG and TNC, respectively. The endocannabinoid system appears to modulate migraine mechanisms, and MAGL may be a promising target for this disorder.

sections.other:
Headache disorders ranked as the third leading cause of years lived with disability in 2019, with migraine accounting for 88.2% of this burden []. Migraine affects ~ 15% of the global population, impacting roughly 1 in 6 Americans [, ]. The most disabling form of migraine is chronic migraine, and ~ 3% of patients transition from episodic to chronic migraine yearly []. Chronic migraine is defined as ≥ 15 headache days/month lasting at least 3 months [, ], and affects 1–2% of the population. A systemic review from 2024 found that disability associated with migraine almost doubled between 2005 and 2018, even though prevalence remained stable []. There is an enormous unmet need for millions of migraine sufferers for whom currently available therapies are only partially effective or poorly tolerated [, ].

The endocannabinoid system has emerged as a promising therapeutic target for headache disorders []. This system includes two primary endogenous ligands, anandamide (AEA) and 2-arachidonoylglycerol (2-AG), which activate two main G-protein coupled receptors: cannabinoid receptor 1 (CB 1 ) and cannabinoid receptor 2 (CB 2 ) [–]. CB 1 receptors are primarily found on neurons within the central nervous system, while CB 2 receptors are predominantly located in the peripheral nervous system and on immune cells []. After their release, AEA is primarily degraded by fatty acid amide hydrolase (FAAH), and 2-AG by monoacylglycerol lipase (MAGL) [].

Interest in the cannabinoids and endocannabinoids as a potential treatment strategy for migraine is growing. Approximately 36% of patients with migraine and headache have reported using exogenous cannabinoids to alleviate symptoms [, ]. In one study, medical marijuana was associated with a significant reduction in migraine frequency []. Chronic migraine is often linked to medication overuse headache, with positive correlations between increased use of triptans or opioids and increased headache days []. Notably, cannabis use was associated with a reduction in opioid use, as well as reduced medication use for migraine treatment []. These findings align with the clinical endocannabinoid deficiency (CECD) hypothesis, which suggests that reduced endocannabinoid tone in migraine patients may contribute to their pain and symptomatology []. Studies have shown that levels of 2-AG and AEA are significantly lower in chronic migraine patients than in controls [, ]. Interestingly, a negative correlation was reported between levels of calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) or nitric oxide, two migraine triggers, and the level of AEA []. Furthermore, increased FAAH levels have been reported in the platelets of women with migraine without aura [], and MAGL mRNA expression was found to be elevated in both episodic and chronic migraine patients [].

Although exogenous cannabinoids may reduce migraine frequency, their effects are unpredictable and associated with adverse effects such as dizziness, dry mouth, nausea, cognitive impairment, psychosis, and abuse liability [, , ]. Given these limitations, cannabis’ Schedule I status, and that cannabinoids are still illegal in many places, alternative strategies are needed. For example, a recent study showed that a peripherally restricted CB1 agonist was effective in a mouse model of migraine with limited tolerance []. Alternatively, enhancing endocannabinoid levels by inhibiting their degradation represents a promising approach. Acute FAAH inhibition produced anti-allodynic effects in an acute nitroglycerin (NTG) migraine model [, ]. Interestingly, in rat trigeminal ganglia, MAGL activity was approximately nine-fold higher than FAAH activity, suggesting that MAGL inhibition could be particularly effective []. Reversible (URB602) and irreversible (JZL184) MAGL inhibitors tested in mice, blocked hyperalgesia induced by NTG, a known human migraine trigger []. Moreover, a dual FAAH/MAGL inhibitor was effective in an acute NTG migraine model as well as blocking meningeal signaling from application of KCl, in a model of migraine aura [–].

Previous studies of irreversible MAGL inhibitors have shown efficacy in pain models such as traumatic nerve injury and chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy []. However, centrally acting inhibitors led to unwanted side effects, including pharmacological tolerance through receptor desensitization, as well as physical dependence []. In migraine models, MAGL inhibitors have been tested in male animals and in acute migraine models, but not in female animals or in chronic states. Recently, a novel potent and selective MAGL inhibitor (ABD-1970, or Lu AG07779) was reported to produce analgesic effects without overt side effects []. Therefore, we aimed to investigate the therapeutic potential of MAGL inhibition using ABD-1970 in acute and chronic models of migraine in male and female mice.
