sections.abstract:
Adverse Childhood Experiences (ACEs) are significant early-life stressors with long-term health impacts. Migraine is a prevalent, debilitating neurological disorder in middle-aged/elderly populations, often accompanied by depression. However, evidence on ACEs’ influence on migraine risk in this demographic and the mediating role of depression is limited in Chinese populations. Using China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS) data, the research investigated the connection of cumulative ACEs exposure with migraine risk in middle-aged/elderly individuals and examined depressive symptoms as a mediator.

8,410 participants (≥ 45 years) from CHARLS (2011–2020) were analyzed. Standardized questionnaires assessed cumulative ACEs, migraine, and depressive symptoms. Multivariable COX regression analyzed the ACEs-migraine association. Bootstrap mediation analysis quantified depression’s mediating role. Mendelian randomization (MR) was used for validation.

After covariate adjustment, each additional ACE point increased migraine risk by 18% (HR = 1.18, 95% CI: 1.13–1.22, p < 0.001). Individuals with ≥ 4 ACEs had remarkably higher migraine risk compared to those with none (HR = 1.99, 95% CI: 1.64–2.41). Depressive symptoms significantly mediated 21.5% (95% CI: 16.3% − 29.0%, P < 0.01) of the connection of ACEs with migraine. ACEs increased migraine risk both directly and indirectly via heightened depressive symptoms. MR confirmed ACEs significantly increased migraine risk (IVW OR = 1.64, 95% CI: 1.20–2.22) and suggested depression mediated 20.1% (95% CI: 4.15% − 36.1%, P = 0.01) of the effect, supporting the primary findings. Genetic correlation between ACEs and migraine was significant (LDSC Rg = 0.23, P < 0.001).

This study confirms cumulative ACEs exposure is a significant risk factor for migraine in middle-aged/elderly Chinese individuals. Depressive symptoms take a substantial mediating role. Findings indicate ACEs have complex effects on later-life neurological health, with depression acting as a key psychological mechanism linking early adversity to migraine.

The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1186/s10194-026-02311-4.
sections.other:
About 1 billion individuals worldwide suffer from migraines, a widespread and incapacitating neurological condition with a 15% global prevalence []. Patients’ quality of life and productivity are severely hampered. At the population level, Global Burden of Disease (GBD) analyses consistently identify migraine as a leading cause of years lived with disability (YLDs), highlighting its substantial contribution to long-term functional impairment and societal burden [, ]. Beyond direct healthcare use, migraine is associated with considerable indirect costs, largely driven by reduced on-the-job performance (presenteeism) and absenteeism [–]. In China, where rapid population aging is underway, recent burden analyses likewise indicate that migraine remains an important contributor to disability, underscoring the relevance of studying migraine among middle-aged and older adults [, ]. Migraines are characterized by a chronic history and usually present as recurring episodes of headaches with accompanying symptoms such phonophobia, photophobia, nausea, and vomiting []. Finding and reducing its underlying risk factors is important for improving preventive as well as management tactics because of its high prevalence and related impairment.

Migraine has a complex etiology that includes aberrant pain processing pathways, central sensitization, neuroinflammatory reactions, and malfunction of the trigeminovascular system [, ]. Although environmental triggers, lifestyle choices, and genetic predisposition have long been identified as risk factors for migraines [, ], mounting data emphasizes the important role that psychological variables play in migraine development. Depression and adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) are two of them that have drawn more attention recently [, ]. Traumatic events that occurred before the age of 18 are referred to as ACEs. These events include physical, emotional, or sexual abuse, physical or emotional neglect, and dysfunctional families, including parental separation, marital violence, and drug misuse []. ACEs are connected to a higher chance of developing a number of illnesses as an adult, including mental health issues including sadness and anxiety [, ]. In particular, ACE exposure has been connected to an increased risk of depression in adulthood, according to a number of studies [, ]. Additional longitudinal and cross-sectional research has shown that migraine and depression are closely related in both directions [, ]. While migraine increases the likelihood of getting depression by 2.5 times [, ], depression itself increases the risk of migraine’s earlier start and worse prognosis []. Importantly, depression may also magnify migraine-related burden: psychiatric comorbidity has been identified as a risk factor for migraine chronification and is associated with greater disability and more complicated clinical management [, ]. In middle-aged and older populations, depressive symptoms are also linked to increased healthcare utilization, suggesting an additional pathway through which depression may exacerbate the real-world burden of migraine in aging societies [].

Although the underlying mechanisms linking ACEs, depression, and migraine are not yet fully elucidated, emerging evidence suggests one potential pathway is that ACEs trigger chronic psychological stress, which subsequently increases the likelihood of developing depression []. This may activate the trigeminovascular system or trigger neuroinflammatory cascades, increasing vulnerability to migraine [].

Despite accumulating evidence, important gaps remain. Prior research on ACEs–migraine links has often relied on cross-sectional designs or non-representative samples, and mediation pathways have not always been quantified with robust causal inference strategies. Therefore, it is essential to examine, within a nationally representative cohort of middle-aged and older Chinese adults, whether ACE exposure confers excess migraine risk and to what extent depressive symptoms mediate this association, while strengthening causal inference using complementary analytic strategies.

The China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS), a nationally representative cohort of Chinese adults aged 45 years and older, provides an ideal platform to address these gaps []. Notably, migraine has been operationalized in CHARLS using items corresponding to the ID-Migraine screening framework in prior studies, supporting its feasibility for large-scale epidemiologic analyses in this cohort [–]. This study innovatively integrates observational analysis with Mendelian Randomization (MR) methods to systematically explore three core scientific questions: First, does cumulative exposure to ACEs remarkably increase the risk of migraine in the Chinese middle-aged as well as elderly population? Second, do depressive symptoms mediate the ACEs-migraine pathway? Third, is this association robust to causal explanations? The findings will provide localized empirical evidence on the long-term neuropsychiatric harms of ACEs, revealing the key mediating pathway of depressive symptoms. This research will offer precise targets for optimizing child protection policies and early depression screening and intervention in high-risk elderly populations, thereby contributing to the implementation of the “healthy aging” national strategy.
sections.methods:
The research is based on data from the CHARLS from the 2011 and 2020 surveys, as well as the 2014 life history survey []. The study population consists of middle-aged and elderly individuals aged 45 as well as older, with a final sample size of 8,410 participants. Exclusion criteria include missing key variables (ACEs, migraine, depressive symptoms) and age < 45 years. The specific process is displayed in Fig. .

ACEs were assessed via a standardized retrospective questionnaire. Physical and emotional abuse, neglect (physical and emotional), as well as family dysfunction (parental divorce or separation, family member incarceration, witnessing domestic violence, substance abuse, or mental health issues within the family) are some of the aspects of early adversity that are covered in the questionnaire (Supplementary Table ). The cumulative ACEs score was calculated based on the number of ACEs reported by the respondent (ranging from 0 to 12 points). Additionally, ACEs were grouped according to clinical standards: 0 (no ACEs), 1–3 (low to moderate exposure), and ≥ 4 (high exposure).

CHARLS does not collect sufficient information to apply full ICHD-3 diagnostic criteria. Therefore, consistent with prior CHARLS-based studies [, ], we operationalized a “probable migraine” phenotype using two concurrent self-reported symptoms assessed at each survey wave: headache and stomach pain. Participants answering “Yes” to both “Do you currently have a headache?” and “Do you currently have stomach pain?” were classified as having migraine-like symptoms. Incident migraine was defined as the first follow-up wave meeting this definition among baseline migraine-free participants.

The Center for Epidemiologic Studies Depression Scale (CES-D) was leveraged to measure depressive symptoms [, ]. A popular tool for assessing the frequency as well as intensity of depression symptoms across a recent time span is the CES-D, which consists of many questions. More severe depressed symptoms are indicated by higher scores.

Based on literature, the following variables were adjusted for.

Demographic variables: age (continuous), gender (male/female), education level (illiterate/primary school/junior high school or above), marital status (married/partnered/separated, widowed/divorced/never married), residential area (urban/rural);

Health behaviors: current smoking (Former/Never/Now), alcohol consumption (yes/no), sleep duration, BMI;

Chronic disease comorbidities: hypertension, diabetes, dyslipidemia, CVD, stroke (based on self-reported physician diagnoses). Missing covariate data were imputed via multiple imputation by chained equations combined with a random forest algorithm. Details of missingness are displayed in Supplementary Table .

Multivariate COX Regression Analysis The relationship between ACEs cumulative score (as a continuous and categorical variable) and probable migraine risk (as a binary: yes/no) was examined using models. The findings were presented as HR with 95% CI, along with the p-value for statistical significance. The following variables were taken into account in the models:

Unadjusted model (only ACEs);

Adjusted for demographic covariates (age, gender, education, marital status, residential area);

Adjusted for all covariates (age, gender, education, marital status, residential area, smoking, alcohol consumption, sleep, chronic diseases, etc.).

Depressive symptoms (continuous CES-D score) were evaluated as a potential mediator of the ACEs–probable migraine association. To support temporal ordering, we used baseline depressive symptoms and modeled incident probable migraine during follow-up among participants without probable migraine at baseline. Bootstrap mediation (5,000 resamples) was used to estimate the total, direct, and indirect (ACEs → depression → migraine) effects on the log-hazard scale and the mediated proportion with 95% confidence intervals, adjusting for all covariates. Given the known bidirectional relationship between migraine and depression, we additionally assessed directionality in the genetic analyses using the MR Steiger test.

The causal link between ACEs and migraine was investigated using MR. Three fundamental presumptions underpin MR analysis [, ]: Pertinence It is assumed that there must be a high correlation between the exposure (ACEs) and the instrumental variables (IVs) employed in the investigation. The independence assumption states that there must be no known or unknown confounders affecting the IVs. The exclusion restriction assumption states that the IVs must only affect the result (migraine) by exposing the patient to ACEs; no other direct causal pathways may be involved. (Fig. A). This investigation was conducted in accordance with the most recent guidelines (STROBE-MR) (Supplementary Table ) [].

Publicly accessible resources were used to get the genetic instrumental variables (IVs) for migraine and ACEs. A study by Warrier et al. that comprised a GWAS meta-analysis of child maltreatment in 185,414 people provided the data on ACEs []. In order to prevent sample overlap, depression data were taken from the PGC consortium’s cross-ancestry GWAS, which used European ancestry data and excluded cases from the UK Biobank []. The FinnGen database (Release 12) provided the migraine data, which included 26,894 cases and 374,605 controls []. To prevent the impact of population stratification, all of the summary data were derived from studies that solely included people of European genetic ancestry.

Genetic instruments for ACEs were selected from large-scale GWAS of European ancestry, applying the following sequential criteria: first, single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) significantly related with ACEs at genome-wide significance ( P < 5 × 10 − 8 ) were identified; second, these SNPs underwent linkage disequilibrium (LD) clumping (r² < 0.001 within 10,000 kb windows) to make sure independence; finally, instrument strength was verified through F-statistics > 10 [].

Causal estimates were primarily computed using inverse-variance weighted (IVW) [], with extensive sensitivity analyses to address pleiotropy and model assumptions: weighted median for robustness to invalid instruments []; MR-Egger with intercept testing for directional pleiotropy []; contamination mixture method to downweight heterogeneous SNPs []; robust adjusted profile score (RAPS) for overdispersion correction []; debiased IVW to mitigate weak instrument bias []; constrained maximum likelihood for balanced pleiotropy assumptions []; and Bayesian weighted MR incorporating prior distributions []. Outlier detection and correction were performed using MR-PRESSO []. Horizontal pleiotropy was formally tested via MR-Egger intercept ( P > 0.05 considered acceptable), with heterogeneity quantified via Cochran’s Q statistic. The Steiger directionality test was also conducted to evaluate the potential impact of reverse causation [].

For mediation analysis, a two-step MR approach was implemented (Fig. B): step one estimated the ACEs-depression effect (β A ), step two quantified the depression-migraine effect (β B ). The mediated proportion was calculated as (β A × β B ) / β total × 100%, with 95% confidence intervals derived from 10,000 bootstrap iterations. Genetic correlation of ACEs with migraine was assessed via LD score regression (LDSC), reporting the rg coefficient and standard error []. All analyses used TwoSampleMR and MRPRESSO packages in R 4.4.3.

sections.results:
8,410 participants were included in the research. The average age of the participants was 58.13 (± 8.40) years, with 46.65% being male. Among the participants, 1,806 (21.67%) reported no ACEs, 5,710 (67.90%) had low to moderate ACEs exposure, and 894 (10.63%) had high ACEs exposure (Table ). After a median follow-up of 108 months, a total of 1,364 participants developed probable migraine outcomes, including 221 cases in no ACEs, 936 cases in moderate ACEs, and 207 cases in high ACEs.

When analyzed as a continuous variable, ACEs scores were significantly positively correlated with migraine in unadjusted, partially adjusted, and fully adjusted models. The hazard ratios (HRs) (95% CI) were 1.19 (1.15–1.23), 1.20 (1.12–1.24), and 1.18 (1.13–1.22), respectively (Table ). When analyzed as a categorical variable, similar trends were observed. In particular, the incidence of migraine was considerably greater for those with ≥ 4 ACEs than for those without ACE exposure (HR = 1.99, 95% CI: 1.64–2.41) in the fully adjusted model, and it was also higher for those with moderate ACE exposure (HR = 1.36, 95% CI: 1.18–1.58). The Kaplan–Meier survival curves demonstrated a remarkable difference in cumulative migraine incidence across the ACEs groups (log-rank test, P < 0.001) (Fig. ).

Depressive symptoms substantially mediated the link of ACEs with migraine, accounting for 21.5% of the association ( p < 0.001), according to mediation analysis. (Fig. ).

In subgroup analyses, the positive association between ACEs and migraine remained consistent across all strata (Fig. ). The hazard ratios ranged from 1.15 to 1.25, and no significant interactions were observed for age, gender, education, marital status, residence, drinking, smoking, or BMI (all P for interaction > 0.05). These findings suggest that the relationship between ACEs and migraine is robust and independent of sociodemographic or lifestyle factors.

After strict variable selection, we identified 9 genetic instrumental variables (IVs) related to ACEs (rs12031035, rs1859100, rs35560901, rs3851357, rs3896224, rs4702, rs4895718, rs611531, rs77987546). We found that ACEs were significantly related with migraine risk (Fig. ): IVW OR = 1.64 [95% CI: 1.20–2.22], P < 0.01. Similar results were observed using other methods. Sensitivity analysis indicated no pleiotropy or heterogeneity ( P > 0.05) (Supplementary Table ). The MR Steiger test showed no evidence of reverse causality ( P < 0.01).

LDSC revealed a remarkable genetic correlation of ACEs with migraine: Rg = 0.23, SE = 0.04, P < 0.001.

Mediation analysis was conducted using two-step MR. In the first step, we demonstrated a remarkable connection of ACEs with depression (OR = 1.23, 95% CI = 1.06–1.43, P < 0.01) (Fig. ). MR-Egger regression and Cochrane Q tests showed no pleiotropy or heterogeneity. In the second step, we confirmed the causal relationship of depression with migraine (OR = 1.59, 95% CI = 1.44–1.75, P < 0.01). MR-Egger regression indicated no pleiotropy ( P > 0.05), but heterogeneity was observed ( P < 0.05). The MR Steiger test also found no evidence of reverse causality ( P < 0.05). Finally, by the product of coefficients method, we calculated the indirect effect and then computed the mediation ratio via dividing the indirect effect by the total effect. Our findings suggest that ACEs influence migraine through depression, mediating 20.1% of the effect (Fig. ).
sections.discussion:
Using a nationally representative cohort of Chinese middle-aged and older adults, this study provides novel evidence that cumulative exposure to ACEs is associated with a higher risk of migraine in later life, supported by both observational analyses and MR. In the cohort analyses, each 1-point increase in the cumulative ACE score was associated with an increased risk of migraine (HR = 1.18, 95% CI: 1.13–1.22), and participants reporting ≥ 4 ACEs had an approximately two-fold higher risk of migraine (HR = 1.99). Mediation analyses suggested that depressive symptoms accounted for 21.5% of the ACEs–migraine association (95% CI: 16.3%–29.0%). Consistent with these findings, MR analyses provided convergent evidence suggesting a comparable mediated proportion (20.1%, 95% CI: 4.15%–36.1%) and indicated a shared genetic architecture between ACEs and migraine (Rg = 0.23, P < 0.001).

Our results indicate that ACE exposure is associated with both depression and migraine. These findings are consistent with prior studies linking ACEs to migraine. For example, evidence from Canadian cohorts suggests that the number and type of ACEs are associated with migraine in adulthood [], and ACE exposure may increase migraine risk in adolescence []. A meta-analysis of 12 studies also reported that ACEs increase migraine risk, highlighting the potential value of interventions aimed at reducing childhood abuse and related adverse behaviors []. In addition, prior research suggests that ACEs may contribute not only to migraine onset but also to migraine chronification []. Leveraging a nationally representative Chinese cohort, our study reinforces and extends current knowledge by confirming the role of ACEs as significant contributors to migraine development in later adulthood. We also observed exposure to ACEs was related with an increased risk of depression, showing a dose-response relationship wherein more severe ACEs correlated with progressively higher risks. These findings align with previously published studies [, ]. A systematic review offered significant evidence suggesting that ACEs, irrespective of their type or number, could contribute to an increased risk of developing depression []. Regardless of sociodemographic traits, Zhang et al. found ACEs increased the likelihood of later depression in Chinese people []. Another research provided more evidence for this, showing exposure to various ACE subtypes, especially sexual and physical abuse, intensifies the severity of depressive symptoms [].

This study further offers insight into potential mechanisms by suggesting that depressive symptoms partially mediate the association between ACEs and migraine. The bidirectional relationship between migraine and depression has been well documented [, , , ]. According to Duan et al., depression was found to be independently and substantially related with both an increased risk of migraine and a larger burden related with migraine []. Furthermore, compared to healthy populations, a number of studies have found that people with migraines had a greater rate of depression []. The effects of moderate and severe ACEs on migraine risk were shown to be partially explained by depression, according to mediation analysis. In particular, higher levels of ACE exposure were associated with higher levels of depressed symptoms, which in turn led to a higher chance of migraine (mediated 21.5%). MR showed that ACEs have a substantial causal impact on migraine risk. Our findings are further supported by the fact that depression mediated 20.1% of this impact. The function of depression as a mediator in the development of different illnesses has been well investigated in earlier research. In the Chinese population, researchers found a strong correlation between cardiovascular illnesses and chronic pain, with depressive symptoms acting as a mediating factor []. According to a different research, chronic pain directly affects cognitive performance and also acts as a mediation factor by indirectly exacerbating cognitive deficiencies through depressed symptoms []. According to Natalia et al., attachment takes a mediating role in the connection of migraine with childhood trauma []. Depression continued to be a major mediator of the relationship between ACEs and migraine in our investigation, even after controlling for age, sex, education, marital status, housing, smoking, alcohol use, as well as chronic conditions. Moreover, these results were corroborated by MR analysis. Consequently, one important mechanism connecting ACEs to migraine risk may be depression. Taken together, these findings support depression as an important pathway linking early-life adversity to migraine risk, even after adjusting for sociodemographic factors and health-related covariates. From a public health perspective, these results underscore the importance of preventing ACEs and strengthening early identification and management of depressive symptoms, which may help reduce migraine risk and related disability among middle-aged and older adults.

Several limitations should be considered. First, migraine in CHARLS was operationalized using two self-reported symptom items (headache and stomach pain) rather than full ICHD-3 diagnostic criteria. This proxy definition may lead to outcome misclassification. If such misclassification is largely non-differential with respect to ACEs, the observed associations would likely be biased toward the null; however, differential reporting cannot be fully excluded. Second, ACEs were assessed retrospectively in later life, so recall bias and mood-congruent reporting are possible, particularly for emotional maltreatment. The use of a structured life history questionnaire and a cumulative ACEs score may reduce random error, and the convergent MR findings provide complementary evidence not subject to recall bias. Third, although we measured depressive symptoms at baseline and focused on incident migraine to improve temporal ordering, depression and migraine have a bidirectional relationship; therefore, reverse causality cannot be completely ruled out and mediation estimates should be interpreted as suggestive rather than definitive. Finally, our two-sample MR analyses relied mainly on European-ancestry GWAS (child maltreatment, depression, and migraine), which may limit the generalizability of causal estimates to Chinese populations due to differences in allele frequencies, linkage disequilibrium patterns, and gene-environment context. Future studies using large East Asian GWAS and prospective life-course cohorts with clinical migraine phenotyping are warranted.

In summary, using a nationally representative sample and complementary MR analyses, this study provides evidence that ACE exposure is associated with increased risks of migraine and depressive symptoms in middle-aged and older adults, with depression partially mediating the ACEs–migraine pathway. These findings suggest that prevention and intervention efforts targeting ACEs and depressive symptoms may reduce migraine risk and improve mental and neurological health in later life. Future research should examine the roles of specific ACE subtypes and migraine phenotypes and explore potential effect modification across sociocultural settings.

title: Vestibular Migraine: A Systematic Literature Search and Narrative Review of Diagnostic Criteria, Pathophysiology, Differential Diagnosis, and Treatment Approaches.
abstract: This review aimed to summarize current evidence on the diagnostic criteria, pathophysiological mechanisms, differential diagnosis, and treatment approaches of vestibular migraine. A systematic literature search was conducted in PubMed/MEDLINE, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library for studies published between May 2021 and May 2026. The search focused on vestibular migraine, migrainous vertigo, migraine-associated vertigo, diagnostic criteria, pathophysiology, treatment, prophylaxis, rehabilitation, and calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP)-related therapies. Study selection followed a PRISMA-informed process, and findings were synthesized narratively because of heterogeneity in study design, populations, interventions, and outcome measures. A total of 663 records were identified, and 72 studies were included in the final synthesis. Current evidence supports vestibular migraine as a complex disorder involving trigeminovascular activation, CGRP signaling, central sensitization, vestibulo-thalamo-cortical networks, and cerebellar compensation. Diagnosis remains primarily clinical and requires careful assessment of attack duration, vestibular symptom type, migraine-associated features, and exclusion of alternative vestibular or vascular disorders. Treatment evidence remains limited and heterogeneous. Lifestyle modification, conventional migraine prophylaxis, vestibular rehabilitation, and CGRP-targeted therapies may be useful in selected patients, but robust vestibular migraine-specific randomized trials are still insufficient. Vestibular migraine should be approached as a multisystem neurovestibular disorder rather than a simple coexistence of migraine and vertigo. Individualized, phenotype-based management and stronger controlled studies are needed to improve diagnostic accuracy and therapeutic decision-making.

sections.other:
The observation that vestibular symptoms, particularly vertigo and head-motion-induced dizziness with nausea, may accompany migraine attacks dates back several decades. The relationship between migraine and vestibular symptoms has historically been described using various terms, such as “migraine-associated vertigo,” “migraine-related vertigo,” “migraine-related dizziness,” “migraine-related vestibulopathy,” and “benign recurrent vertigo.” This terminological confusion became more standardized with the joint diagnostic approach developed in the 2010s by the International Headache Society (IHS) and the Bárány Society , .

Vestibular migraine (VM) is recognized as one of the most important causes of recurrent episodic vestibular symptoms. Its clinical significance stems not only from its prevalence; diagnostic delay, loss of quality of life, functional limitations, anxiety, and its association with chronic dizziness syndromes transform VM into a critical intersection area for neurology, otolaryngology, emergency medicine, and primary care practice , , , . Nevertheless, VM remains underdiagnosed relative to its actual prevalence, and patients are often managed under alternative diagnoses such as benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV), Ménière’s disease, non-specific dizziness, or anxiety disorders.

This review combines a systematic literature search with narrative synthesis to provide a clinically oriented overview of the current evidence on VM. The primary objective is to comprehensively present the epidemiology, diagnostic criteria, pathophysiology, differential diagnosis, and treatment approaches of VM while transparently distinguishing higher-certainty clinical evidence from observational, case-level, and mechanistic evidence.

This narrative review seeks to answer three main research questions:

1) What are the current criteria used for diagnosing VM, and how should their clinical value be interpreted in differential diagnosis?

2) What are the proposed pathophysiological mechanisms for VM?

3) What are the efficacy and safety profiles of acute treatment, prophylactic treatment, vestibular rehabilitation, and new treatment approaches for VM?
sections.methods:
This review was conducted using a systematic literature search and PRISMA-informed study selection process , followed by narrative synthesis. A meta-analysis was not performed because of substantial heterogeneity in study design, diagnostic criteria, populations, interventions, follow-up periods, and outcome measures. Therefore, the results are presented as a narrative synthesis, with explicit attention to the level and certainty of evidence.

The literature search was conducted in PubMed/MEDLINE, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library. The primary disease block consisted of the terms “vestibular migraine,” “migrainous vertigo,” and “migraine-associated vertigo.” The secondary topic block included diagnosis, diagnostic criteria, pathophysiology, treatment, therapy, management, prophylaxis, rehabilitation, calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP), and “calcitonin gene-related peptide.” Searches were adapted to the syntax and field-tag requirements of each database. The literature was searched from May 2021 to May 2026. The database selection was designed to capture the major peer-reviewed biomedical, multidisciplinary, and evidence-synthesis literature relevant to VM. A comprehensive search strategy was employed, incorporating PubMed/MEDLINE to identify biomedical and clinical studies, Web of Science to expand multidisciplinary citation coverage, and the Cochrane Library to capture randomized trials and systematic reviews. In addition, we performed a supplementary targeted search of ClinicalTrials.gov and World Health Organization International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (WHO ICTRP) on 27/06/2026 using the terms “vestibular migraine”, “migrainous vertigo”, “migraine-associated vertigo”. The findings were used to contextualize ongoing or unpublished therapeutic research, but they were not included in the main evidence synthesis because this review was designed as a narrative synthesis. The findings are presented in . We do not have institutional access to Embase. Consequently, this review may therefore overlook unpublished studies, ongoing trials, conference-only reports, negative studies, and regulatory/registry-based evidence. This limitation is of particular pertinence for emerging therapeutic areas, including CGRP-targeted therapies, gepants/ditans, neuromodulation, and other investigational interventions.

An example PubMed query was structured as follows: [“vestibular migraine” (Title/Abstract) OR “migrainous vertigo” (Title/Abstract) OR “migraine-associated vertigo” (Title/Abstract)] AND (diagnosis OR pathophysiology OR treatment OR therapy OR management OR prophylaxis OR rehabilitation OR CGRP OR “calcitonin gene-related peptide”). Field tags and filters were adapted to the syntactic features of the databases.

The relatively modest number of PubMed/MEDLINE records (n=32) reflects the intentionally restrictive title/abstract-based disease block, the recent search window (May 2021 to May 2026), and the prioritization of VM-specific, clinically interpretable records rather than broadly indexed, non-specific dizziness or vertigo records. Broader multidisciplinary coverage was provided by Web of Science, while Cochrane sources were searched to identify randomized trials and evidence syntheses.

Study selection was conducted based on the PRISMA 2020 flowchart. A total of 663 records were identified based on recent database exports. Of these records, 531 were from Web of Science, 88 were from Cochrane CENTRAL/Cochrane Library study records, 32 were from PubMed/MEDLINE, and 12 were from Cochrane Reviews exports.

Duplicate checks were performed based on matching DOI, PMID, study registration numbers, titles, and author information. As a result of this process, 47 duplicate records were removed. After removing duplicates, 616 unique records underwent title and abstract screening. Following title and abstract screening, 516 records were excluded, and 100 reports were selected for full-text evaluation. After full-text evaluation, 72 studies were included in the final synthesis. The PRISMA 2020 flow diagram is summarized in .

No prospective protocol registration was performed for this review. This limits transparency regarding prespecified methods and is acknowledged as a methodological limitation.

Inclusion criteria: human studies; clinical data related to VM or suspected VM; studies using the International Classification of Headache Disorders (ICHD)-3, Bárány Society, or similar diagnostic frameworks; studies contributing to the pathophysiology, differential diagnosis, vestibular testing, or treatment outcomes of VM; randomized controlled trials, systematic reviews, meta-analyses, observational studies, diagnostic criteria/consensus documents, and clinically informative case series.

Exclusion criteria: animal or in vitro studies; general studies of non-specific dizziness, lightheadedness, or vertigo lacking VM-specific analysis; studies published solely as conference abstracts; records with unverifiable full bibliographic information; publications that do not provide clinically interpretable data regarding treatment or diagnosis.

Records were evaluated in two stages: title/abstract screening followed by full-text review according to predefined eligibility criteria. Duplicate records of the same study across databases were merged using DOI, PMID, study registration number, title, and author information. All processes were performed independently by two reviewers. Both reviewers had field-relevant clinical backgrounds and research experience in neurology, migraine, and neurovestibular disorders. Screening and data extraction were performed independently before consensus discussion. Disagreements during eligibility assessment were resolved by consensus. For each included study, the following information was extracted:

- Author/year or study group,

- Design/focus,

- Population,

- Main contribution to this review,

- Key limitation/evidence note.

RoB 2, ROBINS-I, and AMSTAR-2 domains were used as methodological reference frameworks when interpreting randomized trials, non-randomized studies, and systematic reviews/meta-analyses, respectively; however, a formal, study-level risk-of-bias assessment with domain-by-domain judgments was not performed. Therefore, should be interpreted as a methodological interpretive table rather than as a formal risk-of-bias assessment table.

To improve transparency in interpretation, treatment evidence was summarized using a GRADE-informed certainty framework. Because this was a narrative synthesis rather than a formal guideline or meta-analysis, formal outcome-level GRADE ratings were not assigned. Instead, the certainty of evidence was categorized narratively as follows: randomized controlled trials and high-quality systematic reviews were considered higher-certainty evidence; consistent prospective or comparative observational studies were considered moderate- to low-certainty evidence, depending on design limitations; retrospective series and uncontrolled cohorts were considered low-certainty evidence; and case reports, small case series, and preclinical studies were considered hypothesis-generating evidence. Treatment conclusions were then phrased according to this hierarchy. The selected characteristics of key studies are presented in .

Accordingly, the term “GRADE-informed” is used only to indicate that interpretation was guided by GRADE principles such as study design, consistency, directness, precision, and certainty; it should not be read as a formal GRADE assessment, a rating table, or a guideline-level recommendation.

VM is one of the most prominent clinical phenotypes reflecting the relationship between migraine and the vestibular system. Although different studies have reported varying prevalence rates in the general population, VM is recognized as one of the primary causes of recurrent episodic vertigo , , , , .

Its higher prevalence in women suggests a possible contribution of hormonal factors. VM can occur from childhood through old age; however, it is more pronounced in adult women and individuals with a history of migraine.

Although broad complaints, such as dizziness or lightheadedness, may be reported more frequently by patients with migraine than in the general population, these non-specific symptoms do not, by themselves, establish VM. Diagnosis should instead focus on qualifying vestibular symptoms, including spontaneous vertigo, positional vertigo, visually induced vertigo, head-motion-induced vertigo, or head-motion-induced dizziness with nausea , , , , .

However, this association does not always imply VM; diagnosis should therefore be based on the duration of episodes, the type of vestibular symptoms, the migraine-associated symptoms, and the exclusion of alternative vestibular disorders.

The clinical burden is not limited to attack frequency. Recurrent vestibular symptoms, fear of falling, avoidance of movement, visual motion sensitivity, anxiety, depressive symptoms, and sleep disturbances can significantly reduce functional capacity. There may be a bidirectional relationship between VM and persistent postural-perceptual dizziness (PPPD); recurrent vestibular attacks may trigger a cycle of chronic dizziness, avoidance, and hypervigilance.

Both the prevalence of VM and the associated demographic patterns vary by study design; however, population surveys and systematic reviews agree that the prevalence is a low single-digit percentage and that there is a marked predominance among women. Clinically-based series report much higher rates due to referral bias. Prevalence rates from various studies are summarized in , , , , .

Basic demographic characteristics:

- Gender: VM predominantly affects women; tertiary care clinic data report a female-to-male ratio of ~3.3:1, and women constitute the majority in most trial and cohort samples , , .

- Age groups: VM is most commonly diagnosed in young and middle-aged adults; some clinical series show higher rates in younger patients with prevalence decreasing with age, though reports vary and secondary peaks have been identified in older adults; this reflects heterogeneity between the general population, clinical samples, and diagnostic criteria , , .

- Ethnic origin and familial patterns: systematic review data indicate prevalence differences by ethnic origin (reported pooled estimates: Black ~3.13%, White ~2.64%, Asian ~1.07%) and evidence of familial clustering (recurrence rates in siblings indicating increased familial risk), suggesting the presence of both genetic and environmental influences .

- Limitations and heterogeneity: reported prevalence varies significantly depending on the study setting (differences between population-based studies and specialty clinics) and the diagnostic criteria used, which contributes to inconsistent associations with age and sex in some series; these methodological differences account for a large portion of the inconsistencies observed across studies , , .

VM attacks are characterized by recurrent vestibular symptoms, including spontaneous vertigo, positional vertigo, visually induced vertigo, head-motion-induced vertigo or dizziness with nausea. These symptoms may occur with or without a headache and be accompanied by photophobia, phonophobia, visual aura, nausea, vomiting, or motion sensitivity. The clinical phenotype is heterogeneous and may include positional vestibular symptoms, visual motion sensitivity, and auditory hypersensitivity, reflecting multisensory involvement in the syndrome.

In this review, terminology follows the Bárány Society/IHS framework. The umbrella term “vestibular symptoms” is used to refer collectively to the qualifying symptoms of VM. “Vertigo” refers to a false sensation of self-motion or environmental motion, and includes spontaneous, positional, visually- induced, or head-motion-induced vertigo. “Dizziness” is used, as specified in the diagnostic criteria, only when referring to non-vertiginous spatial disorientation—particularly head-motion-induced dizziness with nausea—or when reporting study-specific outcome measures. “Lightheadedness” is not used as a defining VM symptom and is reserved for non-specific or non-vestibular complaints.

• Spontaneous or positional vertigo and head-motion-induced dizziness with nausea are typical qualifying vestibular symptoms and may occur alongside migraine-type headache, photophobia, phonophobia, and nausea , .

• Patients with sensory hypersensitivity typically report motion intolerance and auditory hypersensitivity, such as phonophobia or tinnitus , .

Phenotypic variability in symptoms may be categorized into motion-sensitive, positional vertigo-dominant, auditory-dominant, or mixed types, corresponding to variable involvement of the vestibular, visual, and auditory pathways . In VM, vestibular symptoms may present as spontaneous vertigo, positional vertigo, visually induced vertigo, head-motion-induced vertigo, head-motion-induced dizziness with nausea, or internal/external vertigo. Various types of vertigo may be observed during separate attacks in the same patient. The duration of symptoms typically ranges from minutes to hours; in some patients, symptoms may last for several days. In terms of diagnostic criteria, vestibular symptoms are expected to be moderate or severe in intensity and to last between 5 minutes and 72 hours , .

In some patients, the classic migraine phenotype predominates during the early years of the disease; over time, vestibular symptoms may be added to the clinical picture. In some patients, however, as headache symptoms diminish, vestibular symptoms come to the forefront. Vertigo may occur before, during, or after a headache; it may also arise independently of a headache. In such cases, migraine-associated features such as photophobia, phonophobia, visual aura, nausea, vomiting, osmophobia, and motion sensitivity become important for diagnosis. Tinnitus and a sensation of fullness in the ear may accompany VM attacks; however, persistent, progressive, and marked unilateral hearing loss requires reevaluation for Ménière’s disease or other inner ear pathologies. summarizes the key criteria to be used in the diagnosis of VM and probable VM , , , .

No specific biomarker or standalone diagnostic vestibular test exists for VM. Diagnosis is clinical and relies on a well-structured history, neurological/otological examination, detailed assessment of attack phenomenology, and exclusion of differential diagnoses. Neurological and otological examinations may be normal during the interictal period. The following points should be systematically addressed during the diagnostic interview: duration and frequency of attacks; the type of qualifying vestibular symptom, including spontaneous vertigo, positional vertigo, visually induced vertigo, head-motion-induced vertigo, or head-motion-induced dizziness with nausea; timing and characteristics of headaches; photophobia/phonophobia/aura; nausea/vomiting; the laterality and persistence of hearing symptoms; history of migraine; family history; triggers; anxiety/avoidance behavior; medication use; and vascular risk factors. Vestibular tests should be used primarily for differential diagnosis and phenotyping rather than for establishing a definitive diagnosis. Abnormalities may be detected in tests such as caloric testing, video head impulse test (vHIT), vestibular evoked myogenic potentials (VEMP), and posturography; however, these findings are not specific to VM. Vestibular and audiological assessments should therefore be interpreted as supportive and differential diagnostic tools rather than VM-specific biomarkers. VEMP testing may provide additional supportive information in selected patients, particularly when an overlapping vestibular disorder is suspected; however, abnormal findings are not specific to VM and should be interpreted within the broader clinical context. Pure-tone audiometry is particularly important when Ménière’s disease is considered, because fluctuating or progressive unilateral sensorineural hearing loss should prompt reconsideration of the diagnosis. Vestibular testing and audiological evaluation are most useful when the clinical phenotype is atypical, auditory symptoms are prominent, or possible vascular/neurological contributors are suspected. Significant peripheral vestibular dysfunction on vHIT or caloric testing should be interpreted with caution, particularly regarding Ménière’s disease or concomitant peripheral vestibulopathy , , , .

BPPV is one of the conditions most commonly confused with VM. In BPPV, short-lived typical positional vertigo triggered by head movements and positive Dix-Hallpike or roll tests are expected. While positional symptoms may be present in VM, attack duration may be more variable, migraine-like symptoms may occur, and positional tests may not show the typical BPPV pattern. Ménière’s disease can be particularly difficult to distinguish from VM in the early stages. Tinnitus and a sensation of fullness in the ear may be present in both conditions. In Ménière’s disease, fluctuating, mostly unilateral hearing loss and audiological progression are characteristic features. In VM, hearing complaints are generally bilateral or non-specific; persistent, progressive unilateral hearing loss should prompt reconsideration of the VM diagnosis. PPPD may occur after VM or concurrently with VM. In PPPD, chronic dizziness and persistent symptoms that worsen with standing, movement, and complex visual stimuli predominate. Identifying the episodic attack pattern in VM is important; however, the two conditions are not mutually exclusive. Transient ischemic attacks and strokes involving the posterior circulation should be ruled out, particularly in patients with advanced age, vascular risk factors, new-onset neurological findings, diplopia, dysarthria, ataxia, hemiparesis, new, severe headache, or persistent neurological deficits. In these cases, rather than proceeding with symptomatic treatment based on a provisional diagnosis of VM, an urgent neurological evaluation is required , , , . The differential diagnosis of VM is summarized in .

The pathophysiology of VM has not been fully elucidated; current evidence suggests that a multilevel model—where migraine biology intersects with vestibular networks—is more likely than a single mechanism. This model includes the trigeminovascular system, brainstem nuclei, vestibular nuclei, thalamus, temporo-parieto-insular vestibular cortex, cerebellum, and visual-vestibular sensory integration networks , , , , .

CGRP, expressed in trigeminal ganglion neurons, has been linked to the pathophysiology of migraine, and agents targeting this peptide or its receptors have been developed as treatments for migraine. CGRP receptors expressed in the peripheral and central vestibular systems may also be involved in the pathophysiology of VM , . During a migraine attack, trigeminovascular activation and CGRP release may affect not only pain pathways but also structures anatomically and functionally linked to the vestibular system. Trigeminal innervation and CGRP expression in inner ear structures are interpreted as a biological bridge between migraine biology and otologic/vestibular symptoms , , . The ability of CGRP-targeted therapies to improve VM symptoms indirectly supports the clinical significance of these pathways , , .

Functional imaging studies suggest altered metabolic and activation patterns among the temporo-parieto-insular regions, the thalamus, and the visual cortex during a VM attack. The disruption of reciprocal inhibition between the visual and vestibular systems may explain visual motion sensitivity and vertigo-like visual symptoms. Gray matter changes reported in structural imaging studies have been associated with recurrent sensory overstimulation and adaptive/plastic changes , .

Central sensitization is an increasingly important mechanism in VM. Phenotypes associated with widespread cutaneous allodynia, sleep disturbances, tinnitus, depressive symptoms, and high disability can be interpreted as clinical manifestations of increased sensitivity in thalamocortical sensory processing . Therefore, in some patients, VM may not be limited to episodic vestibular symptoms but may manifest as a multisensory hypersensitivity syndrome.

The role of cerebellar and vestibulo-cerebellar networks is also significant. Studies showing changes in cerebellar functional activity following vestibular rehabilitation support the possibility of treatment-induced compensation and neuroplasticity . On the other hand, the presence of peripheral vestibular abnormalities in vHIT or caloric tests in some patients indicates that VM should not be interpreted as a purely central disorder in all patients .

Evidence suggests that attacks are primarily caused by abnormal central processing and integration of vestibular, visual, and nociceptive inputs, rather than by entirely peripheral labyrinthine insufficiency. Studies have identified impairments in canal-otolith integration, alterations in vestibulo-ocular responses, and dysfunction in the vestibulo-thalamocortical and cerebellar networks that process multisensory vestibular signals.

• Patients with abnormal integration exhibit reduced motion detection thresholds and delayed formation of tilt perceptions during combined canal-otolith stimulation; this likely implies central synthesis defects of cerebellar origin .

• Vestibulo-thalamocortical dysfunction: functional imaging and physiological data support a modulation disorder in multimodal cortical networks that normally balance vestibular with visual/auditory cues, a condition that causes motion intolerance and vertigo , .

• The brainstem and cerebellar nuclei, vestibular nuclei, and vestibulocerebellum have repeatedly been identified as sites where vestibular and nociceptive (trigeminal) signals interact; this interaction may trigger vestibular symptoms in migraine episodes , .

Trigeminal nociceptive pathways interact with vestibular nuclei, which generate central sensitivity during attacks. Experimental models demonstrate both glutamatergic projections from the caudal trigeminal nucleus to the vestibular nuclei and increased neuronal activation in vestibular centers following migraine provocation.

• The trigemino-vestibular projection is glutamatergic, originates in the caudal trigeminal nucleus, and projects to the vestibular nuclei, where it mediates vestibular dysfunction in chronic nitroglycerin migraine models; silencing this projection reduces vestibular dysfunction .

• Vestibular nucleus sensitivity: in chronic migraine models, increased expression of the immediate-early gene (c-fos) and neuronal activation are observed in the vestibular nuclei, accompanying vestibular behavioral abnormalities .

• Synaptic plasticity: following chronic migraine paradigms, abnormal synaptic protein expression and altered synaptic morphology have been reported in the vestibular nucleus, consistent with central sensitization processes .

The mechanisms summarized in are supported by the literature.

The evidence base for VM treatment remains heterogeneous and generally limited. Therefore, treatment recommendations should be interpreted according to the certainty of the evidence. Higher-certainty evidence is available only for a limited number of VM-specific interventions evaluated in randomized trials or systematic reviews. Observational studies may support real-world feasibility and signals of benefit, but they cannot establish definitive treatment effects. Case reports, small case series, and preclinical studies are useful for biological plausibility and hypothesis generation, but should not be used as the basis for strong clinical recommendations.

Sleep patterns, regular meals, hydration, caffeine/alcohol management, stress management, and recognition of personal triggers are fundamental components of migraine management. Patients should be informed that vestibular symptoms in VM may decrease in parallel with the headache burden. Lifestyle modifications are particularly important for patients with mild-to-moderate attack frequency, those who do not wish to use medication, or those requiring additional support alongside pharmacological treatment .

In acute attacks, short-acting antiemetics and vestibular suppressants may be used for short-term symptom control; however, prolonged use of vestibular suppressants is not recommended because it may interfere with central compensation. Evidence specific to acute VM treatment remains limited. Triptans have been used in clinical practice, but randomized VM-specific evidence is of low or very low certainty and does not establish a consistent, clinically meaningful benefit. Other acute options, including 5-HT1F agonists, gepants, and neuromodulation, should be considered investigational or individualized until supported by adequately powered VM-specific trials , .

Overall, evidence for acute VM-specific pharmacological treatment remains of low to very low certainty. Short-term antiemetics and vestibular suppressants may be used symptomatically in selected patients, but this practice is supported mainly by clinical experience and by extrapolation from vertigo and migraine management, rather than by robust VM-specific randomized evidence. Triptans have limited and inconsistent support from VM-specific trials, and newer acute agents, such as gepants and ditans, as well as neuromodulation approaches, should be considered investigational until adequately powered VM-specific randomized trials are available.

Acute treatment aims to halt the migraine process and reduce vestibular symptoms (e.g., nausea and motion intolerance); evidence regarding specific emergency medications for VM is insufficient and largely derived from studies of migraine headaches. Randomized data are limited to small-scale trials involving triptans; other commonly used agents are supported by observational data and expert consensus rather than by high-quality randomized controlled trials.

• Triptans—two randomized studies tested 10 mg rizatriptan and 2.5 mg zolmitriptan for acute VM attacks; the combined evidence was assessed as being of very low certainty and showed little or no significant benefit compared to placebo at 2 hours .

• Antiemetics and vestibular suppressants—agents such as dimenhydrinate, promethazine, and benzodiazepines are frequently used symptomatically to control nausea and reduce severe vestibular symptoms during attacks, but evidence from controlled trials is insufficient , .

• Antihistamines—vestibular sedatives/antihistamines are recommended as symptomatic treatment options in reviews and clinical practice guidelines , .

• Corticosteroids—they have been reported as a potential acute option in some practice guidelines, but evidence specific to VM is limited .

• Practice guidelines—current practice guidelines recommend the use of symptomatic vestibular medications alongside migraine-specific abortive treatment (when appropriate) and the personalization of treatment selection based on comorbidities and contraindications; however, recommendations at the official guideline level are limited due to low-quality evidence , .

Assess red flags: Before attributing symptoms to BPPV, rule out stroke and other acute vestibular syndromes (standard diagnostic procedure) . Tailor treatment to the individual: consider cardiovascular contraindications before using triptans, and select antiemetics/vestibular suppressants based on their side effect profiles and the patient’s comorbidities , . Evidence quality: most acute interventions are supported by low-quality observational data or extrapolations from migraine headaches; high-quality randomized controlled trials are largely absent , .

Small published series investigating non-pharmacological acute rescue approaches are available; however, controlled evidence is either preliminary or absent. Several devices and novel drug approaches show promise, but larger randomized trials are required.

• Non-invasive vagus nerve stimulation (nVNS): small case series and retrospective cohorts report rapid improvement in vertigo, headache, and ictal nystagmus following nVNS application during VM attacks; however, the evidence is Class IV and uncontrolled, so the benefit remains under investigation , .

• CGRP pathway agents and gepants—emerging small-scale studies and early reports are investigating CGRP receptor antagonists (e.g., rimegepant) for acute VM, but randomized results specific to VM have not yet been established in the published literature presented here , .

• Research gap: reviews and systematic reviews emphasize the urgent need for sufficiently powered, placebo-controlled trials targeting both pharmacological and device-based rescue strategies for acute VM , .

Prophylaxis should be considered in cases of frequent, prolonged, or severe attacks that significantly impair quality of life. Agents used in traditional migraine prophylaxis—such as beta-blockers, tricyclic antidepressants, topiramate, valproate, and flunarizine—are also used in VM. Cochrane reviews and network meta-analyses indicate that, due to limitations in the number and quality of studies, it is difficult to definitively identify a first-line agent; however, selected agents may be beneficial in reducing the frequency of vestibular symptoms and disability. Treatment selection should be based on comorbidities: tricyclic antidepressants for insomnia or anxiety; beta-blockers for hypertension or tachycardia; and topiramate may be considered for obesity and high migraine frequency. Pregnancy, childhood, old age, cardiac conduction disorders, depression, a history of kidney stones, and cognitive side effects should be considered when selecting medications , , , , .

CGRP-targeted therapies represent a biologically plausible and clinically promising approach for selected patients with frequent or refractory VM; however, the certainty of the evidence differs substantially by study type. The strongest direct evidence currently comes from limited VM-specific randomized clinical data. Prospective and retrospective observational studies provide supportive but lower-certainty evidence because of selection bias, lack of randomization, placebo effects, and heterogeneous outcome definitions. Case reports should be interpreted as hypothesis-generating only. Preclinical studies support the biological plausibility of CGRP involvement in vestibular pathways, but do not establish clinical efficacy in human VM.

CGRP-targeted monoclonal antibodies represent a promising mechanism-based approach in VM, particularly for frequent or refractory phenotypes. A placebo-controlled randomized clinical trial with galcanezumab reported improvement in VM-specific disability and dizziness-day measures , and systematic reviews and real-world data suggest potential benefit , . However, the overall evidence base remains limited by the number of VM-specific randomized trials, follow-up duration, cost considerations, and uncertainty regarding patient-selection criteria and response markers.

CGRP is expressed in the trigeminal and vestibular pathways and contributes to VM by increasing excitability and sensitivity, both centrally (vestibular nuclei and trigeminal pathways) and peripherally (inner ear efferent synapses). Blocking CGRP signaling alleviates these changes in preclinical models and reduces vestibular symptoms in clinical cohorts.

• Anatomical expression: CGRP is found in the vestibular cerebellum, vestibular nuclei, and cochlear/vestibular efferent fibers, providing the anatomical substrates for direct CGRP effects on vestibular function .

• Central sensitization: following repeated migraine triggers, CGRP levels and CGRP receptor components (calcitonin receptor-like receptor and receptor activity-modifying protein 1) are upregulated in the vestibular nuclei, and in animal models, local CGRP inhibition or CGRP receptor antagonism reduces c-fos activation and vestibular dysfunction , .

• Intracellular signaling: CGRP1 receptor activity in the vestibular nucleus activates the PKC/ERK/CREB pathways and alters synaptic transmission; blocking CGRP1 receptors reverses abnormal synaptic protein expression and structural synaptic changes in the VN in chronic migraine models .

• Peripheral modulation: systemic CGRP administration alters the electrophysiological potentials of the semicircular canals and vestibular end organs and leads to behavioral phonophobia and postural instability in rodents; this indicates that there is a site of action in peripheral end organs in addition to central effects .

• Clinical effects of blockade: monoclonal antibodies targeting CGRP or its receptor have been associated with reductions in vestibular symptom frequency, dizziness-day measures, and disability in observational clinical series, and with normalization of certain vestibular test abnormalities; this supports a possible pathogenic role for CGRP in human VM , , .

• Localization of the effect: in at least one clinical case, symptomatic improvement was observed following administration of a CGRP receptor inhibitor without any detectable changes in inner ear imaging or vestibular evoked potentials, suggesting that the primary mechanism of action involves the trigeminal/central vestibular pathways rather than reversing peripheral inner ear structural findings .

• Evidence for acute termination is lacking: evidence that CGRP antagonism can reliably terminate an acute VM attack has not been established in the current literature; existing data instead support prevention or reduction of attack frequency and of central sensitization rather than confirming the rapid termination of individual attacks, and overall evidence is insufficient.

Clinical cohorts and animal studies suggest that targeting CGRP signaling may reduce vestibular hypersensitivity and improve vestibular symptoms; however, the certainty of the evidence differs by study type. Randomized clinical evidence remains limited; observational studies are supportive but prone to bias; and animal studies are mechanistic rather than directly practice-changing. Representative clinical reports and key experimental findings are summarized in , , .

• Preclinical studies showed that CGRP receptor antagonists (e.g., BIBN4096BS) and CGRP inhibition reduced vestibular nucleus hyperactivity, corrected synaptic abnormalities, and improved vestibular behavior in chronic migraine animal models , .

• The mechanistic consistency observed in clinical symptoms with anti-CGRP agents is consistent with preclinical evidence that CGRP increases vestibular nucleus excitability and alters inner ear electrophysiology, establishing a mechanistic bridge from molecule to symptom , , .

Due to the non-systematic nature of the search for trial registries and grey literature, the current synthesis may underrepresent unpublished, ongoing, negative, or inconclusive studies of CGRP-targeted therapies. Therefore, the apparent benefit of these agents should be interpreted with caution until additional registered and peer-reviewed VM-specific trials become available.

Vestibular rehabilitation may be a useful non-pharmacological adjunct for patients with recurrent vestibular symptoms, visual motion sensitivity, persistent imbalance, or a tendency toward chronicity following VM. The Cochrane review of non-pharmacological interventions and subsequent systematic reviews suggest potential benefit as measured by tools such as the Dizziness Handicap Inventory, but protocols and evidence quality remain heterogeneous , , , . Rehabilitation should be gradual, individualized, and adjusted to patient tolerance to avoid exacerbating migraine triggers. Nevertheless, the certainty of the evidence remains limited by heterogeneity in rehabilitation protocols, outcome measures, comparator groups, and blinding procedures. Therefore, vestibular rehabilitation should be presented as a supportive, individualized intervention rather than as a uniformly established treatment.

Approaches such as greater occipital nerve block, nVNS, manual cervical therapy, and acupuncture have been reported in the literature. However, most of these methods are supported by small studies, protocols, or case series. These interventions should therefore be interpreted as investigational or adjunctive, rather than as established routine treatment options, until larger controlled studies using VM-specific outcome measures are available.

A summary of the available evidence, stratified by treatment category, study design, certainty level, and key limitations, is provided in to support cautious interpretation of treatment options , , , .

VM in childhood and childhood recurrent vertigo phenotypes should be evaluated using distinct diagnostic criteria and developmental characteristics . Children may have limited ability to describe vestibular symptoms precisely: parental observation, history of motion sickness, family history of migraine, and school or activity loss are important. In elderly patients, new-onset vertigo combined with headache should prompt investigation with a lower threshold for vascular and structural causes beyond VM. During pregnancy and breastfeeding, the selection of pharmacological prophylaxis should prioritize safety, and non-pharmacological approaches and lifestyle modifications should be preferred. In the presence of comorbid anxiety, depression, sleep disorders, PPPD, BPPV, or Ménière’s disease, treatment should not be limited to migraine prophylaxis alone , .
sections.discussion:
This PRISMA-informed systematic literature search with narrative synthesis demonstrates that VM is a clinically common yet diagnostically challenging neurovestibular syndrome , , , . Although current diagnostic criteria provide a standardized framework, diagnosis still depends on careful clinical history, neurological and otological examination, and exclusion of alternative or coexisting vestibular disorders , , . This dependence on clinical interpretation creates a risk of both overdiagnosis and underdiagnosis, particularly in patients with atypical vestibular symptoms, prominent auditory complaints, or chronic dizziness patterns.

Historically, vertigo in migraine was often conceptualized either as a non-specific accompanying symptom of headache or as a functional/psychogenic dizziness label when otological findings were unrevealing , , , . The evidence synthesized in this review supports a more specific neurovestibular model. In this framework, vestibular symptoms are not merely an incidental extension of migraine pain; rather, they may arise from interactions between migraine biology and vestibular network dysfunction.

From a pathophysiological perspective, VM should be considered a complex disorder situated at the intersection of trigeminovascular, vestibular, thalamocortical, cerebellar, and visual-vestibular integration systems , , . Trigeminovascular activation and CGRP signaling provide a biological bridge between migraine mechanisms and vestibular symptoms , , . Central sensitization, altered thalamocortical sensory processing, and cerebellar compensation may further explain motion sensitivity, visual dependence, and the tendency toward chronic dizziness in some patients , , . This network-based interpretation has practical consequences: patients with recurrent vertigo and migraine features should not be categorized solely by headache frequency but also by attack phenomenology, vestibular symptom type, auditory profile, motion sensitivity, and chronification risk.

A key finding of this synthesis is that VM frequently phenotypically overlaps with common neurotological disorders. Positional vertigo may resemble BPPV, whereas tinnitus and aural fullness may resemble early Ménière’s disease , , . Chronic visually induced dizziness may suggest PPPD, and late-onset acute vestibular symptoms may mimic posterior circulation ischemia , , . These overlaps do not invalidate the diagnosis of VM, but they require a diagnostic strategy that actively searches for distinguishing features, such as canal-specific nystagmus, progressive unilateral sensorineural hearing loss, persistent neurological deficits, vascular risk factors, or chronic non-episodic dizziness patterns. Thus, VM should be approached as a diagnosis requiring positive clinical criteria and careful exclusion of alternative or coexisting vestibular disorders rather than as a residual diagnosis after normal testing , , .

In daily neurotological and audiological practice, the findings support a structured assessment pathway. A detailed attack history should be accompanied, when clinically indicated, by pure-tone audiometry and targeted vestibular testing such as vHIT, caloric testing, VEMP, and positional maneuvers , , . These tests should not be interpreted as stand-alone diagnostic biomarkers for VM. Their main value lies in identifying Ménière’s disease, BPPV, vestibular neuritis, bilateral vestibulopathy, or central red flags and phenotyping patients with persistent imbalance or visual dependence. Audiological follow-up is particularly important when auditory symptoms are unilateral, progressive, or disproportionate to the vestibular attack pattern , .

Therapeutically, the reviewed evidence argues against applying a uniform treatment ladder to all patients. Acute symptomatic medications may be appropriate for short-term control of severe nausea and vertigo, but prolonged vestibular suppression should be avoided , , , . Conventional migraine prophylaxis remains clinically relevant, yet the choice of beta-blockers, tricyclic antidepressants, topiramate, valproate, flunarizine, or other agents should be individualized according to comorbidities, contraindications, pregnancy potential, age, cognitive side effects, and patient preference , , , . Vestibular rehabilitation should be considered early when motion sensitivity, imbalance, visual dependence, or PPPD overlap is present, because these domains may persist even after headache frequency improves , , , .

Emerging data on CGRP-targeted therapies represent one of the most important changes in the therapeutic landscape of VM , , . The available randomized and observational findings suggest benefit in selected frequent or refractory VM phenotypes , , , . However, replication studies, longer follow-up, cost-effectiveness analyses, and predictors of response are still needed before these agents can be positioned as definitive first-line therapy for VM. For clinicians, the most appropriate current implication is cautious escalation: CGRP-targeted treatment may be considered when conventional prophylaxis is ineffective, poorly tolerated, or contraindicated, particularly in patients with strong migraine biology and substantial vestibular disability.

The synthesis also highlights the need for closer collaboration between neurology, otolaryngology, audiology, vestibular physiotherapy, and primary care. VM management should include patient education, recognition of red flags, documentation of attack frequency and dizziness-related disability, and assessment of anxiety, sleep disturbance, and PPPD comorbidity , , . Follow-up should use comparable outcome measures, preferably dizziness-day counts and disability scales. Such a multidisciplinary approach may reduce diagnostic delay, avoid unnecessary repeated imaging or vestibular procedures, and improve alignment of mechanism-based treatment with the patient’s dominant clinical phenotype.

This review has several limitations. Although the literature search and study selection were structured according to PRISMA-informed principles, the synthesis was narrative rather than quantitative because of heterogeneity in study design, diagnostic criteria, interventions, and outcomes. Although a supplementary targeted search of ClinicalTrials.gov and WHO ICTRP was performed, Embase was not searched because of a lack of institutional access, and a comprehensive grey literature search was not undertaken. Registry findings were used to contextualize ongoing or unpublished therapeutic research but were not incorporated into the main evidence synthesis; therefore, the possibility of publication and selective reporting bias remains. This limitation may result in an overrepresentation of positive findings in the published literature, particularly in rapidly evolving treatment areas such as CGRP-targeted therapies and other pharmacological or device-based interventions. Consequently, conclusions regarding these therapies should be interpreted as provisional and based primarily on the available published evidence rather than on the totality of completed or ongoing research. No prospective protocol registration was performed. The included evidence base spans randomized trials, observational studies, systematic reviews, case series, and preclinical studies; therefore, conclusions should be interpreted in accordance with the certainty of the evidence rather than as uniform clinical recommendations. Finally, VM-specific outcome measures remain heterogeneous, limiting direct comparisons across treatment studies.

These limitations are particularly relevant to the treatment sections. Acute therapies, CGRP-targeted therapies, vestibular rehabilitation, and experimental interventions are supported by evidence of varying levels of certainty; therefore, the manuscript avoids ranking all interventions equally and emphasizes individualized, phenotype-based management.

Future research should prioritize four clinically relevant areas: development of standardized VM-specific outcome measures; adequately powered randomized trials for acute, preventive, CGRP-targeted, and rehabilitation-based interventions; biomarker and vestibular testing studies that help distinguish VM from Ménière’s disease, BPPV, PPPD, and posterior circulation disorders; and longitudinal studies evaluating chronification, PPPD overlap, disability, and treatment response. Machine learning-based diagnostic models, combinations of VEMP/vHIT/caloric testing, and attack-monitoring approaches that use wearable technologies may contribute to future clinical decision support, but these tools require external validation, interpretability, and clinical applicability beyond algorithmic accuracy.

In the future, evidence syntheses should incorporate Embase, prospective trial registries, and grey literature sources. This will reduce publication bias and more effectively capture ongoing or unpublished therapeutic studies.

VM is not merely the concurrent occurrence of migraine and vertigo; it is a complex neurovestibular disorder involving the trigeminovascular system, central sensitization, vestibulo-thalamic-cortical networks, CGRP signaling, and cerebellar compensation. Diagnosis should be structured according to ICHD-3 and Bárány Society criteria, but differential diagnosis must be performed carefully for each patient. Treatment should be individualized and guided by the certainty of available evidence. Lifestyle modification and conventional migraine-preventive strategies may be considered according to phenotype, comorbidities, contraindications, and patient preference, although VM-specific evidence remains limited for many agents. Vestibular rehabilitation may be useful as an adjunct in selected patients with motion sensitivity, imbalance, or overlap with PPPD. CGRP-targeted therapies are promising for selected, frequent, or refractory phenotypes, but current evidence remains insufficient to establish them as the definitive first-line VM therapy. Stronger VM-specific randomized trials, standardized outcome measures, and biomarker-based phenotyping are needed to transform clinical practice in this field.

title: [Migraine and contraception].
abstract: Migraine is a common pathology in women. Migraine disease is well defined by the International Headache Society and has to be distinguished from others types of headaches. The occurrence of migraine attacks is frequently linked to the menstrual cycle. Many studies have related a connexion with hormonal fluctuations and migraine event. Migraine with aura is currently identified as a stroke risk factor and this risk dramatically increases in case of oestroprogestative pill intake and smoking. The World Health Organization established guidelines about oestroprogestative intake in case of migraine while strictly contraindicating oestroprogestative intake in patients with migraine with aura. This review explains the influence of different contraceptive intake, oral contraceptive regimens, and type of oestrogen in oestroprogestative contraceptive on migraine occurrence.
