sections.methods:
This scoping review followed the methodological framework established by Arksey and O’Malley,[] as refined by Levac et al.,[] and adhered to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) guidelines.[]

Studies were selected using a predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria framework. The population included individuals of all ages diagnosed with primary migraine according to the International Classification of Headache Disorders, 3 rd edition criteria.[] Interventions or exposures involved either measurement of serum 25[OH]D levels or administration of vitamin D supplementation. Comparators included placebo, no treatment, or control groups. Primary outcomes encompassed migraine frequency, severity, disability scores (e.g., Migraine Disability Assessment [MIDAS], Headache Impact Test-6 [HIT-6]), and vitamin D deficiency prevalence. Eligible study designs were RCTs, cohort studies, case-control studies, and cross-sectional analyses published between January 1, 2000, and June 30, 2025. We excluded studies investigating secondary headaches, nonEnglish publications (due to resource constraints for translation, though we acknowledge this may introduce language bias), conference abstracts, narrative reviews, and those utilizing nonstandard vitamin D biomarkers such as 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D.

A systematic search was conducted across MEDLINE/PubMed, Scopus, and Embase using controlled vocabulary (MeSH and Emtree terms) combined with keywords related to vitamin D and migraine concepts (full search strategy provided in Supplementary Material 1).

Two independent reviewers (AM, SV) performed the selection process using Rayyan Qatar Computing Research Institute (QCRI) software,[] with inter-rater reliability assessed via Cohen’s kappa (κ = 0.86). The process included: (1) removal of duplicates, (2) title and abstract screening against eligibility criteria, and (3) full-text review of potentially relevant articles. Disagreements were resolved through consensus discussions or adjudication by a third reviewer (S.D.). The selection process, including detailed exclusion reasons, is presented in a PRISMA-ScR flow diagram [].[]

Data extraction was performed using a standardized form pilot-tested on 10% of included studies. The exact extraction template is provided in Supplementary Material 2; no modifications were made during the review process. Extracted variables included study characteristics (country, funding source); population demographics (age, migraine subtype); vitamin D metrics (deficiency threshold <20 ng/mL, assay method); clinical outcomes (headache days/month, disability scores); and covariates (skin phototype, supplement dosage). Ethical approval status and informed consent procedures from original studies were systematically recorded; all included studies reported Institutional Review Board approval where applicable.

To address clinical heterogeneity, predefined subgroup analyses were conducted. Outcomes were categorized by migraine subtype, dosage tier, and population characteristics for narrative comparison, with explicit acknowledgment of methodological limitations. Geographic modifiers were operationalized by classifying studies based on whether they were conducted above or below 40°N latitude. This allowed exploration of potential variations in vitamin D deficiency prevalence and its association with migraine across geographic regions. Studies reporting mixed populations from both latitudinal zones were analyzed separately when feasible to preserve the integrity of the geographic modifier analysis. These comparisons were exploratory, recognizing potential confounding factors such as diet, genetics, cultural practices, and healthcare access.

Vitamin D dosage regimens were grouped into three categories: high-dose (≥50,000 IU/week), moderate-dose (4,000–49,999 IU/week), and low-dose (<4,000 IU/week) to examine differential treatment effects. However, formal comparisons between dosage tiers were limited due to inconsistent reporting and small sample sizes within each category. Population subtypes were stratified by age group (<18 vs. ≥18 years), migraine chronicity (chronic migraine defined as ≥15 headache days/month vs. episodic), and treatment resistance (refractory migraine classified as ≥2 failed preventive therapies). These analyses remained hypothesis-generating rather than confirmatory, consistent with scoping review methodology.

Findings were synthesized narratively through evidence mapping. Frequency ranges and directional trends were reported without statistical pooling. Methodological rigor was assessed using discipline-specific tools: the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale for observational studies,[] the Cochrane Risk of Bias Tool 2.0 for RCTs,[] and A Measurement Tool to Assess Systematic Reviews 2 (AMSTAR 2) for systematic reviews.[] Overall, most studies demonstrated moderate-to-high quality; common limitations included variability in assay methods and unadjusted confounders such as sun exposure and dietary habits. Quality scores are summarized in .

As this study involved secondary analysis of publicly available data, institutional ethics approval was not required. International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO) registration was not pursued, as scoping reviews are exempt from preregistration requirements under PRISMA-ScR guidelines when synthesizing evidence without meta-analysis.[]

sections.results:
The systematic search identified 3,447 records from PubMed (n = 1,875), Scopus (n = 470), and Embase (n = 1,102). After removing 377 duplicates and excluding 2,832 during title/abstract screening (not addressing research topic/question), 238 full-text articles were retrieved and assessed for eligibility. Of these, 208 were excluded, and 30 studies were included in the final scoping review.[] The PRISMA-ScR flow diagram outlines the number of records identified, screened, eligible, and included, along with detailed exclusion reasons [].

The 30 included studies comprised 14 observational studies (n = 27,482 participants), 9 RCTs (n = 1,710 participants), and 7 systematic reviews.[] All studies are summarized in . Geographically, 48% originated from latitudes >40°N (predominantly Europe and North America), 32% from Asia and the Middle East, and 20% from other regions. Geographic disparities were evident: Africa and South Asia accounted for only 10% (3/30) of included studies,[] compared to 48% (14/30) from high-latitude regions.

Vitamin D deficiency prevalence ranged from 65% to 88% across studies. Chronic migraine patients exhibited higher deficiency rates (80%–92%) than those with episodic migraine (60%–75%).[] Geographically, individuals residing at latitudes >40°N showed elevated deficiency prevalence (75%–90%) compared to those at ≤40°N (60%–85%).[] In pediatric populations, deficiency frequencies were lower (60%–72%) than in adults (70%–88%).[] Assay methodology also appeared to influence estimates; liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry reported 12% lower deficiency rates than immunoassays in comparable populations.[]

Studies consistently reported inverse associations between vitamin D status and headache frequency (median r = –0.42; range: –0.08 to –0.67).[] The strongest correlations were observed in episodic migraine cohorts. Disability outcomes also showed negative trends across standardized scales (MIDAS, HIT-6), particularly among patients with chronic migraine.[] Notably, Haro et al. found no significant association in chronic migraine (r = 0.08).[]

Due to substantial clinical heterogeneity—including variations in dosing regimens (1,000–50,000 IU/week), patient populations (episodic vs. chronic migraine), and outcome measures (headache days vs. disability scores)—the therapeutic efficacy of vitamin D supplementation was evaluated through narrative synthesis. Direct quantitative comparisons between studies are therefore cautioned. In vitamin D-deficient adults, high-dose regimens (≥50,000 IU/week), resulted in a 50%–72% relative reduction in monthly migraine attacks across three RCTs,[] corresponding to an absolute reduction of 3.2–4.8 fewer headache days per month. This aligns with meta-analytic estimates showing approximately 2.7 fewer headache days per month.[] However, effects on attack severity and duration were inconsistently reported.

Distinct therapeutic responses were observed in special populations. In pediatric cohorts, combining vitamin D 3 (2,000 IU/day) with topiramate led to a 72% reduction in migraine attacks—substantially greater than the 48% reduction seen with topiramate alone.[] Refractory migraine cases showed promising results when probiotics ( L. rhamnosus ) were coadministered with high-dose vitamin D, yielding a 54% attack reduction,[] potentially reflecting synergistic gut–brain axis modulation. This finding supports emerging evidence for combination therapies targeting neuroinflammation[]; however, it is based on a single trial and requires validation in larger studies.[]

Conversely, individuals with sufficient baseline vitamin D levels (≥30 ng/mL) consistently experienced minimal benefit from supplementation.[] Collectively, these findings demonstrate that clinical efficacy is critically dependent on baseline vitamin D status.

These results illustrate that vitamin D’s role in migraine is highly context-dependent rather than universal (it is not a “one-size-fits-all” intervention]. Treatment responses and deficiency patterns vary significantly based on geographic location (with higher deficiency rates at latitudes above 40°N), migraine subtype (chronic vs. episodic), and age group (adults vs. children). Importantly, lower vitamin D levels consistently correlate with increased symptom burden and greater disability. These associations highlight the need for further investigation into how vitamin D modulates neurological pathways relevant to migraine pathophysiology. The key findings of the studies are tabulated in A,B,C and the global map depicting the studies is given in .
sections.discussion:
This scoping review synthesizes evidence from 30 studies examining the role of vitamin D across diverse migraine populations and geographic regions. We identified three consistent patterns: First, vitamin D deficiency (serum 25(OH)D <20 ng/mL) is highly prevalent (65%–88%) among individuals with migraine, particularly those with chronic migraine (80%–92%) and residents of high-latitude regions (>40°N; 75%–90%).[] Second, moderate inverse correlations exist between baseline vitamin D levels and both headache frequency (median r = –0.42) and migraine-related disability severity.[] Third, therapeutic effects of vitamin D supplementation are context-dependent: high-dose regimens (≥50,000 IU/week) reduced migraine attacks by 50%–72% in deficient adults, whereas replete populations showed minimal benefit.[] These findings underscore the importance of baseline 25(OH)D testing before initiating supplementation.

These results have important implications for clinical practice. Baseline serum 25(OH)D testing should be considered for all migraine patients, especially those with chronic migraine or living at higher latitudes, to identify those who may benefit from targeted intervention. For patients confirmed as deficient, high-dose vitamin D supplementation (e.g., 50,000 IU/week) may serve as an effective adjunctive therapy to reduce attack frequency. This approach supports a personalized treatment strategy, tailoring interventions based on individual vitamin D status. Conversely, clinicians should recognize the limited efficacy of supplementation in patients with sufficient baseline levels, reinforcing the need for stratification prior to initiation of therapy. A practical clinical algorithm could include (1) routine 25(OH)D testing in migraine patients, (2) administration of high-dose vitamin D if deficiency is confirmed, and (3) ongoing monitoring of both treatment response and serum calcium to prevent toxicity.

The relationship between vitamin D and migraine appears complex and potentially bidirectional. While the observed associations align with proposed mechanisms involving modulation of trigeminovascular and neuroinflammatory pathways—including suppression of CGRP and regulation of IL-17/Transforming Growth Factor (TGF)-β[]—they raise critical questions about causality: Is vitamin D deficiency a driver or consequence of migraine? What underlies the observed latitude gradients in deficiency prevalence? Most existing studies employ cross-sectional designs, limiting causal inference. Although we observed strong and consistent patterns—especially among chronic migraineurs and high-latitude populations—these likely reflect interwoven biological and behavioral factors. Notably, reverse causation remains plausible: photophobia and reduced outdoor activity during migraine episodes may impair cutaneous vitamin D synthesis,[] a mechanism particularly relevant in chronic migraine, where deficiency rates are highest (83.7%) and symptom-driven sun avoidance creates self-perpetuating cycles of deficiency.[] Additionally, comorbid conditions such as depression or anxiety may further influence lifestyle behaviors and sun exposure.

Geographic confounding also warrants attention. Factors such as skin pigmentation (melanin density), dietary intake of vitamin D-fortified foods or fatty fish, and cultural practices affecting clothing coverage may independently influence vitamin D status and partially explain regional differences in deficiency prevalence. Together, these complexities highlight the need for longitudinal studies to clarify the temporal dynamics between vitamin D status and migraine development.

This scoping review reflects limitations inherent to the current literature on vitamin D and migraine. Confounding by geographic and demographic variables is common, and the predominance of cross-sectional designs limits causal interpretation. Therapeutic heterogeneity—arising from variations in dosing regimens, outcome measures, and follow-up durations—also complicates comparisons. Inconsistent assay methodologies for measuring 25(OH)D further contribute to diagnostic variability and interpretative challenges across studies.

Critical gaps remain in understanding the role of vitamin D in migraine pathophysiology and management. First, the temporal relationship between vitamin D deficiency and migraine onset remains unclear, necessitating longitudinal studies to establish causality. Second, most trials focus primarily on migraine frequency, with insufficient data on severity, duration, or disability. Third, mechanistic insights into how vitamin D influences pathways such as CGRP release, IL-17 signaling, and neuronal excitability are largely theoretical and require in vivo validation. There is also limited evidence regarding the safety and efficacy of long-term vitamin D supplementation in pediatric populations. Finally, significant disparities persist in the global evidence base, particularly among populations with darker skin tones and underrepresented geographic regions.

To advance this field, future research should prioritize mechanistic RCTs incorporating baseline 25(OH)D stratification and exploring interactions within the gut–brain axis. Global standardization of vitamin D assays through coordinated initiatives is essential to reduce diagnostic inconsistencies. Clinical trials must adopt more comprehensive endpoints, including severity, duration, and disability, while accounting for migraine subtypes (chronic vs. episodic) and aura status in participant stratification. The potential synergies of vitamin D with adjunctive therapies—such as probiotics, statins, or lifestyle interventions—deserve investigation in larger, well-controlled trials. Collaborative, consortia-driven efforts like HEADACHE-MEND[] offer a promising framework to address global evidence gaps, particularly in populations disproportionately affected by vitamin D deficiency but currently underrepresented in the literature.[]

Vitamin D deficiency shows consistent associations with increased migraine burden, especially among individuals with chronic migraine and residents of high-latitude regions. While high-dose supplementation demonstrates promise in deficient populations, its effects on headache severity, duration, and outcomes in nondeficient individuals require further prospective study. Vitamin D supplementation should be considered an adjunct therapy for deficient patients rather than a universal prophylactic measure. Addressing current evidence gaps—particularly through mechanistic research, combination therapy studies, investigations in high-melanin populations, and work in underrepresented regions—alongside establishing pediatric safety frameworks, will support equitable global translation of findings.

There are no conflicts of interest.

This scoping review is based entirely on published, publicly available literature. All data supporting the findings are derived from the cited references. No new datasets were generated. The full search strategy, PRISMA-ScR checklist, and data extraction tables are available as supplementary materials and from the corresponding author upon reasonable request.

sections.abstract:
the purpose of this study is to evaluate both macular thickness and vascular density in patients with new- onset migraine using optical coherence tomography angiography (OCTA).

This prospective case-control study included 109 participants divided into two groups: Group (A), which comprised patients with New- onset migraine (n=54) and group (B), which included healthy control group (n= 55). Both groups were evaluated ophthalmologically and imaged by optical coherence tomography angiography (OCTA) to evaluate both retinal thickness and vasculature.

Both groups were well matched regarding age, sex, best corrected visual acuity (BCVA), axial length, spherical equivalent (SER) and intraocular pressure (IOP), with no significant difference. The migraine group demonstrated a significant decrease in all vascular parameters in comparison with control group p-value is significant (p < 0.05), Furthermore, when comparing migraine patients with aura to those without aura; patients with aura were significantly more affected.

Patients with migraine, even at their first diagnosis, exhibit abnormal retinal microvasculature. Furthermore, those with aura demonstrate a higher susceptibility to retinal vascular involvement.

sections.other:
Migraine is a prevalent neurological disorder characterized by episodic attacks of headache accompanied by autonomic gastrointestinal tract (GIT) changes []. additionally, Visual symptoms reported in many cases of migraine are frequently associated with periorbital pain [].

Although The pathogenesis of migraine is still unclear, both vascular and neurologic theories have been proposed to explain its nature. the vascular theory attributes the occurrence of migraine to a transient decrease in cerebral blood flow, which triggers the aura []. Conversely The neurogenic theory attributes its occurrence to neuronal dysfunction that leads to vascular changes []. Recently, migraine has been conceptualized as a mixed neurovascular disorder involving cortical spreading depression (CSD). Indeed, Microvascular biometrics in the brain have demonstrated altered vascular density and hemodynamics. Migraine could be classified as cerebral small vessel disease (CSVD).

The trigeminal vascular system (TGVS) plays pivotal role in the pathogenesis of migraine. The trigeminal vascular system (TGVS) provides sensory innervation to both cranial blood vessels and extracranial tissue. Its activation during the attack leads to ocular manifestations particularly during the aura, as it is in charge of regulating the vascular tone and transmitting the signals of pain [].

Based on the presence of aura, migraine is classified into two types: migraine with aura (MA) and migraine without (MWA). The aura phase is characterized by focal neurological symptoms that typically precede the onset of headache attacks [].

Previous studies have reported that both ocular and cerebral flow decreases in migraine with aura (MA). In addition, this hypoperfusion directly affects the optic nerve head (ONH) and the retina, potentially inducing ganglion cell loss due to oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction [, ]. similar patterns of retinal hypoperfusion and altered retinal structural integrity could be found in other neurological disorders such as multiple sclerosis (MS) [].

Recent advancements in optical coherence tomography angiography (OCTA) have made it possible to keep track of the microvascular abnormalities in both macula and the optic nerve head (ONH). This technique enables the segmentation of superficial and deep capillary networks with the use of amplitude or phase decorating technology. This allows for the visualization of posterior segment vascularity at a 3D resolution of 5 μm [].

The purpose of this study was to investigate the perfusion of both retina and the optic nerve head (ONH) in the new- onset migraine patients compared to healthy controls.

Hany Mahmoud wrote the manuscript, Dalia Tohamy investigated the cases, Ahmed Ezzat investigated migraine cases, Islam Saad revised the manuscript, and Mohamed Salah collected and revised data.

No funding.

This prospective case-control study was conducted using data from 109 patients recruited from both ophthalmology and neurology departments of Sohag and Assiut University Hospitals. In order to be conducted, it received its approval from Sohag Faculty of Medicine’s ethical committee; number (Soh-Med-24-06-06PD). It adheres to the tenets of the Helsinki Declaration. The evaluated eyes were divided into two groups: group (A) which comprised patients with the new- onset migraine patients, and group (B) which included the healthy controls undergoing routine ophthalmic examination.

The inclusion criteria for the study group required patients with confirmed diagnosis of new- onset migraine. The diagnosis was confirmed by a senior neurologist according to official diagnostic criteria. additionally, these patients have free neurological examination with no prior history of neurological disorders. The control group consisted of healthy individuals recruited from ophthalmology department among individuals presenting for routine eye examinations and had no history of neurologic disease.

new-onset migraine patients are recruited and classified into migraine with aura (MA) and migraine without aura (MWA). According to International classification of headache disorders-3 (ICHD-3) [].

Exclusion criteria comprised patients with other neurological or cognitive disorder, diabetes, hypertension, cardiac patients, coagulation disorders. additionally, participants with ocular disorders such as glaucoma, abnormal axial length, high refractive errors, or ocular hypertension were excluded. History of ocular surgery with the exception of uncomplicated cataract surgery, also served as a basis for exclusion.

A comprehensive examination of the eyes was performed on all participants, which included uncorrected visual acuity (UCVA) and best corrected visual acuity (BCVA) in the form of logarithm of minimum angle of resolution (log MAR), axial length, spherical equivalent (SER), slit lamp biomicroscopy, measurement of intraocular pressure (IOP) using Goldmann applanation tonometry.

Optical Coherence Tomography Angiography (OCTA; Optovue, Inc., Fremont, CA) was used to evaluate the parameters including macular thickness, peripapillary retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL) thickness and vascular density in both the peripapillary and the macula regions. Patients were examined by the same operator with 3 × 3 mm scan area centered on the macula and 4.5 × 4.5 mm scan area centered on the optic disc.

Scans were excluded if Signal strength index (SSI) was less than 55, and if automated quality index (AQI) was less than 6. Scans with artifacts were excluded. The measurements obtained automatically and verified manually for more accuracy [].

The optical coherence tomography angiography (OCTA) was done in between the attacks, with one week of attack free period. The medications were stopped one week before the examination.

Both eyes of each case were examined, only one eye of each patient included in the statistical analysis, the included eye was chosen randomly to avoid bias, and the records of the other eye were added to the patients’ registered data.

In order to compute the size of the sample, the G*Power statistical program V. 3.1.9.4. was used based on the following assumptions: means ± SDs of whole image macular VD were 15.57 ± 0.53 and 15.8 ± 0.32 of migraine and control groups respectively according to results of a previous study which used optical coherence tomography angiography (OCTA) to make assessments of the perfusion of the macula and optic nerve in cases diagnosed with migraine compared to healthy control participants, making an effect size of 0.55 (2), α = 0.05, and power = 0.80. Computing the size of the sample size included 54 participants for each study group.

The data collected for the purposes of the present study were analyzed and presented using the Statistical Package for the Social Sciences (SPSS) V.26 program for data entry and analysis. Descriptive statistics were used to summarize data; in the form of numbers and percentages for qualitative data and mean ± standard deviation concerning quantitative data. The Kolmogorov-Smirnov test was employed in order to make assessments of how normal the data were. The association between groups was detected by independent sample t test or Mann-Whiteny U test according to normality distribution. Significance was assessed at a p-value < 0.05.

Data are available upon request from the corresponding author.

sections.discussion:
Migraine is a neurovascular phenomenon; many studies have reported retinal vascular alternations in patients with migraine []. Central spreading depression (CSD), which is a large depolarizing wave related to calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP), causes generalized short congestion in the cortical grey matter followed by prolonged hypoperfusion. The hypoperfusion and the resultant microangiopathy contribute to the pathophysiology of migraine and support the occurrence of retinal vascular changes [].

Retinal vascular density is decreased in migraine cases, with a more pronounced decrease in cases with aura []. These alternations support the brain vascular changes that occur in migraine patients and could reflect subclinical ischemic damage and microcirculation disorders in the retinal vasculature. Since The brain and the retina share the same embryological origin, these ocular findings are considered a “window” into cerebral circulation.

Additionally, many studies have shown alternations in retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL) thickness, especially in the nasal quadrant, along with macular thinning []. the retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL) thinning is due axonal loss, with the nasal quadrant being more affected due to its weaker vascular supply. macular thinning results from vascular insult and hypoxia; furthermore, repeated migraine attacks aggravate this damage over time.

In these previous studies, the study group consisted of migraine patients undergoing treatment; moreover, the duration of the disease had a significant impact on vascular and retinal changes, as repeated prolonged vasoconstriction could induce permanent microvascular abnormalities [, ]. These repeated episodes of vasoconstrictions cause endothelial cell damage and microvascular remodeling. Over time, this cumulative ischemic stress becomes irreversible, leading to greater retinal involvement and diminished central vision.

Certain medications can significantly impact retinal thickness and vasculature, particularly those that induce vasoconstriction, which may lead to vascular insult and ischemia. Specifically, Triptans and ergot alkaloids cause direct vasoconstriction; while beta-blockers can decrease overall ocular perfusion. consequently, strict monitoring is necessary to detect any medications-induced changes [].

We studied new- onset migraine patients who were assessed regarding their retinal and vascular changes immediately upon diagnosis. The findings revealed significant alternations in vascular density, characterized by a decrease in the superficial and deep layers of both macula and the optic nerve head (ONH).

When the thicknesses of the macula and retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL) were investigated, no significant differences were observed between the control and migraine groups. The lack of significant changes could be due to several factors. We hypothesized that such alternations might only occur in long-standing migraine cases, driven by prolonged ischemia or the use of vasoconstrictive drugs.

Additionally, there were no significant changes between the migraine with aura (MA) and migraine without aura (MWA) groups regarding macular and retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL) thicknesses, however, the vascular changes were significant between the two groups. The findings support the vascular theory and suggest that vascular involvement occurs prior to the onset of structural thickness alternations. previous studies have found that patients with aura show pronounced alternations in the macular and retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL) thicknesses compared to patients without aura.

Many studies have found that genetics play a crucial role in pathogenesis of migraine, since these genes are related to vascular structure, such changes can be found even before clinical attacks are established []. furthermore, calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) plays a crucial role in central spreading depression (CSD).

The genetic basis accounts for the vascular changes detected even in new-onset migraine patients. suggesting that genetic predisposition is a crucial factor in the early development of the disease.

The vascular changes are more prevalent in patients with aura, thereby reinforcing the vascular link to the pathogenesis of the disease. Consequently, the Early detection of these alternations combined with meticulous follow up can significantly impact the management of ocular vascular consequences of migraine.

First, the small sample size limited the statistical power of the study. Second, the Lack of longitudinal designs precluded the assessment of the cascade of subsequent vascular and structural thickness alterations.

In conclusion, retinal vascular alternations occur in the new-onset migraine patients, with a more pronounced effect observed in those with aura. These findings strongly reinforce the theory of vascular alternation in migraine patients. further studies are warranted to support these preliminary findings.

title: Pathophysiology of migraine.
abstract: Our understanding of migraine pathophysiology is a work in progress. As more is learned about migraine, it seems that the probability of identifying a single unifying explanation for this common disorder becomes less and less. Although the neuroanatomy and elements of pain physiology underlying migraine attacks are probably shared pathophysiologic elements, the emerging complexity of migraine genetics suggests that the acute attack may be the final common expression of more than one type of initiating abnormality. After a brief summary of the neuroanatomic structures involved in the generation of migraine attacks and the traditional theories of migraine, the author focuses on the current understanding of migraine genetics and reviews recent data from the neuroimaging and the neurophysiology of migraine.

title: Epigenome-wide DNA methylation profiling reveals risk genes for migraine and its subtypes.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Migraine is a highly disabling neurovascular disorder, yet its underlying molecular mechanisms remain incompletely understood. Emerging evidence implicates epigenetic modifications, particularly DNA methylation, in migraine pathophysiology, but whether these changes play a causal role has not been established. METHODS: We integrated large-scale brain and blood methylation quantitative trait loci (mQTL) datasets with genome-wide association study (GWAS) data to investigate the causal role of DNA methylation in migraine and its subtypes. Two-sample Mendelian randomization (MR) was applied to evaluate the effects of cytosine-phosphate-guanine (CpG) methylation on migraine risk. Significant CpG sites were annotated to genes and refined through a multi-step prioritization framework incorporating colocalization, expression QTL (eQTL)-MR, two-step MR, and gene-based association analyses. Functional enrichment, protein-protein interaction, and drug-gene analyses were then performed to explore biological mechanisms and therapeutic potential. RESULTS: We identified 169 CpG sites with causal effects on migraine, mapping to 68 genes. Subtype analyses revealed 10 additional genes associated with MA and MO, including three genes specific to MA and one to MO, expanding the total to 72 non-overlapping migraine risk genes. Integrative prioritization highlighted 12 high-confidence genes, among which CFDP1, ICA1L and SERPING1 was supported by all five analytical approaches. Functional characterization indicated significant enrichment in calcitonin-like ligand receptors, axon development and neurovascular regulation, while drug-gene interaction analyses suggested therapeutic potential for targets such as MAPT and CALCA. CONCLUSION: Our findings provide robust evidence that DNA methylation contributes causally to migraine risk and its subtypes, identify genes of biological and therapeutic relevance, and offer novel insights into the epigenetic mechanisms underlying migraine pathophysiology.

sections.other:
Migraine is a highly disabling neurovascular disorder, clinically characterized by a severe throbbing unilateral headache, often accompanied by nausea, vomiting, photophobia, and phonophobia. It is the fourth leading cause of disability worldwide and the second leading cause among young women []. In addition to markedly impairing patients’ quality of life, migraine imposes a substantial social and economic burden [–]. Clinically, it is broadly classified into two major subtypes: migraine without aura (MO), characterized by the absence of preceding neurological symptoms, and migraine with aura (MA), which is preceded by transient sensory disturbances, such as visual or motor changes []. However, the molecular mechanisms underlying migraine remain poorly understood, limiting the development of effective preventive and therapeutic strategies [].

Epigenetics is the study of heritable changes in gene expression that occur without alterations in the underlying DNA sequence, and it plays a key role in regulating gene activity and mediating interactions between genetic and environmental factors []. Among various epigenetic mechanisms, DNA methylation is the most extensively studied, primarily involving the covalent addition of a methyl group to cytosines at cytosine-phosphate-guanine (CpG) sites. By influencing chromatin structure and transcription factor binding, DNA methylation can exert long-lasting effects on gene activity. Several recent studies have implicated DNA methylation in the pathophysiology of migraine [–]. However, most available evidence is observational, making it difficult to establish causality. Determining whether DNA methylation changes are causal in migraine could provide critical insights for biomarker discovery and targeted therapeutic development.

Mendelian randomization (MR) is a powerful analytic framework that uses genetic variants robustly associated with an exposure as instrumental variables (IVs) to infer a causal effect of that exposure on an outcome [–]. By leveraging the natural random allocation of alleles at conception, MR emulates the design principles of randomized controlled trials, thereby minimizing confounding and reverse causation and offering stronger evidence for causality. The rapid expansion of large-scale genome-wide association studies (GWAS) and molecular quantitative trait loci (QTL) resources has created new opportunities to dissect the regulatory mechanisms linking genetic variation to complex diseases. In particular, integrating methylation QTL (mQTL) data with MR enables the identification of DNA methylation sites that have causal effects on disease risk, thereby revealing causal epigenetic modifications and their target genes, and offering novel biomarkers and therapeutic targets with potential implications for disease prevention, diagnosis, and treatment.

In this study, we integrated large-scale mQTL and GWAS summary statistics to perform MR analyses, with the aim of identifying DNA methylation sites with potential causal effects on migraine and its subtypes (MA and MO). Significant CpG sites identified from the mQTL–MR analyses were first mapped to genes, providing an initial set of candidate genes. To further refine these candidate genes, we then implemented a comprehensive gene prioritization framework, which included: (1) colocalization analysis between mQTL and migraine to identify shared causal variants; (2) expression QTL (eQTL)-based MR to test whether genetically regulated gene expression influences migraine risk; (3) colocalization analysis between eQTL and migraine to determine whether gene expression and migraine share the same causal variant; (4) two-step MR to assess whether the effects of DNA methylation on migraine are mediated through gene expression; and (5) gene-based association analysis using MAGMA to prioritize migraine risk genes. This was followed by functional enrichment analysis, protein–protein interaction (PPI) network analysis, and drug–gene interaction analysis to evaluate the biological relevance and therapeutic potential of the candidate genes mapped from significant CpG sites. Collectively, our study provides a comprehensive view of the potential causal role of DNA methylation in migraine and highlights novel opportunities for biomarker discovery and precision medicine interventions. sections.methods:
We obtained summary statistics for migraine and its two major subtypes—MA and MO—from the largest available GWAS meta-analysis, which included approximately 1.3 million individuals of European ancestry. This dataset comprised 79,495 cases and 1,259,808 controls for overall migraine, 16,603 cases and 1,336,517 controls for MA, and 11,718 cases and 1,330,747 controls for MO []. For mQTL data, we included two tissue-specific datasets. Brain mQTL data were derived from Qi et al. [], based on a meta-analysis of three European cohorts with an effective sample size of 1,160, while peripheral blood mQTL data were obtained from a meta-analysis of the Brisbane Systems Genetics Study (BSGS) and the Lothian Birth Cohorts (LBC), totaling 1,980 individuals of European ancestry [, ]. For eQTL data, brain cis-eQTL summary statistics were sourced from Qi et al. [], comprising 2,865 brain cortex samples from 2,443 unrelated individuals of European ancestry, and blood cis-eQTL data were obtained from the eQTLGen Consortium ( https://eqtlgen.org/cis-eqtls.html ), which includes 31,684 samples [].

We employed a two-sample MR approach to assess the causal effects of DNA methylation on migraine and its subtypes (i.e., mQTL–MR), using the TwoSampleMR R package (Version 0.6.17, https://mrcieu.r-universe.dev/TwoSampleMR ) []. The validity of MR relies on three core assumptions: the IVs are robustly associated with the exposure, are independent of confounding factors, and affect the outcome only through the exposure []. To satisfy the first assumption, we selected single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) from mQTL datasets that were significantly associated with methylation levels at genome-wide significance ( P < 5 × 10 − 8 ) as IVs. To minimize bias from linkage disequilibrium, SNPs passing this threshold were clumped for independence using PLINK (Version 2.0, https://www.cog-genomics.org/plink2/ ) [] with the European reference panel from the 1000 Genomes Project []. A stringent threshold of R² < 0.001 within a 10,000 kb window was applied. We then harmonized effect alleles between the exposure and outcome datasets to ensure consistency of effect direction, and removed palindromic SNPs with intermediate allele frequencies to avoid strand ambiguity. Instrument strength was evaluated using the F -statistic, with values >10 considered indicative of sufficiently strong instruments. When a single SNP was available as an IV, we applied the Wald ratio method; when two or more SNPs were available, we used the inverse-variance weighted (IVW) method. Multiple testing correction was performed using the Bonferroni method, with significance defined as P < 0.05/ N , where N is the number of CpG sites tested. To assess potential horizontal pleiotropy and heterogeneity, we performed MR-Egger intercept tests and Cochran’s Q tests when at least three IVs were available. These procedures were implemented to ensure the robustness and validity of the causal inferences.

Significant CpG sites identified from the mQTL–MR analyses were mapped to genes using the annotation file provided by the GEO platform ( https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo , GPL13534 , Illumina HumanMethylation450 BeadChip), which assigns CpG sites to genes based on genomic context (e.g., transcription start site [TSS]1500, 5’ untranslated region [5’UTR], 3’UTR]). For CpG sites lacking annotations in this resource, ANNOVAR ( http://www.openbioinformatics.org/annovar/ ) was employed to annotate them to the nearest genes [].

To refine candidate genes mapped from significant CpG sites, we implemented a multi-step gene prioritization framework comprising five complementary analyses. First, we.

performed colocalization analysis between mQTL and migraine (and its subtypes) using the coloc R package (Version 5.2.3, https://github.com/chr1swallace/coloc ), considering all genetic variants within ± 500 kb of each CpG site. Colocalization assessed the posterior probabilities of five hypotheses: H0, no causal variants for either traits; H1, association with DNA methylation only; H2, association with migraine or its subtype only; H3, distinct causal variants for the two traits; and H4, both traits associated and sharing a single causal variant []. A posterior probability for H4 (PP.H4) ≥ 0.8 was regarded as strong evidence that methylation and migraine share the same causal variant. Second, we conducted two-sample MR analyses using brain and blood eQTL datasets as exposures (i.e., eQTL–MR) to test whether genetically regulated gene expression influences migraine risk. Statistical significance for these analyses was defined at the nominal threshold of P < 0.05. Third, we performed colocalization between eQTL signals and migraine GWAS within TSS ± 500 kb for all candidate genes mapped from significant CpG sites, with PP.H4 ≥ 0.8 regarded as strong evidence of colocalization. Fourth, to evaluate whether the effect of DNA methylation on migraine is mediated through gene expression, we restricted the analysis to CpG sites that showed a significant causal association with migraine or its subtypes in the mQTL–MR analyses (used as exposures), and genes with nominally significant causal effects on migraine in the eQTL–MR analyses (used as mediators). We first estimated the causal effect of DNA methylation on gene expression, then incorporated the corresponding effect of gene expression on migraine from the eQTL–MR results. Indirect effects were quantified using the product of coefficients method, and the proportion mediated was calculated as the ratio of the indirect effect to the total effect. Statistical significance for the mediation pathways was determined using a Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons. Finally, we performed gene-based association testing on GWAS summary statistics for overall migraine as well as its two subtypes (MA and MO) using MAGMA (Version 1.09, https://cncr.nl/research/magma/ ) []. A total of 19,070 protein-coding genes were tested, and Bonferroni correction was applied to account for multiple comparisons. Genes surpassing the corrected threshold ( P < 0.05/19,070 = 2.62 × 10 − 6 ) were considered genome-wide significant. This analysis provided additional, genome-wide evidence to prioritize migraine risk genes, complementing the QTL-based approaches described above.

Based on these five analytical approaches, we defined prioritized genes in a three-tiered framework, reflecting the strength and integration of supporting evidence. Tier 1 genes were those identified by the two-step MR framework, which requires both significant mQTL–MR and eQTL–MR associations and further demonstrates that the effect of DNA methylation on migraine is mediated through gene expression. Tier 2 genes were those supported by at least three of the remaining four approaches (mQTL colocalization, eQTL–MR, eQTL colocalization, and gene-based association), indicating robust convergence across independent lines of evidence. Tier 3 genes consisted of candidates mapped from causal CpG sites in the mQTL–MR analysis but not meeting Tier 1 or Tier 2 criteria, representing preliminary yet weaker evidence.

To further investigate the biological relevance of the candidate risk genes identified from mQTL–MR analyses, we performed comprehensive functional characterization. Gene Ontology (GO) and Reactome pathway enrichment analyses were conducted using KOBAS-i ( http://bioinfo.org/kobas ) [], with multiple testing corrected using the Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) method ( q < 0.05). Tissue-specific enrichment was evaluated using the GENE2FUNC function in FUMA ( https://fuma.ctglab.nl/ ) [], utilizing GTEx v8 expression data from 30 tissue categories. Statistical significance for tissue-specific enrichment was determined using Bonferroni correction with a threshold of P < 0.05. To delineate functional networks, PPI analysis was carried out in STRING (Version 12.0, https://cn.string-db.org/ ), with a minimum interaction score of 0.4 to retain medium-to-high confidence interactions. The enrichment in interactions of the list of proteins is reflected by the probability of obtaining such a number of interactions by chance (PPI enrichment P -value). Cytoscape (Version 3.10.3, https://cytoscape.org/ ) [] was used for network visualization, and hub genes were prioritized via cytoHubba based on maximal clique centrality (MCC) scores []. Finally, potential therapeutic targets were explored by mapping drug–gene interactions through the DGIdb (Version 5.0.9, https://www.dgidb.org ) [, ], and further filtered against the GREP (Genome for REPositioning drugs) database (Version 1.0.0, https://github.com/saorisakaue/GREP ) [] to highlight compounds with established therapeutic or repositioning potential.
sections.results:
Utilizing brain mQTL data, we identified a total of 106 CpG sites (i.e. DNA methylation probes) that were causally associated with overall migraine after Bonferroni correction ( P < 0.05/ 183,827 = 2.72 × 10 − 7 , Fig. a, Supplementary Table ). Among these, increased methylation at 52 CpG sites was associated with a reduced risk of overall migraine, whereas increased methylation at the remaining 54 sites was linked to an elevated risk. The most significant association was observed at cg10233454 (Odds Ratio [ OR ] = 0.865, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.847–0.884, P = 1.32 × 10 − 40 ), followed by cg16766632 ( OR = 0.770, 95% CI: 0.740–0.802, P = 1.24 × 10 − 36 ), both of which are located within the gene body of LRP1 . These 106 significant sites were annotated to 50 genes (Supplementary Table ), with 14 genes were mapped by more than three CpG sites, including ARTN, CALCA, CFDP1, HEY2, INPP5B, LINC02523, LRP1, MANEAL, MEF2D, MIR9-1HG, MRVI1, PRDM16, STAT6 and TRPM8 .

Using blood mQTL data, we identified 97 CpG sites that showed significant causal effects on overall migraine ( P < 2.72 × 10 − 7 , Fig. b, Supplementary Table ). The most significant association was again observed at cg10233454 in LRP1 ( OR = 0.816, 95% CI: 0.791–0.841, P = 4.20 × 10 − 39 ), followed by cg15470658 ( OR = 0.764, 95% CI: 0.733–0.796, P = 2.73 × 10 − 37 ). These 97 significant sites were annotated to 51 genes, among which 17 genes were mapped by more than three sites, including ABHD16A, ACTRT2, B4GALT2, CALCA, CFDP1, FHL3, HEY2, LY6G5C, MANEAL, MEF2D, MIR130A, MIR9-1HG, MRVI1, PRDM16, SERPING1, TRPM8 , and TTC34 (Supplementary Table ). Of note, PRDM16 was annotated by the largest number of CpG sites ( n = 17).

By integrating the results from brain- and blood-based analyses, a total of 169 unique CpG sites were identified as exerting causal effects on overall migraine, annotated to 68 candidate risk genes. The majority of these sites were located within the gene body, followed by intergenic regions and TSS1500 regions. Importantly, 34 CpG sites showed significant associations with overall migraine in both brain and blood datasets, of which 33 demonstrated consistent directions of effect across the two tissues (Fig. c).

We further conducted stratified MR analyses by migraine subtype. For MA, one significant CpG site was identified in brain mQTL data and five in blood mQTL data, annotated to three genes, namely RSPO2,CNRIP1 , and CACNA1A (Fig. , Supplementary Tables –). The most significant association was observed for cg03242834 in blood, annotated to CACNA1A ( OR = 1.271, 95% CI: 1.166–1.384, P = 3.96 × 10 − 8 ). For MO, 17 CpG sites were detected in brain mQTL data and nine in blood mQTL data (Fig. , Supplementary Table ), annotated to seven genes: MEF2D, TRPM8, KIAA0776, STAT6, LRP1, MAPT, and IQGAP3 (Supplementary Table ). Notably, all six CpG sites identified for MA (cg24891846, cg11660879, cg18060171, cg06059616, cg03242834, cg24171907) were not detected in the overall migraine analysis, suggesting that their associated genes ( CNRIP1, CACNA1A , and RSPO2 ) may be specific to MA. Similarly, cg26163368 annotated to MAPT , which was identified for MO, was absent from the overall migraine findings, highlighting potential subtype-specific effects.

In total, we identified 72 unique genes associated with migraine across overall and subtype-stratified analyses, comprising 68 genes from the integrated brain- and blood-based analyses and four additional subtype-specific genes ( RSPO2, CNRIP1, CACNA1A , and MAPT ).

Of the 203 CpG sites identified from brain and blood mQTL–MR analyses, 106 (~ 52%) exhibited strong evidence of colocalization with overall migraine GWAS signals (PP.H4 ≥ 0.8), corresponding to 55 out of 68 mapped genes (Supplementary Table ). For instance, the CpG sites cg08130307 in brain tissue, annotated to FALEC and ADAMTSL4 , exhibited the strongest colocalization signal (PP.H4 = 1.000), with rs6693567 being the most likely causal variant (Fig. a). Subtype-specific analyses revealed that 2 out of 6 CpG sites for MA and 12 out of 26 for MO, respectively, colocalized with their corresponding subtype GWAS signals, with cg24171907 ( CNRIP1 ; PP.H4 = 0.946) for MA and cg10233454 ( LRP1 ; PP.H4 = 0.994) for MO showing the strongest signals (Supplementary Table ).

Using brain and blood eQTL datasets, we next performed two-sample MR to investigate whether genetically regulated gene expression influences migraine risk. This analysis identified 20 distinct genes with causal effects on overall migraine (16 based on brain eQTL data and 14 based on blood eQTL data), with 10 genes shared across both tissues (Supplementary Table ). Subtype analyses further revealed that expression of CACNA1A in blood was causally associated with MA, and STAT6 expression in blood was causally associated with MO (Fig. b, Supplementary Table ). Colocalization analyses between eQTL signals and migraine GWAS were performed within ± 500 kb of TSS of the mQTL–MR significant genes. The expression levels of nine genes displayed strong evidence of colocalization with overall migraine, including UTP11, SERPING1, RNF213, LY6G5C, FHL3, CFDP1, DOT1L, ICA1L , and HEY2 , with LY6G5C showing the strongest signal (PP.H4 = 0.999). Subtype-specific colocalization was also observed: the expression of DOT1L colocalized with MA, whereas the expression of UTP11 and FHL3 colocalized with MO (Supplementary Table ).

By pairing CpG sites identified through mQTL–MR with genes from eQTL–MR across brain and blood tissues, we constructed CpG–gene–migraine mediation pathways. Among these, 357 pathways had valid instruments to test the intermediate step from DNA methylation to gene expression, and were subsequently evaluated in the two-step MR framework, with the Bonferroni-corrected threshold set at P < 1.40 × 10⁻⁴ (0.05/357). For overall migraine, we identified 87 putative causal mediation pathways involving 54 unique CpG sites and 11 mediator genes (Supplementary Table ). For example, decreased methylation at cg13521797 increased ICA1L expression, which in turn elevated overall migraine risk ( β = − 0.087, P = 2.82 × 10 − 8 , mediated proportion = 97.2%, Fig. a). Similarly, CFDP1 mediated the effect of cg10425698 on overall migraine ( β = 0.104, P = 4.76 × 10 − 8 , mediated proportion = 87.5%, Fig. b), and FHL3 mediated the effect of cg03103611 on overall migraine ( β = 0.103, P = 1.32 × 10 − 6 , mediated proportion = 81.8%, Fig. c). For the subtypes, seven mediation pathways were identified for MO, all involving STAT6 as the mediator (Supplementary Table ), while no significant mediation were detected for MA.

Finally, gene-based association testing using MAGMA identified 63 genome-wide significant risk genes for overall migraine ( P < 2.62 × 10 − 6 ), four for MA and twelve for MO (Fig. d, Supplementary Table ). Integrating the results from mQTL colocalization, eQTL–MR, eQTL colocalization, two-step MR and MAGMA, we prioritized 12 Tier 1 high-confidence genes, 22 Tier 2 genes, and 38 Tier 3 genes (Supplementary Table ). Among these, CFDP1, ICA1L and SERPING1 was supported across all five analytical approaches (Fig. e), and seven Tier 1 genes ( CCDC30, FHL3, DOT1L, NOC3L, LY6G5C, IPO13 , and WDR12 ) emerged as novel candidates not previously implicated in genetic studies of migraine.

Based on the 72 unique genes identified from the mQTL–MR analyses, enrichment analysis revealed significant associations with 30 GO terms and 4 Reactome pathways (Fig. a, Supplementary Table ), including calcitonin-like ligand receptors (FDR q = 0.021), negative regulation of excitatory postsynaptic potential (FDR q = 0.021) and axon development (FDR q = 0.024), highlighting biological processes central to synaptic transmission and neuronal development. Tissue-specific enrichment analysis showed significant enrichment in brain and pancreas (Fig. b, Supplementary Table ).

The PPI network comprised of 54 nodes and 200 edges (PPI enrichment P < 1.0 × 10 − 16 ) (Fig. c). Central nodes such as LY6G6C and LY6G5B displayed the highest degree (degree = 22), suggesting their key roles as core members in the network. Hub analysis using MCC approach further prioritized LY6G6C, LY6G5B, LY6G6E, LY6G6F, and LY6L as the top-ranked hub proteins.

To further evaluate their therapeutic potential, drug–gene interaction analysis revealed that 16 of the 72 genes were targeted by 67 drugs (Supplementary Table ). The strongest interaction score was observed between ASTN2 and isoniazid (score = 5.8; Fig. d). Among these, MAPT showed the highest number of unique drug interactions ( n = 33), followed by CALCA ( n = 9), underscoring their potential as therapeutic targets or candidates for drug repositioning.
sections.discussion:
To our knowledge, this is the first study to investigate the causal role of DNA methylation in migraine and its subtypes by integrating large-scale mQTL and GWAS datasets. We identified 169 CpG sites with significant causal effects on overall migraine, which were mapped to 68 candidate genes. Notably, 33 CpG sites were supported by both brain and blood mQTL datasets with consistent directions of effect, underscoring the robustness of these associations. Subtype-stratified analyses revealed distinct associations, with RSPO2, CNRIP1 , and CACNA1A implicated in MA and MAPT in MO, highlighting heterogeneity across clinical subtypes. We further defined 12 high-confidence genes, of which seven represent novel candidates. Collectively, the identified CpG sites and prioritized genes represent promising targets for functional validation and may inform the development of novel therapeutic strategies for migraine prevention and treatment.

By integrating evidence from brain- and blood-based mQTL datasets, we identified 169 CpG sites exerting causal effects on migraine risk, which were annotated to 68 candidate risk genes. Notably, cg10233454, located within the body region of LRP1 , exhibited the most significant causal effect in both brain and blood analyses. LRP1 encodes a low-density lipoprotein receptor family member, its precursor protein is cleaved by furin into 515 kDa and 85 kDa subunits, which together assemble into the mature receptor []. Prior studies have highlighted the critical involvement of LRP1 in migraine pathophysiology [, , ]. In addition, PRDM16 was annotated by the greatest number of causal CpG sites, and its relevance to migraine has been supported by independent genetic studies [, ].

Subtype-specific MR analyses for MA and MO revealed distinct DNA methylation signatures that were not captured in the overall migraine analysis. This underscores that treating migraine as a single entity may obscure subtype-specific signals and emphasizes the need to dissect molecular mechanisms according to clinical subtype. For MA, three genes— CNRIP1, CACNA1A , and RSPO2 —were uniquely associated, absent from both the overall migraine and MO analyses. CNRIP1 and RSPO2 , predominantly expressed in brain tissue, have not been previously implicated in migraine, pointing to novel neuronal signaling pathways potentially contributing to MA-specific pathophysiology. CACNA1A , which encodes the alpha-1 A subunit of the P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channel, represents a well-established susceptibility gene in familial hemiplegic migraine [] and episodic ataxia []. Our findings are consistent with previous studies, suggesting that CACNA1A is specially associated with MA [, ]. For MO, MAPT emerged as a subtype-specific gene, it encodes tau, a key regulator of microtubule stability and axonal transport, and has been implicated in several neurodegenerative disorders, such as Alzheimer’s disease [], Pick’s disease [], and frontotemporal dementia []. These findings highlight the value of subtype-specific analyses in uncovering biologically relevant genes and provide insight into distinct epigenetic pathways underlying migraine heterogeneity.

Our tiered gene prioritization analysis yielded a refined catalog of candidate genes that integrates evidence from multiple complementary strategies, including mQTL colocalization, eQTL–MR, eQTL colocalization, two-step MR, and gene-based association testing. This framework reduces reliance on any single method and enhances the robustness of causal inference. Among the prioritized genes, CFDP1, ICA1L and SERPING1 were supported by all five approaches, highlighting their strong candidacy as a migraine susceptibility gene. In addition, we identified 12 Tier 1 genes through two-step MR mediation, of which seven— CCDC30, FHL3, DOT1L, NOC3L, LY6G5C, IPO13 , and WDR12 —represent novel findings not previously linked to migraine. These genes may contribute to migraine pathogenesis through various mechanisms such as ribosome rescue, RNA binding, signal transduction, and regulation of neural function. For example, NOC3L , which enables RNA binding activity and is predicted to be involved in DNA replication initiation, has been reported to be associated with brain resting-state networks []. DOT1L , the protein encoded by this gene, is a histone methyltransferase that methylates lysine-79 of histone H3 []. It plays a key role in regulating the proliferation and differentiation of neural progenitor cells and modulating synaptic function, and dysregulation of DOT1L has been linked to multiple neurological disorders []. Subtype-specific prioritization further uncovered distinct patterns, with DOT1L colocalizing with MA signals and FHL3 with MO, suggesting mechanistic heterogeneity between migraine subtypes.

Functional enrichment analysis revealed that the candidate risk genes were significantly involved in calcitonin-like ligand receptors. This finding is consistent with previous studies recognizing the neuropeptide calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) as a critical mediator in migraine pathophysiology [–]. Tissue-specific enrichment was strongest in the brain and pancreas, reflecting the interplay between neurovascular regulation and metabolic–endocrine pathways that are increasingly recognized in migraine biology [, ]. These molecular pathways may also represent potential targets through which environmental influences exert their effects on brain function and disease vulnerability. Recent advances in environmental neuroscience have highlighted that cumulative environmental exposures across the life course—the exposome—can shape brain structure and function via both genetic and epigenetic mechanisms []. In line with this concept, growing evidence shows that environmental factors such as air pollution, urbanicity, and psychosocial stress can modulate neural and molecular pathways related to inflammation and oxidative stress []. Furthermore, druggability analysis revealed 45 potential drug–gene interaction pairs, underscoring opportunities for therapeutic translation and drug repositioning. Together, these findings reinforce the biological plausibility of the prioritized genes identified by our MR framework and provide a mechanistically informed set of candidates for future functional validation and therapeutic development in migraine.

Several limitations of this study should be acknowledged. First, all GWAS, mQTL, and eQTL datasets used in this analysis were derived from individuals of European ancestry, which may restrict the generalizability of our findings to other populations with distinct genetic architectures. Future studies in non-European cohorts will be essential to evaluate the transferability of the identified CpG sites and risk genes. Second, although MR minimizes confounding and reverse causation, it cannot completely eliminate potential biases such as horizontal pleiotropy, measurement error in QTL estimates, or weak instrument bias, which may influence the robustness of causal inferences. Third, our analyses were restricted to CpG sites and gene expression measured in bulk tissues (brain cortex and whole blood), which may obscure cell-type–specific regulatory mechanisms that are critical in the pathogenesis of migraine. Single-cell multi-omics data could provide more granular insights in future research. Fourth, although we integrated multiple prioritization approaches—including colocalization, eQTL–MR, two-step MR, and MAGMA—some genes were supported by limited lines of evidence, meaning their prioritization should be interpreted with caution. Fifth, it should be noted that this study focuses specifically on DNA methylation and does not incorporate other epigenetic mechanisms, such as histone modifications, chromatin remodeling, or non-coding RNA regulation, which may also contribute to migraine pathophysiology. Future studies integrating multiple layers of epigenetic regulation will be essential to obtain a more comprehensive understanding of the epigenomic mechanisms underlying migraine and its subtypes. Finally, the functional characterization of candidate risk genes was based on bioinformatic enrichment, protein–protein interaction, and drug–gene interaction analyses, which provide valuable hypotheses but require experimental validation. Further mechanistic studies in cellular and animal models, as well as pharmacological investigations, will be necessary to confirm the causal roles of these genes and assess their therapeutic potential.

In summary, by integrating large-scale mQTL and GWAS datasets, our study provides robust evidence that DNA methylation exerts causal effects on migraine risk and identifies a set of candidate genes with biological and therapeutic relevance. Through a comprehensive prioritization strategy, we highlighted several high-confidence genes, including subtype-specific signals that underscore the heterogeneous molecular architecture of migraine with and without aura. Functional enrichment analyses revealed involvement in calcitonin-like ligand receptors, axon development and neurovascular regulation, while drug–gene interaction screening pointed to potential opportunities for therapeutic development. Collectively, these findings establish DNA methylation as a mechanistic bridge between genetic risk and migraine pathophysiology, expand the catalog of migraine-associated genes, and provide new directions for biomarker discovery and precision medicine.

title: Ketogenic diet in refractory migraine: possible efficacy and role of ketone bodies-a pilot experience.
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Refractory migraine is a particularly disabling form of chronic migraine, unresponsive to multiple prophylactic strategies. Ketogenic diet (KD) is useful to treat migraine but poorly tested for refractory migraine. OBJECTIVE: We started exploring the efficacy and safety of KD, as compared to a non-ketogenic dietary regimen similar in reduction of carbohydrate intake (low-carb diet, LCD), in refractory migraine. Secondary objective was to explore whether ketones have a role in the prophylaxis induced by KD on migraine. RESULTS: In a first trial, 22 patients with refractory migraine were included and completed the study. Thirteen (mean age 36.8 ± 12.9 years, 11 females, 2 males) were assigned to the KD arm and eight (mean age 50.9 ± 10.8 years; all females), not eligible for KD, to LCD. Patients treated with KD showed a significant reduction in the frequency of migraine attacks, intensity of headache, and amount of drug intake. No significant benefit was seen in the LCD group. A relationship between ketone production and effect on headache was observed among patients with a good response to KD. In a second study, additional 31 refractory migraineurs were treated with these two dietary regimens, 26 with the same KD scheme and 5 with a LCD. Results were comparable with those of the first study. CONCLUSIONS: KD might be a useful option in refractory migraine. Ketones seem to have a role in migraine modulation and their regular measurement might be useful to monitor KD in migraineurs. Larger, randomized, and controlled trials are needed to confirm these data.

title: Resistance training for migraine in females: mechanistic review of hormonal, CGRP, autonomic, vascular and nociceptive pathways.
abstract: Migraine is the second leading cause of years lived with disability worldwide and disproportionately affects women, in whom the disorder tends to be more frequent, longer-lasting and functionally more disabling than in men. This female preponderance, which emerges after menarche, is tightly linked to changes in estrogen levels, reproductive phases and sex-specific responsiveness of the trigeminovascular and calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) systems. Against this backdrop, non-pharmacological interventions that modulate the same physiological processes involved in migraine are particularly attractive. Resistance training (RT) has emerged from recent systematic reviews and network meta-analyses as one of the exercise modalities with the largest effect sizes on monthly migraine frequency, yet its mechanistic rationale in women is rarely addressed as a coherent biological argument. In this narrative review we integrate the pathophysiology of migraine in females with the adaptations induced by structured RT across four convergent axes: autonomic regulation, neurovascular and endothelial function, systemic and neurogenic inflammation, and endogenous pain modulation. We interpret the current clinical evidence in light of these mechanisms, outline how the hormonal milieu in females may shape individual responsiveness, and propose a translational framework for prescribing RT as part of a comprehensive, sex-informed migraine management plan. We explicitly distinguish between robust findings, emerging signals and hypotheses that remain to be tested, and highlight the main methodological barriers that should be addressed before RT can be firmly embedded in clinical guidelines for women with migraine.

title: A comparison of the effects of greater occipital nerve blockade and combined greater occipital-supraorbital nerve blockade on headache in chronic migraine.
abstract: ObjectiveTo evaluate and compare the effects of isolated greater occipital nerve (GON) blockade versus combined GON-supraorbital nerve (SON) blockade on headache severity, frequency, duration, and quality of life in patients with chronic migraine.MethodsThis retrospective study included 80 patients with CM who had not responded to adequate medical prophylaxis. Forty patients received isolated GON blockade, while the remaining 40 received combined GON-SON blockade. Nerve blockades were administered weekly during the first month and monthly for the subsequent two months. Headache frequency, duration, severity, analgesic use, and scores on the Migraine Disability Assessment Scale (MIDAS) and Headache Impact Test-6 (HIT-6) were recorded at baseline (month 0) and after treatment (month 3). Outcomes were analyzed both within and between groups.ResultsBoth groups showed significant improvements from baseline to post-treatment (weeks 1-3, month 1, and month 3) in attack frequency, duration, VAS pain scores, analgesic use, and MIDAS and HIT-6 scores (p ConclusionBoth blockade treatment approaches resulted in clinical improvement in patients with chronic migraine. However, the combined GON and SON blockade demonstrated more favorable outcomes than GON blockade in terms of headache burden and quality of life during specific follow-up periods. this is the first study to directly compare these two treatment modalities in patients with CM.

title: Effectiveness and tolerability of pharmacological prophylaxis in migraine patients with prior preventive treatment failure: A systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
abstract: BackgroundDespite advances in migraine management, some patients fail to respond to preventive treatments for migraine. We aimed to assess the comparative effects of available pharmacological prophylaxis in adults with a treatment failure history.MethodsWe searched Medline, Embase, Cochrane Central, PsycINFO, Web of Science, and Scopus up to July 2025. Pairs of reviewers independently screened titles, abstracts, and full-text articles to identify randomized controlled trials of prophylactic pharmacological interventions that enrolled adults diagnosed with chronic or episodic migraine and a prior preventive treatment failure. We performed a frequentist random-effects network meta-analysis and used the GRADE approach to assess the certainty of evidence.ResultsWe included 18 randomized trials (7281 participants). Compared to placebo, low certainty evidence suggest fremanezumab [mean difference (MD) -3.30 (95% CI: -4.11 to -2.49)], eptinezumab [MD -3.35 (95% CI: -4.38 to -2.32)], galcanezumab [MD -2.73 (95% CI: -3.43 to -2.03)], atogepant [MD -2.30 (95% CI: -3.47 to -1.13)], and erenumab [MD -2.20 (95% CI: -2.72 to -1.68)] may be among the most effective in reducing the monthly migraine headache days. Low to moderate certainty evidence suggests that, compared with placebo, galcanezumab [relative risk (RR) 1.94 (95% CI: 1.52 to 2.48)], fremanezumab [RR 3.98 (95% CI: 2.40 to 6.59)], atogepant [RR 2.80 (95% CI: 1.73 to 4.54)], erenumab [RR 2.56 (95% CI: 2.01 to 3.26)], and eptinezumab [RR 2.35 (95% CI: 1.61 to 3.42)] may increase the likelihood of achieving a 50% response rate.ConclusionEvidence for migraine patients with prior preventive treatment failure is limited. Low- to moderate-certainty data suggest that CGRP-targeted therapies may provide some benefit and are generally tolerable, but the available evidence is driven by a few industry-sponsored trials. Additional independent, well-powered studies with longer follow-up are needed to strengthen the evidence base.Registration numberPROSPERO (CRD42024547860).

title: Migraine susceptibility is modulated by food triggers and analgesic overuse via sulfotransferase inhibition.
abstract: BACKGROUND/AIM: Certain constituents in migraine food triggers and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) inhibit sulfotransferases (SULTs) that detoxify drugs/chemicals and play role in the metabolism of neurotransmitters. We aimed to dissect SULT1A1 modulation of CSD susceptibility and behavior in an in vivo experimental model using hesperidin, a SULT1A1 inhibitor found in citrus fruits (known migraine triggers) and mefenamic acid (SULT1A1 inhibitor), an NSAID to simulate medication overuse. METHODS: Hesperidin was used as SULT1A1 inhibitor found in citrus fruits, known migraine triggers and mefenamic acid (NSAID), another SULT1A1 inhibitor, was used to induce MO in rats. The groups were; 1) Hesperidin (ip) or its vehicle-DMSO (ip) 2) Chronic (4 weeks) mefenamic acid (ip) or its vehicle (ip) 3) Chronic mefenamic acid+hesperidin (ip) or DMSO (ip). CSD susceptibility was evaluated and behavioral testing was performed. SULT1A1 enzyme activity was measured in brain samples. RESULTS: Single-dose of hesperidin neither changed CSD susceptibility nor resulted in any behavioral change. Chronic mefenamic acid exposure resulted in increased CSD susceptibility, mechanical-thermal hypersensitivity, increased head shake, grooming and freezing and decreased locomotion. Single dose hesperidin administration after chronic mefenamic acid exposure resulted in increased CSD susceptibility and mechanical-thermal hypersensitivity, increased freezing and decreased locomotion. SULT1A1 enzyme activity was lower in mefenamic acid and mefenamic acid+hesperidin groups compared to their vehicles. CONCLUSION: Mefenamic acid and hesperidin have synergistic effect in modulating CSD susceptibility and pain behavior. Sulfotransferase inhibition may be the common mechanism by which food triggers and NSAIDs modulate migraine susceptibility. Further investigations regarding human provocation studies using hesperidin in migraine patients with medication overuse are needed.

sections.other:
Migraine is a neurovascular disorder with recurrent headache attacks and signs and symptoms of hypersensitivity to mutiple sensory stimuli accompanying these attacks. It is triggered by various factors in genetically susceptible individuals. Headache attacks are accompanied by nausea and vomiting and hypersensitivity to visual, auditory, olfactory and tactile stimuli. Medication overuse usually underlies the chronification of migraine and medication overuse headache affects approximately 1–2% of the population [].

It is known that stress, noise, hunger, insomnia and various foods such as chocolate, citrus, coffee, tea and red wine trigger migraine. Although migraine food triggers are well defined, it is still not shown how they start a migraine attack. Some substances in these migraine triggers inhibit a group of enzymes known as sulfotransferases. Sulfotransferases are involved in detoxification of drugs, chemicals and metabolism of neurotransmitters. For example, quercetin and catechin in chocolate, hesperidin in orange and lemon, quinic and caffeic acids in coffee, epicatechin gallate in tea and red wine cause inhibition in SULT1A1 and SULT1A3 enzymes []. SULT1A enzymes are also involved in the metabolism of hormones and neurotransmitters such as catecholamines especially dopamine. Several previous studies have shown decreased sulfotransferase activities in platelets in migraine patients [–]. Littlewood et al. reported that sulfotransferase activity in platelets was lower in migraine patients who had a history of migraine attacks with migraine food triggers compared to non-dietary migraine and healthy controls []. Migraine triggers could initiate a migraine attack by inhibiting SULT1A enzymes, which have a role in deactivation of neurotransmitters, thus, inhibition of these enzymes would cause the levels of neurotransmitters such as cathecolamines including dopamine to fluctuate and may alter migraine susceptibility.

Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) used in acute migraine attacks such as mefenamic acid, diflunisal, nimesulide, diclofenac, salicylic acid, ketoprofen, indomethacin, ibuprofen, ketorolac and naproxen have also been shown to inhibit SULT1A1 enzymes []. Medication overuse usually occurs in migraine patients. Medication overuse by inhibiting these enzymes could make the migraine patients more susceptible to triggers and triggers even in subthreshold amounts could result in chronic daily headache.

Cortical hyperexcitability has been shown in animal models of medication overuse headache (MOH). When cortical spreading depression (CSD) is induced with topical KCl 1 hour after acute paracetamol (200 mg/kg, intraperitoneal) administration, c-fos activation was reduced in the parietal cortex and trigeminal nucleus caudalis (TNC) but CSD frequency was not altered whereas, chronic paracetamol administration (200 mg/kg daily dose for 30 days, intraperitoneal) caused an increase in c-fos activation and CSD frequency []. CSD threshold was also shown to be reduced in another animal model of MOH where sumatriptan was administered by a subcutaneous pump for 6 days []. In another experimental study using functional magnetic resonance imaging in rats, after 7 days of sumatriptan administration with osmotic minipumps, bright light stress produced CSD-like responses in sumatriptan group but not in the control group []. Medication overuse may increase the sensitivity of migraine patients to triggers, worsen the headache attacks and increase the headache frequency and since both NSAIDs and migraine food triggers inhibit SULT1A enzymes, SULT1A inhibition may be one of the underlying mechanisms for the modulation of migraine susceptibility by such food items and NSAIDs.

We hypothesized that SULT1A inhibition was the common mechanism by which food triggers and NSAIDs modulate migraine susceptibility, in a way that to explain food triggers of migraine attacks and medication overuse (MO) headache. Since both NSAIDs and food triggers inhibit SULT1A enzymes, in migraine patients with medication overuse, SULT1A involvement would cause increased susceptibility to triggers by changing cortical excitability where subthreshold triggers would be enough to cause headache. SULT1A3 is only found in primates and humans but not in rodents and other lower order animals [, ]. Therefore, we aimed to dissect SULT1A1 modulation of CSD susceptibility and behavior in an in vivo experimental model using hesperidin, a SULT1A1 inhibitor found in citrus fruits (known migraine triggers) and mefenamic acid (SULT1A1 inhibitor), an NSAID to simulate medication overuse.
