sections.methods:
This study strictly adhered to the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology using Mendelian Randomization (STROBE-MR) guidelines [, ] (see Additional file 1: Table). To explore the potential causal relationship between gut microbiota abundance and chronic pain, and to evaluate the mediating role of brain structural connectivity, the study was conducted in four stages. In the first stage, we assessed the causal effects of genetic variants associated with gut microbiota abundance on 15 chronic pain phenotypes, as well as the reverse causal effects of chronic pain on gut microbial taxa with potential associations. In the second stage, we examined the causal effects of genetic variants related to brain structural connectivity on the same chronic pain phenotypes, together with the reverse causal effects of chronic pain on brain structural connectivity traits showing potential associations. In the third stage, we assessed the potential causal effects of gut microbiota-related genetic variants on brain structural connectivity. In the fourth stage, a mediation model was constructed to evaluate the mediating role of brain structural connectivity in the gut–brain axis pathway influencing chronic pain, thereby revealing the causal involvement of the gut–brain axis in the pathogenesis of chronic pain. The analytical framework of this study is illustrated in Fig. .

The MiBioGen consortium hosts one of the most comprehensive GWAS datasets linking host genetics to the gut microbiome, providing SNP-level data related to gut microbial traits. The study includes 24 cohorts from 11 countries or regions, encompassing diverse ethnic backgrounds, with a total of 18,340 participants of European ancestry []. Researchers collected 16S rRNA gene sequencing and genotyping data from these individuals to investigate the associations between human autosomal genetic variants and gut microbiota composition. The analysis focused on 211 taxonomic units across five taxonomic ranks: 9 phyla, 16 classes, 20 orders, 35 families, and 131 genera. After excluding 15 taxa that were unclassified at the family or genus level, a total of 196 microbial traits were retained for further analysis.

Human brain structural connectivity data, derived from DTI, is obtained from the GWAS database ( https://www.ebi.ac.uk/gwas ), with study accession numbers ranging from GCST90302648 to GCST90302853. This dataset, assembled by Wainberg et al., integrates DTI imaging data from 26,333 participants in the UK Biobank, encompassing 206 phenotypes related to the brain’s structural connectome, specifically focusing on white matter structural connectome phenotypes []. The study quantitatively assesses white matter fiber density and connectivity between paired brain regions across 214 brain areas, which include 200 cortical subdivisions as delineated by the Schaefer atlas and 14 subcortical regions as identified by the Harvard–Oxford atlas. Following this, a GWAS was conducted to investigate the relationship between the 206 indices of white matter structural connectivity and 9,423,516 genetic variants identified within the UK Biobank. The 206 connectivity indices are classified into three categories: (1) three hemisphere-level connectivity indices, which include left hemisphere connectivity, right hemisphere connectivity, and interhemispheric connectivity; (2) 105 network-level connectivity indices that assess white matter structural connectivity across seven functional networks in both hemispheres. Among these, fourteen indices pertain to white matter connectivity within the networks, while 91 indices pertain to connectivity between networks. These measurements are based on 14 large-scale brain networks that encompass both hemispheres, collectively referred to as the "Yeo 7" network [], which includes the visual network (VN), somatomotor network (SN), dorsal attention network (DAN), SAN/VAN, limbic network (LN), control network (CN), and DMN; (3) cortical-subcortical connectivity indices, totaling 98, which involve white matter connectivity between seven functional networks in both hemispheres and seven subcortical structures, namely the thalamus, caudate, putamen, pallidum, hippocampus, amygdala, and accumbens.

To avoid sample overlap, genomic data for 15 chronic pain subtypes were obtained from the FinnGen consortium (version 11) []. The specific subtypes of chronic pain and their corresponding participant characteristics are summarized in Table . It is noteworthy that the data utilized in this study are derived from publicly accessible GWAS, and all individuals included have obtained ethical approval from their respective institutions, thereby negating the necessity for additional informed consent or ethical approval.

In MR analysis, instrumental variables (IVs) [] representing genetic variations must satisfy three key assumptions: (1) relevance assumption, which requires that the genetic IVs be significantly associated with the exposure; (2) independence assumption, which states that the genetic IVs must be independent of potential confounding factors to prevent bias in the identified associations; (3) exclusion assumption, which ensures that the genetic IVs influence the outcome solely through the exposure. To satisfy the relevance assumption, a significance threshold of P < 5 × 10⁻⁸ was initially employed to identify SNPs associated with gut microbiota abundance and brain structural connectivity. However, given the limited number of SNPs meeting this threshold, additional thresholds were introduced to enhance the robustness of the analysis. Based on the suggestions of previous studies, we relaxed the significance threshold for gut microbiota-associated SNPs to P < 1 × 10⁻ 5 [], for brain structural connectivity-associated SNPs to P < 5 × 10⁻⁶ [], and for chronic pain subtype-associated SNPs to P < 5 × 10⁻⁶. Furthermore, to improve the accuracy of the analysis, SNPs in linkage disequilibrium (LD) were removed to retain the most representative variants. LD refers to the non-random association of alleles at different loci, where their co-occurrence probability exceeds that predicted by random distribution. To control for LD, a clumping window size of 10,000 kb and R 2 < 0.001 were set as filtering criteria. This step was crucial in minimizing redundancy among selected SNPs and ensuring the independence of IVs. Finally, to satisfy the independence and exclusion assumptions, LDlink ( https://ldlink.nih.gov/?tab=home ) was used to identify SNPs potentially influenced by confounding factors such as body mass index (BMI), age, and sex, thereby minimizing their potential impact on the study outcomes. Additionally, the F-statistic for each SNP was calculated to assess the strength of the IVs. SNPs with F-statistics < 10 were excluded to reduce bias arising from weak instruments. The F-statistic was computed as F = β 2 /se 2 , where β represents the effect size of the exposure-associated SNP, and se denotes the standard error.

Mediation analysis plays a crucial role in assessing the mediating effects of exposure on outcomes in causal inference. Therefore, this study employs mediation analysis to investigate whether brain structural connectivity mediates the relationship between gut microbiota abundance and chronic pain. Specifically, mediation MR analysis consists of three primary stages. In the first stage, TSMR analysis is conducted to evaluate the association between gut microbial abundance and chronic pain. Significant results ( P < 0.05) are denoted by the beta value (β_total), representing the total effect of gut microbiota abundance on chronic pain. In the second stage, TSMR analysis is performed to assess the association between brain structural connectivity and chronic pain, where significant results ( P < 0.05) are denoted by β_b, representing the direct effect of brain structural connectivity on chronic pain. Additionally, In the third stage TSMR analysis is employed to evaluate the relationship between significantly positive gut microbiota abundance and brain structural connectivity, where significant results are indicated by β_a, reflecting the effect of gut microbiota abundance on brain structural connectivity. This study utilizes a two-step MR approach for mediation analysis, calculating the mediation effect using the product-of-coefficients method (β_a × β_b). The proportion of the mediation effect is subsequently determined as the ratio of the mediation effect to the total effect [(β_a × β_b)/β_total].

In this study, multiple MR methods were employed, including Weighted Mode [], Weighted Median [], MR Egger [], IVW [], and Simple Mode, with IVW serving as the primary analytical method. Results were considered statistically significant and retained for further analysis when the IVW estimate reached the nominal threshold ( P < 0.05) and showed a consistent effect direction across all five MR methods. For the primary MR results, Bonferroni correction was applied to account for multiple testing, calculated as 0.05 divided by the number of exposures tested in each analysis stage ( P < 0.05/ n ) []. The Bonferroni-adjusted significance thresholds were as follows: for gut microbiota—phylum level: 5.56 × 10⁻ 3 (0.05/9), class: 3.13 × 10⁻ 3 (0.05/16), order: 2.50 × 10⁻ 3 (0.05/20), family: 1.56 × 10⁻ 3 (0.05/32), genus: 4.20 × 10⁻ 4 (0.05/119); for brain structural connectivity: 2.43 × 10⁻ 4 (0.05/206). Causal associations were considered statistically significant when the IVW P -value was below the Bonferroni threshold and no evidence of horizontal pleiotropy or heterogeneity was detected. Associations with P -values < 0.05 but exceeding the Bonferroni threshold, while passing all sensitivity analyses, were classified as indicative associations, suggestive of potential causal effects [, ]. Additionally, a series of sensitivity analyses were conducted to ensure the robustness of the findings, including heterogeneity tests, pleiotropy tests, and leave-one-out analyses. For the heterogeneity test, Cochran’s Q test was employed to assess the degree of heterogeneity in the results []. A p-value greater than 0.05 indicated minimal heterogeneity. For the pleiotropy test, the MR-Egger intercept method and the MR Pleiotropy RESidual Sum and Outlier (MR-PRESSO) global test [] were used to evaluate the potential influence of other factors on the causal effect, thereby testing the exclusion hypothesis. An intercept that was not significantly different from zero ( P > 0.05) suggested the absence of directional pleiotropy. Furthermore, a leave-one-out analysis was conducted, involving the sequential removal of each IVs and the recalculation of the IVW estimate using the remaining IVs. This analysis assessed whether any specific SNP influenced the significance of the results, thus further validating the robustness of the findings. These analytical approaches collectively ensured a comprehensive and reliable investigation of the causal relationships in the data. All analyses were performed using R Studio software (version 4.3.2). Several R packages were employed during the analysis, including “TwoSampleMR” (version 0.6.6), “ieugwasr” (version 1.0.0), “data.table” (version 1.15.4), “MRPRESSO” (version 1.0), “dplyr” (version 1.1.4), “plyr” (version 1.8.9), and “forestploter” (version 1.1.1).
sections.results:
This study systematically evaluated the potential causal associations between the abundance of 196 gut microbial abundance as exposures and 15 chronic pain conditions as outcomes. The IVW method in MR was employed as the primary analytical approach to estimate the genetically predicted effects of gut microbiota abundance on the risk of chronic pain. A total of 101 gut microbiota–chronic pain pairs demonstrated potentially robust causal associations (see Forest Plot in Fig. ), with detailed results presented in Additional file 1: Table S5. Among them, 48 gut microbiotas were identified as potential risk factors, while 53 gut microbiotas were predicted to exert potential protective effects against chronic pain. Specifically, potential causal associations were observed between gut microbiota abundance and the following pain subtypes: 4 gut microbiotas with TN (Fig. a), 14 with PHN (Fig. b), 3 with small fiber neuropathy (Fig. c), 4 with diabetic neuropathy (Fig. d), 10 with sciatica (Fig. e), 5 with atypical facial pain (Fig. f), 4 with idiopathic peripheral autonomic neuropathy (Fig. g), 7 with intercostal neuropathy (Fig. h), 5 with thoracic spine pain (Fg. i), 6 with drug-induced polyneuropathy (Fig. j), 9 with alcohol-induced polyneuropathy (Fig. k), 8 with migraine (Fig. l), 12 with migraine with aura (Fig. m), 6 with migraine without aura (Fig. n), and 4 with cluster headache (Fig. o). The detailed results of the reverse MR analyses are provided in Additional file 1: Table S6.

Furthermore, six gut microbiota demonstrated bidirectional effects, showing both risk-increasing and protective associations depending on the chronic pain phenotype. For example, genetically predicted genus Parabacteroides was inversely associated with alcohol-induced polyneuropathy (IVW OR = 0.2285; 95% CI = 0.0588–0.8883; P = 0.0331), but positively associated with cluster headache (IVW OR = 2.0630; 95% CI = 1.0320–4.1243; P = 0.0405). Genus Candidatus Soleaferrea was associated with an increased risk of PHN (IVW OR = 1.8041; 95% CI = 1.0418–3.1242; P = 0.0352) but a decreased risk of migraine (IVW OR = 0.8989; 95% CI = 0.8120–0.9951; P = 0.0398). Similarly, genus Veillonella showed protective effects on PHN (IVW OR = 0.4256; 95% CI = 0.1881–0.9631; P = 0.0403), but increased the risk of sciatica (IVW OR = 1.1358; 95% CI = 1.0135–1.2728; P = 0.0285). Genus RuminococcaceaeUCG014 showed inverse associations with thoracic spine pain (IVW OR = 0.8357; 95% CI = 0.7006–0.9968; P = 0.0460) and drug-induced polyneuropathy (IVW OR = 0.2746; 95% CI = 0.1189–0.6346; P = 0.0025). Genus RuminococcaceaeUCG002 was positively associated with drug-induced polyneuropathy (IVW OR = 2.5944; 95% CI = 1.2148–5.5408; P = 0.0138), but negatively associated with alcohol-induced polyneuropathy (IVW OR = 0.4789; 95% CI = 0.2532–0.9058; P = 0.0235). Finally, genus Christensenellaceae R.7 group increased the risk of diabetic neuropathy (IVW OR = 1.4715; 95% CI = 1.0596–2.0436; P = 0.0211), while decreasing the risk of migraine with aura (IVW OR = 0.7961; 95% CI = 0.6583–0.9627; P = 0.0187).

After applying Bonferroni correction for multiple testing, five gut microbiotas remained statistically significant. At the phylum level, genetically predicted Tenericutes was associated with a reduced risk of alcohol-induced polyneuropathy (IVW OR = 0.3297; 95% CI = 0.1575–0.6904; P = 0.0033). At the class level, Bacteroidia was associated with an increased risk of thoracic spine pain (IVW OR = 1.4183; 95% CI = 1.1472–1.7535; P = 0.0012). At the order level, Bacteroidales showed the same effect (IVW OR = 1.4183; 95% CI = 1.1472–1.7535; P = 0.0012), while Bifidobacteriales was associated with a lower risk of migraine (IVW OR = 0.8268; 95% CI = 0.7541–0.9065; P = 0.0001). At the family level, Bifidobacteriaceae also exhibited a protective association with migraine (IVW OR = 0.8268; 95% CI = 0.7541–0.9065; P = 0.0001).

This study further evaluated 206 brain structural connectivity traits as potential mediators to investigate their causal roles in 15 types of chronic pain. The IVW method in MR analysis was employed to uncover potential causal associations between brain structural connectivity and chronic pain. A total of 127 potentially robust causal relationships were identified (see Forest Plot in Fig. ), with detailed results provided in Additional file 1: Table S7. Among these, 73 connectivity traits were predicted to act as potential risk factors, whereas 54 were suggested to confer protective effects. Regarding specific chronic pain phenotypes, potential causal associations were observed between brain connectivity and: 7 traits for TN (Fig. a), 8 for PHN (Fig. b and Fig. ), 5 for small fiber neuropathy (Fig. c), 8 for diabetic neuropathy (Fig. d), 7 for sciatica (Fig. e), 10 for atypical facial pain (Fig. f), 6 for idiopathic peripheral autonomic neuropathy (Fig. g), 8 for intercostal neuropathy (Fig. h), 11 for thoracic spine pain (Fg. i), 7 for drug-induced polyneuropathy (Fig. j), 8 for alcohol-induced polyneuropathy (Fig. k), 11 for migraine (Fig. l), 9 for migraine with aura (Fig. m), 9 for migraine without aura (Fig. n), and 13 for cluster headache (Fig. o). Notably, 24 brain structural connectivity traits showed potentially robust causal associations with various types of chronic pain, primarily involving the DMN, DAN, SAN/VAN, control network (CN), VN, and several key subcortical structures (e.g., amygdala, nucleus accumbens, thalamus, putamen, and globus pallidus). The detailed results of the reverse MR analyses are provided in Additional file 1: Table S8.

Among the brain structural connectivity indicators, ten were identified as risk factors for chronic pain. For example, genetically predicted connectivity from the left-hemisphere CN to the putamen was associated with an increased risk of PHN (IVW OR = 3.1624; 95% CI = 1.3059–7.6580; P = 0.0107) and atypical facial pain (IVW OR = 1.9060; 95% CI = 1.1237–3.2330; P = 0.0167). Similarly, connectivity from the left-hemisphere SN to the thalamus was linked to elevated risks of PHN (IVW OR = 2.6341; 95% CI = 1.1893–5.8345; P = 0.0170) and alcohol-induced polyneuropathy (IVW OR = 2.8378; 95% CI = 1.0126–7.9529; P = 0.0473). Additionally, genetically predicted right-hemisphere CN to pallidum connectivity increased the risk of small fiber neuropathy (IVW OR = 2.0777; 95% CI = 1.0334–4.1773; P = 0.0402) and idiopathic peripheral autonomic neuropathy (IVW OR = 6.0540; 95% CI = 1.0489–34.9427; P = 0.0441). Further risk associations included left-hemisphere SN to left-hemisphere DAN connectivity with diabetic neuropathy (IVW OR = 1.3620; 95% CI = 1.0112–1.8346; P = 0.0420) and intercostal neuropathy (IVW OR = 3.2904; 95% CI = 1.0283–10.5283; P = 0.0447); right-hemisphere LN to putamen connectivity with sciatica (IVW OR = 1.1395; 95% CI = 1.0155–1.2786; P = 0.0263) and atypical facial pain (IVW OR = 1.6494; 95% CI = 1.0932–2.4887; P = 0.0171); right-hemisphere SAN/VAN to amygdala connectivity with intercostal neuropathy (IVW OR = 4.7023; 95% CI = 1.2788–17.2905; P = 0.0198) and cluster headache (IVW OR = 1.8097; 95% CI = 1.0384–3.1538; P = 0.0363). Moreover, left-hemisphere DAN to DAN connectivity was associated with increased risks of alcohol-induced polyneuropathy (IVW OR = 3.9295; 95% CI = 1.1362–13.5892; P = 0.0306) and migraine (IVW OR = 1.1603; 95% CI = 1.0124–1.3298; P = 0.0326). Connectivity from the right-hemisphere VN to right-hemisphere CN predicted higher risks of alcohol-induced polyneuropathy (IVW OR = 2.8137; 95% CI = 1.0492–7.5455; P = 0.0398), migraine (IVW OR = 1.1528; 95% CI = 1.0178–1.3057; P = 0.0253), and migraine with aura (IVW OR = 1.3004; 95% CI = 1.0868–1.5559; P = 0.0041). Additionally, left-hemisphere DAN to left-hemisphere LN connectivity was linked to migraine (IVW OR = 1.1536; 95% CI = 1.0170–1.3085; P = 0.0262) and migraine with aura (IVW OR = 1.3204; 95% CI = 1.0964–1.5901; P = 0.0034). Similarly, left-hemisphere LN to accumbens connectivity increased the risk of migraine (IVW OR = 1.1824; 95% CI = 1.0229–1.3667; P = 0.0234) and migraine without aura (IVW OR = 1.2915; 95% CI = 1.0268–1.6245; P = 0.0288), while right-hemisphere VN to hippocampus connectivity was associated with migraine (IVW OR = 1.1862; 95% CI = 1.0515–1.3382; P = 0.0055) and migraine with aura (IVW OR = 1.2147; 95% CI = 1.0049–1.4681; P = 0.0443).

Five brain structural connectivity indicators were identified as protective factors against chronic pain. Genetically predicted connectivity within the right-hemisphere SAN/VAN was associated with a reduced risk of PHN (IVW OR = 0.3599; 95% CI = 0.1418–0.9136; P = 0.0315) and migraine (IVW OR = 0.8740; 95% CI = 0.7674–0.9954; P = 0.0424). Similarly, right-hemisphere CN to accumbens connectivity was linked to decreased incidences of small fiber neuropathy (IVW OR = 0.4085; 95% CI = 0.1873–0.8910; P = 0.0245) and intercostal neuropathy (IVW OR = 0.1187; 95% CI = 0.0295–0.4781; P = 0.0027). Connectivity from the left-hemisphere LN to the left-hemisphere CN was associated with lower risks of idiopathic peripheral autonomic neuropathy (IVW OR = 0.1331; 95% CI = 0.0210–0.8450; P = 0.0325) and cluster headache (IVW OR = 0.4688; 95% CI = 0.2812–0.7813; P = 0.0036). Additionally, genetically predicted right-hemisphere SN to caudate connectivity reduced the risk of thoracic spine pain (IVW OR = 0.7373; 95% CI = 0.5716–0.9511; P = 0.0190) and migraine with aura (IVW OR = 0.8061; 95% CI = 0.6693–0.9707; P = 0.0230). Finally, left-hemisphere SN to accumbens connectivity was linked to decreased incidence of atypical facial pain (IVW OR = 0.5687; 95% CI = 0.3304–0.9787; P = 0.0416) and migraine with aura (IVW OR = 0.7739; 95% CI = 0.6006–0.9973; P = 0.0476).

Nine brain structural connectivity indicators exhibited bidirectional effects across different chronic pain conditions. Genetically predicted connectivity from left-hemisphere LN to amygdala showed a potential causal association with TN (IVW OR = 1.7127; 95% CI = 1.0455–2.8057; P = 0.0326) and alcohol-induced polyneuropathy (IVW OR = 0.2407; 95% CI = 0.0719–0.8056; P = 0.0208). Similarly, connectivity from the right-hemisphere LN to the nucleus accumbens was linked to TN (IVW OR = 0.4484; 95% CI = 0.2499–0.8047; P = 0.0072) and idiopathic peripheral autonomic neuropathy (IVW OR = 12.5769; 95% CI = 1.4059–112.5099; P = 0.0235). Genetically predicted left-hemisphere DAN to left-hemisphere SAN/VAN connectivity was associated with PHN (IVW OR = 0.3749; 95% CI = 0.1471–0.9554; P = 0.0398), atypical facial pain (IVW OR = 1.8887; 95% CI = 1.1828–3.0160; P = 0.0077), and drug-induced polyneuropathy (IVW OR = 3.6573; 95% CI = 1.0934–12.2335; P = 0.0353). Right-hemisphere SN to putamen connectivity showed potential causal relationships with small fiber neuropathy (IVW OR = 0.4862; 95% CI = 0.2786–0.8485; P = 0.0111) and diabetic neuropathy (IVW OR = 1.4080; 95% CI = 1.0718–1.8496; P = 0.0140). Left-hemisphere CN to right-hemisphere VN connectivity was linked to diabetic neuropathy (IVW OR = 1.3991; 95% CI = 1.0019–1.9538; P = 0.0487) and thoracic spine pain (IVW OR = 0.7277; 95% CI = 0.5552–0.9538; P = 0.0213). Connectivity from the left-hemisphere CN to right-hemisphere CN showed associations with diabetic neuropathy (IVW OR = 1.3448; 95% CI = 1.0167–1.7786; P = 0.0379) and migraine with aura (IVW OR = 0.8336; 95% CI = 0.7160–0.9706; P = 0.0191). Right-hemisphere VN to right-hemisphere LN connectivity exhibited potential causal links with atypical facial pain (IVW OR = 1.5810; 95% CI = 1.0196–2.4515; P = 0.0407), intercostal neuropathy (IVW OR = 0.3105; 95% CI = 0.0994–0.9698; P = 0.0441), and thoracic spine pain (IVW OR = 1.3358; 95% CI = 1.0088–1.7690; P = 0.0433). Additionally, left-hemisphere VN to right-hemisphere DAN connectivity was associated with idiopathic peripheral autonomic neuropathy (IVW OR = 0.1562; 95% CI = 0.0267–0.9156; P = 0.0396) and thoracic spine pain (IVW OR = 1.2793; 95% CI = 1.0140–1.6140; P = 0.0378). Finally, connectivity from the left-hemisphere LN to right-hemisphere DAN showed potential causal relationships with idiopathic peripheral autonomic neuropathy (IVW OR = 5.8790; 95% CI = 1.3415–25.7643; P = 0.0188) and migraine without aura (IVW OR = 0.8159; 95% CI = 0.6834–0.9741; P = 0.0244).

However, after applying Bonferroni correction for multiple testing, two brain structural connectivity indicators remained statistically significant. Specifically, genetically predicted connectivity from the right-hemisphere SAN/VAN to putamen was associated with a decreased risk of sciatica (IVW OR = 0.7113; 95% CI = 0.6005–0.8425; P = 0.0001). Similarly, connectivity from the left-hemisphere DAN to the pallidum was linked to a reduced incidence of migraine (IVW OR = 0.3579; 95% CI = 0.2111–0.6065; P = 0.0001).

Building upon previous studies, we further investigated the causal relationships between gut microbiota abundances significantly associated with chronic pain and brain structural connectivity. The results revealed ten potential robust causal links. Specifically, the results indicate that, for PHN, genetically predicted genus LachnospiraceaeNK4A136 was positively correlated with an increased risk of connectivity from left-hemisphere DAN to left-hemisphere SAN/VAN (IVW OR = 1.0947; 95% CI = 1.0263 to 1.1676; P = 0.0060). For diabetic neuropathy, genetically predicted genus Senegalimassilia was positively correlated with the risk of connectivity from left-hemisphere VN to right-hemisphere VN (IVW OR = 1.1171; 95% CI = 1.0209 to 1.2223; P = 0.0160). For sciatica, genetically predicted genus eubacterium brachy was negatively correlated with the risk of connectivity from right-hemisphere SAN/VAN to putamen (IVW OR = 0.9521; 95% CI = 0.9075 to 0.9989; P = 0.0451). Additionally, genetically predicted genus Ruminiclostridium6 was positively correlated with the risk of connectivity from left-hemisphere SAN/VAN to right-hemisphere SAN/VAN (IVW OR = 1.1045; 95% CI = 1.0415 to 1.1714; P = 0.0009), as well as the risk of connectivity from Left-hemisphere VN to right-hemisphere SAN/VAN (IVW OR = 1.0956; 95% CI = 1.0281 to 1.1675; P = 0.0049). For atypical facial pain, genetically predicted order Pasteurellales was negatively correlated with the risk of connectivity from left-hemisphere CN to putamen (IVW OR = 0.9490; 95% CI = 0.9011 to 0.9994; P = 0.0473). Moreover, the genetically predicted family Pasteurellaceae also showed a negative correlation with the risk of connectivity from left-hemisphere CN to putamen (IVW OR = 0.9490; 95% CI = 0.9011 to 0.9994; P = 0.0473). For intercostal neuropathy, genetically predicted genus RuminococcaceaeUCG010 was positively correlated with the risk of connectivity from right-hemisphere CN to accumben (IVW OR = 1.1059; 95% CI = 1.0008 to 1.2221; P = 0.0483). For migraine, genetically predicted genus Marvinbryantia was negatively correlated with the risk of connectivity from left-hemisphere SAN/VAN to right-hemisphere CN (IVW OR = 0.9014; 95% CI = 0.8288 to 0.9804; P = 0.0155). For cluster headache, genetically predicted genus Parabacteroides was negatively correlated with the risk of connectivity from right-hemisphere SAN/VAN to right-hemisphere DMN (IVW OR = 0.8920; 95% CI = 0.8077 to 0.9851; P = 0.0240). However, after applying Bonferroni correction for multiple testing, no gut microbiota taxa reached the threshold for statistical significance.

Comprehensive findings from the sensitivity analyses are presented in the Additional file 1: Table. The application of Cochran’s Q test further corroborated these findings, revealing no significant heterogeneity among the studies ( P > 0.05). Moreover, the results obtained from the MR-Egger regression intercept method indicated that genetic pleiotropy did not influence the outcomes. The MR-PRESSO test similarly showed no evidence of horizontal pleiotropy within our MR analysis ( P > 0.05). Additionally, the robustness of the MR results was affirmed through a leave-one-out sensitivity analysis, which exhibited consistent reliability. Collectively, these findings reinforce the dependability of our analysis and provide further validation of the robustness of the MR results.

The identification of the gut–brain axis as a significant contributor to the onset of chronic pain necessitates a deeper exploration of the mediating factors involved. Employing a two-step methodology, ten brain structural connectivity phenotypes were discerned as mediators in the relationship between gut microbiota and chronic pain. Based on these observations, ten mediation models illustrating the pathways of the gut–brain axis were developed. As depicted in Figs. , and Table , genetically predicted brain structural connectivity demonstrated notable mediating effects across various neuropathic pain conditions. The most pronounced mediation effect was noted in the connectivity from the right-hemisphere CN to the accumbens, which negatively mediated the correlation between genus RuminococcaceaeUCG010 and intercostal neuropathy (β = − 0.2146), with a mediation proportion of 14.99%. For sciatica, the connectivity from the right-hemisphere SAN/VAN to the putamen exhibited a positive mediation effect between the genus Eubacterium brachy and sciatica (β = 0.0167), with a mediation proportion of 27.07%. Additionally, the left-hemisphere VN to the right-hemisphere SAN/VAN demonstrated a positive mediation effect between the genus Ruminiclostridium6 and sciatica (β = 0.0194), with a mediation proportion of 22.90%. Furthermore, the connectivity from the left-hemisphere SAN/VAN to the right-hemisphere SAN/VAN exhibited a positive mediation effect between the same genus Ruminiclostridium6 and sciatica (β = 0.0163), with a mediation proportion of 18.87%. Regarding headache-related conditions, the connectivity from the left-hemisphere SAN/VAN to the right-hemisphere CN showed a positive mediation effect between genus Marvinbryantia and migraine (β = 0.0190), with a mediation proportion of 18.32%. The right-hemisphere SAN/VAN to the right-hemisphere DMN mediated the relationship between genus Parabacteroides and cluster headache (β = 0.0565), with a mediation proportion of 7.80%. For diabetic neuropathy, the left-hemisphere VN to the right-hemisphere VN exhibited a positive mediation effect between genus Senegalimassilia and diabetic neuropathy (β = 0.0308), with a mediation proportion of 9.91%. For atypical facial pain, the left-hemisphere CN to the putamen demonstrated a negative mediation effect on the relationships between order Pasteurellales and atypical facial pain (β = − 0.0338), as well as family Pasteurellaceae and atypical facial pain (β = − 0.0338), both with a mediation proportion of 10.36%. Lastly, the left-hemisphere DAN to the left-hemisphere SAN/VAN exhibited a negative mediation effect on the association between genus LachnospiraceaeNK4A136 and PHN (β = − 0.0887), with a mediation proportion of 11.48%. Collectively, these findings highlight the intricate interplay between specific gut microbiota abundances and brain structural connectivity in the context of chronic pain, thereby enhancing our understanding of the mechanisms underlying gut–brain interactions in chronic pain modulation.
sections.discussion:
This study integrated MR analysis with mediation analysis to systematically investigate the potential genetic causal relationships among gut microbiota abundance, brain structural connectivity, and 15 types of chronic pain, based on GWAS data. The results identified 101 gut microbiota and 127 brain connectivity features that were potentially causally associated with various chronic pain conditions. Subsequent two-step mediation analysis revealed 10 robust mediation pathways linking gut microbiota abundance to chronic pain through specific brain connectivity features, with the mediation effects quantitatively evaluated. These findings provide novel insights into the regulatory mechanisms and mediation processes along the "gut microbiota-brain structural connectivity-chronic pain" axis and offer a theoretical foundation for developing targeted therapeutic strategies based on microbial and neuroimaging biomarkers.

This study provides genetic evidence suggesting a potential causal relationship between alterations in gut microbiota composition-particularly changes in the relative abundance of Firmicutes , Bacteroidetes , and Proteobacteria -and the risk of chronic pain. As one of the most complex and diverse microbial ecosystems in the human body, the gut microbiota plays critical physiological roles in maintaining intestinal barrier integrity, protecting against pathogen invasion, and promoting neural development []. Emerging evidence indicates that the gut microbiota is not only associated with visceral and abdominal pain but may also contribute to the onset and progression of neuropathic pain and headache disorders []. Several studies have identified significant differences in microbial diversity and composition between individuals with chronic pain and healthy controls [, ]. For example, a cross-sectional study involving 27 patients with PHN and 27 healthy controls reported a marked reduction in the abundance of Helicobacteraceae , Ruminococcaceae , and members of the Veillonellales order in PHN patients []. Our findings corroborate these observations, suggesting that decreased abundance of these taxa may increase the risk of PHN. Similarly, in a mouse model of diabetic neuropathy, researchers observed a significant reduction in Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium populations, along with an increased Firmicutes/Bacteroidetes ratio []. In clinical research involving 45 PDN patients and 35 matched controls, elevated levels of Firmicutes , Actinobacteria , Escherichia-Shigella , Clostridium , Megasphaera , and Ruminococcus were identified in the PDN group, whereas the abundance of Bacteroidetes , Bacteroides , and Faecalibacterium was significantly decreased []. Moreover, a recent systematic review and meta-analysis confirmed that chronic pain patients exhibit significantly lower relative abundance of Helicobacteraceae , Faecalibacterium , Roseburia , and Prevotella []. Consistent with these findings, our study not only reinforces the causal link between gut dysbiosis and neuropathic pain but also offers novel insights into the microbial underpinnings of other chronic pain types, including headaches. Increasing epidemiological evidence indicates a higher prevalence of gastrointestinal disorders among migraine sufferers compared to the general population []. In a non-randomized controlled trial involving 29 migraine patients, a 12-week probiotic intervention resulted in significant reductions in both migraine frequency and severity []. Likewise, a placebo-controlled randomized clinical trial with 63 migraine participants demonstrated that probiotic treatment significantly reduced migraine severity scores []. Furthermore, a double-blind randomized controlled trial demonstrated that a 10-week supplementation of 14 probiotic strains significantly reduced both the frequency and severity of episodic migraine attacks. An 8-week intervention also alleviated symptoms in patients with chronic migraine []. Other studies have reported that supplementation with strains such as Lactobacillus acidophilus , Lactobacillus bulgaricus , and Bifidobacterium improved quality of life scores in migraine patients []. These findings, along with our results, support the hypothesis that gut dysbiosis may influence individual susceptibility to chronic pain by modulating the abundance of specific microbial taxa. Specifically, decreased levels of Helicobacteraceae , Ruminococcaceae , and Barnesiellaceae may increase pain risk, whereas increased levels of Firmicutes , Proteobacteria , Actinobacteria , Megasphaeraceae , and Bifidobacteriaceae may exert protective effects. Growing evidence highlights the key regulatory roles of microbial families such as Helicobacteraceae , Megasphaeraceae , Lactobacillaceae , Bacteroidaceae , and Bifidobacterium in the development and progression of chronic pain, possibly through metabolic pathways involving short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs). SCFAs—particularly acetate, propionate, and butyrate—are critical gut-derived metabolites that help maintain intestinal barrier integrity and regulate host immune responses []. Recent studies suggest that SCFAs may also contribute to neuropathic pain alleviation [, ]. In animal models, butyrate administration significantly reduced neuropathic pain behaviors in chronic constriction injury models []. In humans, PHN patients were found to have significantly lower serum butyrate levels compared to healthy controls []. Moreover, gut-derived metabolites such as SCFAs, neurotransmitters, and neuromodulators may act on pain-related receptors and signaling pathways, thereby modulating both central and peripheral sensitization. In the central nervous system, these molecules can activate blood–brain barrier endothelial cells, microglia, and infiltrating immune cells, contributing to the initiation and maintenance of central sensitization []. Peripherally, they may enhance the excitability of primary nociceptive neurons, thereby promoting peripheral sensitization. These mechanistic insights have paved the way for microbiota-targeted therapies as promising strategies for chronic pain management. Interventions such as probiotic supplementation and FMT have shown encouraging results. In one study, transplantation of gut microbiota from healthy donors into a cisplatin-induced neuropathic pain mouse model significantly alleviated pain behaviors within 21 days []. Other animal studies have also confirmed the efficacy of FMT in relieving neuropathic pain induced by peripheral nerve injury, chemotherapy, or diabetes [].

To elucidate the pathophysiological mechanisms of the gut–brain axis in chronic pain, this study further investigated the central role of brain structural connectivity in pain perception and regulation. Structural connections between brain regions form the anatomical backbone of neural networks, and their integrity is essential for sensory processing and cognitive integration. Advances in DTI and structural connectomics have revealed that chronic pain-particularly neuropathic pain and headache-is commonly associated with aberrant brain connectivity. Specific brain networks and subcortical structures are involved not only in the transmission of nociceptive signals but also in their perception, modulation, and chronification. As the most structurally complex organ of the central nervous system, the brain possesses highly integrated sensory recognition and response capabilities, allowing it to efficiently detect and regulate harmful stimuli. Despite the high degree of phenotypic heterogeneity in clinical pain syndromes, the anatomical pathway of nociceptive transmission remains relatively conserved. Peripheral noxious stimulation activates sensory neurons, which transmit signals through the dorsal root ganglion (DRG) to the dorsal horn of the spinal cord. The signals then ascend via the spinothalamic tract to the contralateral ventral posterolateral nucleus (VPL) of the thalamus and are subsequently projected to the primary and secondary somatosensory cortices, insula, cingulate gyrus, and prefrontal cortex [, ]. This ascending pathway is finely regulated by descending modulatory systems, which include the prefrontal cortex, amygdala, periaqueductal gray (PAG), and the rostral ventromedial medulla (RVM). The RVM projects bilaterally to the spinal dorsal horn and enables bidirectional modulation of multisegmental nociceptive input; its structural and functional integrity is critical in pain sensitization and chronic maintenance. At the genetic level, our study identified 127 significant causal relationships between brain structural connectivity and 15 chronic pain phenotypes. Neuroimaging evidence consistently highlights the involvement of DMN, DAN, and SAN/VAN in pain perception, emotional regulation, and attentional allocation. Functional impairment in these networks has been shown to intensify pain experience and promote the transition from acute to chronic pain [, ]. At the regional level, multiple studies have reported persistent structural and functional disruptions of the DMN in individuals with chronic pain. For instance, patients with PHN exhibit decoupling between the DMN, SN, and VN, as well as marked alterations in intra-DMN connectivity [, ]. Abnormalities in brain structural connectivity primarily cluster within the so-called “pain matrix,” encompassing regions such as the thalamus, insula, amygdala, parahippocampal gyrus, and prefrontal cortex []. Patients with TN exhibit disrupted connectivity between DMN and SAN. Chronic migraine sufferers show enhanced connectivity between the hypothalamus and both the DMN and dorsal visual network (DVN), accompanied by reduced intra-DMN connectivity. These alterations closely correlate with heightened pain sensitivity and increased nociceptive perception []. Similarly, patients experiencing bone metastasis pain demonstrate dysfunctional activity within the DMN and SN []. The DMN, as a core brain network, is implicated in self-referential processing, interoception, and emotional regulation, playing a critical role in the maintenance of chronic pain. Abnormal DMN connectivity exacerbates negative affect and pain perception, reflecting the complex interplay among pain, cognitive, and emotional systems. During mind-wandering, reduced DMN deactivation in response to painful stimuli suggests its importance in maintaining environmental vigilance []. Pain sensitization induces functional reorganization of the DMN and related networks, leading to maladaptive regulation and emotional disturbances. Moreover, significant structural connectivity abnormalities have been reported in DAN and SAN of patients with TN and migraine. A study including patients with chronic and episodic migraine, TN, and healthy controls found increased DAN connectivity in chronic craniofacial pain, with particularly pronounced coupling between the somatomotor cortex and DAN in TN patients []. The SN and VAN remain persistently active in pain-related attentional control, even during non-attentive states []. In tension-type headache, continuous activation of these two networks closely relates to pain sensitivity and emotional disorders []. The DAN predominantly mediates top-down attentional modulation, and its dysfunction manifests as hypervigilance toward noxious stimuli—an important neural signature of cognitive-emotional remodeling in chronic pain. The SN and VAN are responsible for detecting salient stimuli and reallocating attentional resources; as hubs mediating emotion-pain interactions, their dysfunction is particularly prominent in chronic pain patients with comorbid anxiety and depression. These findings further underscore the critical role of these attention-related networks in the chronification of pain.

Moreover, the limbic system plays a critical role in the development and modulation of chronic pain. Our study revealed significant structural connectivity abnormalities in key limbic regions among chronic pain patients, reflecting their essential functions in the emotional, cognitive, and motivational processing of pain. The limbic system, comprising the amygdala, putamen, nucleus accumbens, hippocampus, and thalamus, is involved in pain perception as well as the regulation of associated emotions, memory, and attentional biases. The amygdala, a central hub for emotional memory and fear conditioning, contributes to pain modulation and related affective disorders such as anxiety and depression []. Both animal and human studies have demonstrated neuroplastic changes among the amygdala, putamen, and nucleus accumbens that facilitate pain chronification and complexity []. Amygdala dysfunction is particularly pronounced in patients with trigeminal neuralgia and cluster headache. Structural and functional abnormalities of the nucleus accumbens reflect a pathological shift from reward processing toward avoidance behavior, potentially leading to motivational deficits and anhedonia, which exacerbate the vicious cycle of pain, avoidance, and emotional disorders. The hippocampus participates in pain-related cognitive appraisal and memory processes, and its dysfunction is widely reported across various pain conditions. As a relay for nociceptive signals, the thalamus exhibits reduced structural connectivity closely associated with chronic pain []. Notably, limbic system abnormalities demonstrate pain phenotype specificity. For instance, patients with sciatica show increased connectivity between the amygdala and medial prefrontal cortex, potentially mediating pain catastrophizing and attentional bias, which further aggravate pain perception and movement avoidance. In migraine and cluster headache, the limbic system acts as a hub for emotional comorbidity, autonomic responses, and sensory regulation, contributing to headache initiation and maintenance. Studies indicate marked activation of the amygdala and hypothalamic-limbic pathways during cluster headache attacks, while patients with comorbid affective disorders exhibit impaired limbic system function that exacerbates negative emotional modulation of pain, increasing headache frequency and severity. Further analysis suggests that abnormalities in limbic structural connectivity may be influenced by genetic variation. Polymorphisms modulate white matter connectivity efficiency in specific brain regions, impacting pain regulatory networks. Neuronal plasticity, through dynamic synaptic remodeling, facilitates nociceptive signal transmission and central modulation. Extensive research confirms that structural and functional plasticity of the brain is vital for the initiation, progression, and maintenance of neuropathic pain, particularly involving the somatosensory cortex, thalamus, insula, and hippocampus. Plasticity-induced synaptic remodeling aggravates central sensitization, promotes the formation of pain-related affective states, and contributes to the persistence of chronic pain.

A key finding of this study lies in the identification and quantification of the mediating role of brain structural connectivity in the relationship between gut microbiota and chronic pain. As a pioneering effort to investigate the potential genetic causal pathways linking gut microbiota, brain structural connectivity, and chronic pain, this study demonstrates that the influence of gut microbiota on pain is not exerted through direct mechanisms, but rather mediated via structural alterations in specific brain networks. Specifically, gut microbiota may modulate the structural connectivity between regions involved in sensory processing, attention, cognition, emotion regulation, and reward, including DMN, SAN, and limbic system. These findings provide empirical evidence supporting the role of the gut–brain axis in the neural mechanisms of chronic pain and offer a theoretical foundation for identifying targeted clinical interventions. Moreover, the mediation pathways identified between specific microbial taxa and brain structural connections may serve as potential neuroimaging biomarkers. These biomarkers could help identify individuals at risk, assess disease susceptibility, and monitor therapeutic responses, thus contributing to the development of personalized pain assessment frameworks. Modulating the abundance of key microbial taxa-via probiotic supplementation, dietary interventions, or other microbiota-targeted approaches-may indirectly enhance structural connectivity between relevant brain regions and alleviate pain perception. Additionally, this gut–brain mechanism may synergize with non-pharmacological neuromodulation techniques, such as transcranial magnetic stimulation or neurofeedback, offering a multimodal and individualized therapeutic strategy for chronic pain management.

This study presents notable strengths in both dataset selection and methodological rigor, offering a more systematic and comprehensive genetic investigation into the causal relationships among gut microbiota, brain structural connectivity, and chronic pain. Compared with previous research, our work expands the analytical scope and enhances the reliability of findings. Specifically, we included 15 chronic pain phenotypes-comprising 11 types of neuropathic pain and 4 headache subtypes-and utilized updated GWAS summary statistics from the FinnGen Consortium R11. These datasets provide broader phenotype coverage and richer sample information, substantially improving the robustness, accuracy, and generalizability of our results. From a methodological perspective, we implemented multiple strategies to strengthen causal inference. Firstly, IVs were stringently selected by excluding SNPs associated with known confounders and calculating F-statistics based on R 2 to ensure sufficient strength and minimize multicollinearity. Secondly, we retained only those causal associations that showed consistent directional effects across all MR methods and conducted extensive sensitivity analyses to confirm the stability and reliability of the results. Furthermore, we quantified the mediating role of brain structural connectivity between gut microbiota and chronic pain, offering novel mechanistic insights into the gut–brain axis in pain regulation. This provides a mechanistic foundation for viewing both gut microbiota and brain structural connectivity as modifiable targets for precision chronic pain therapies. Our results thus inform future directions for functional validation studies, biomarker development, and individualized intervention strategies based on the gut–brain–chronic pain axis. Despite these innovations, several limitations should be acknowledged. Firstly, chronic pain encompasses a highly heterogeneous set of conditions. The involvement of divergent pathophysiological mechanisms across different pain types introduces potential confounding that may restrict the broader applicability of our findings. Secondly, although we applied stringent criteria for IV selection, gene–environment interactions and residual confounding cannot be entirely ruled out. Psychological factors, such as mood and affective disorders—particularly anxiety and depression—are highly prevalent among patients with chronic pain. These factors may influence both gut microbiota composition and brain structure and function through multiple mechanisms, including neural plasticity, inflammatory responses, and regulation of stress hormone levels. Such mechanisms could potentially affect the results of our MR analyses, adding complexity to causal inference. In addition, other lifestyle factors (e.g., sleep quality, dietary habits, physical activity) and psychosocial stressors may concurrently act on the gut–brain axis, further modulating chronic pain-related phenotypes. Given its relatively low heritability, the potential for genetic instruments to be linked with unmeasured environmental confounders remains a methodological challenge. Thirdly, while some of the identified associations did not surpass the Bonferroni-corrected threshold for statistical significance, they may still carry biological relevance. Although multiple testing correction is crucial for reducing false positives, it may also mask suggestive signals with potential mechanistic implications. Importantly, our study is exploratory in nature and aims to generate novel scientific hypotheses rather than deliver definitive causal conclusions. Thus, the findings should be interpreted as preliminary and require further replication and functional validation. Lastly, the GWAS datasets employed in this study were predominantly derived from European populations, limiting the generalizability of our conclusions to other ethnic groups. Given the well-documented variations in gut microbiota composition, brain structural connectivity, and chronic pain susceptibility across populations, future studies involving multi-ethnic cohorts are essential to validate our findings and enhance their translational relevance in clinical practice.

In summary, this study systematically revealed the genetic causal mechanisms through which specific gut microbiota influences chronic pain via brain structural connectivity, combining genetic IVs and brain imaging phenotypes to clarify the important role of the "gut–brain-pain” pathway. The study emphasizes the pivotal role of gut microbiota and central nervous networks in the regulation of chronic pain, providing a new perspective on the understanding of chronic pain mechanisms and the development of precise intervention strategies. In the future, the integration of multi-omics and neuroimaging technologies could lead to the development of personalized pain management strategies based on gut microbiota and brain network axes.

title: Positioning rimegepant in migraine prophylaxis: updated evidence and emerging perspectives.
abstract: IntroductionMigraine is among the most disabling neurological disorders worldwide and preventive treatment remains a cornerstone for reducing disease burden. Recent advances in mechanism-based therapies have positioned calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) and its main receptor as central targets for migraine prophylaxis.Areas coveredThis updated narrative overview summarizes the pharmacological profile, clinical efficacy, safety and regulatory status of rimegepant, integrating evidence published through 2025 and highlighting emerging real-world and clinical trends. Relevant literature was identified through searches in PubMed/MEDLINE and Scopus (last search: 19 November 2025) using predefined combinations of terms related to rimegepant and migraine. The review also examines emerging concepts such as situational prevention, potential combination approaches with traditional or novel preventives and exploratory use in other CGRP-mediated headache disorders.Expert opinionRimegepant represents a significant addition to migraine prophylaxis by offering a flexible and well-tolerated option that bridges acute and preventive care. Its role may expand through rational combinations and investigation in other headache disorders. Persistence and long-term safety require careful monitoring, and reimbursement frameworks will determine its future clinical adoption.

title: Migraine mimics.
abstract: The symptoms of migraine are non-specific and can be present in many other primary and secondary headache disorders, which are reviewed. Even experienced headache specialists may be challenged at times when diagnosing what appears to be first or worst, new type, migraine status, and chronic migraine.

title: Mediators of the association between depression and migraine: a mendelian randomization study.
abstract: BACKGROUND: An association between depression and migraine has been reported in observational studies; however, conventional observational studies are prone to bias. This study aims to investigate the causal relationship between depression and migraine and to quantify the mediating effects of known risk factors. METHODS: We applied two-sample Mendelian randomization and utilized single nucleotide polymorphisms as genetic instruments for exposure (depression) and mediators (sleep traits). We utilized summary data on genome-wide association studies for depression, sleep-related traits mediators and migraine. For depression, genome-wide association studies (depression) were utilized as a test cohort for the primary analysis. Moreover, genome-wide association studies (major depressive disorder) were utilized to test the stability of the results for the validation cohort. IVW and MR-Egger regression were applied to test the heterogeneity, and Cochran's Q statistics were calculated to quantitatively evaluate the heterogeneity. MR-PRESSO analyses were utilized to examine and correct possible horizontal pleiotropy through removing outliers, and leave-one-out analyses were utilized to identify outlier SNPs. RESULTS: Genetically predicted depression was associated with migraine (OR = 1.321, 95% CI: 1.184-1.473, p < 0.001). Furthermore, risk factors insomnia was associated with migraine risk (OR = 1.766, 95% CI: 1.120-2.784, p = 0.014). sections.abstract: BACKGROUND: An association between depression and migraine has been reported in observational studies; however, conventional observational studies are prone to bias. This study aims to investigate the causal relationship between depression and migraine and to quantify the mediating effects of known risk factors. METHODS: We applied two-sample Mendelian randomization and utilized single nucleotide polymorphisms as genetic instruments for exposure (depression) and mediators (sleep traits). We utilized summary data on genome-wide association studies for depression, sleep-related traits mediators and migraine. For depression, genome-wide association studies (depression) were utilized as a test cohort for the primary analysis. Moreover, genome-wide association studies (major depressive disorder) were utilized to test the stability of the results for the validation cohort. IVW and MR-Egger regression were applied to test the heterogeneity, and Cochran's Q statistics were calculated to quantitatively evaluate the heterogeneity. MR-PRESSO analyses were utilized to examine and correct possible horizontal pleiotropy through removing outliers, and leave-one-out analyses were utilized to identify outlier SNPs. RESULTS: Genetically predicted depression was associated with migraine (OR = 1.321, 95% CI: 1.184-1.473, p < 0.001). Furthermore, risk factors insomnia was associated with migraine risk (OR = 1.766, 95% CI: 1.120-2.784, p = 0.014). The mediator insomnia accounted for 19.5% of the total effect of depression on migraine. CONCLUSION: These results support a potential causal effect of depression on migraine, partly mediated by insomnia. title: [CGRP antibodies in migraine prophylaxis : The new standard in migraine treatment?].
abstract: Migraine is associated with a high individual level of suffering. Therefore, an effective preventive treatment is highly important. The spectrum of classical prophylactic drugs has now been expanded to include monoclonal antibodies against calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) and its receptor. These antibodies have shown reliable efficacy compared to placebo and a rapid onset of action with a low rate of side effects and negligible interactions in pivotal studies. Recently, the efficacy of the antibody was shown in many studies even on drug-refractory migraine and migraine associated with medication overuse. Comprehensive head to head comparisons with previously established drugs and among the antibodies are not yet available; however, initial studies suggest better tolerability and efficacy compared to conventional drugs and other antibodies. The role of antibodies in established treatment cascades still needs to be clarified.

title: Prevalence and Clinical Characteristics of Migraine in Adults with Reduced Vitamin D Levels in Yunnan, China: A Cross-Sectional Study
abstract: Abstract Background For migraine patients residing in the low-latitude, high-altitude region of Yunnan, China, the current lack of data regarding vitamin D status and its impact on migraine characteristics has limited both research into vitamin D supplementation as a therapeutic approach and its clinical application. This study aimed to investigate the prevalence of reduced serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D (25(OH)D) levels in adult migraine patients in Yunnan Province and to explore its correlation with the clinical characteristics of migraine. Methods A total of 678 adult migraine patients who underwent serum 25(OH)D concentration testing at the outpatient clinic of the Department of Neurology, First People's Hospital of Yunnan Province, between January 1, 2023, and August 31, 2025, were consecutively enrolled. They were divided into three groups: deficient group ( 30 ng/mL). The differences in monthly headache attack frequency, monthly headache days, Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) score, and Headache Impact Test-6 (HIT-6) score were compared among the three groups. Pearson correlation analysis was used to assess the correlations. Results Among the 678 patients, the prevalence of reduced vitamin D was 64.31% (436/678), with 18.29% (124/678) classified as deficient and 46.02% (312/678) as insufficient. Additionally, body mass index (BMI) differed significantly among the three groups ( P P P = 0.057). Correlation analysis showed that serum 25(OH)D levels were negatively correlated with monthly headache attack frequency, monthly headache days, and HIT-6 scores. Conclusion The prevalence of reduced vitamin D levels among adult migraine patients in Yunnan Province was as high as 64.31%. Reduced serum 25(OH)D levels were negatively correlated with monthly headache frequency, monthly headache days, and HIT-6 scores. In addition, a significant association was found between increased BMI and reduced vitamin D levels, suggesting that BMI, as a contributing factor to vitamin D deficiency, may exacerbate the disease burden of migraine.

title: From Predictive Coding to Preventive Processing: Forecast-Triggered Pre-Emptive Treatment of Migraine
abstract: Migraine pharmacotherapy still divides into two temporal strategies: continuous prevention, taken every day against attacks that occupy a minority of days, and acute treatment, taken after pain has begun. The PRODROME trial opened a third window: ubrogepant taken during the prodrome left 46% of treated prodromal events free of moderate or severe headache within 24 h, against 29% with placebo. Access to that window currently runs through the patientʹs ability to recognise their own prodrome reliably, which was an entry criterion of the trial rather than a general property of migraine. I argue that this dependence need not be permanent. On an active-inference reading, the prodrome is the physiological trace of a failing allostatic regulation loop; it perturbs autonomic output in ways that wrist-worn sensors record every night, and individualised machine-learning models have begun, modestly, to forecast next-day attacks f rom t hose r ecordings. C oupling calibrated forecasts to short-acting CGRP receptor antagonists would turn prevention from a standing pharmacological state into a triggered event. This paper sets out the computational rationale for such preventive processing, weighs the wearable and pharmacoepidemiological evidence, including the parts that resist the argument, and speciﬁes the regimen-randomised trial on which the proposal should be judged.

title: Characteristics and Treatment Patterns in People with Burden of Migraine: A Subgroup Analysis of the OVERCOME Japan 2nd Study.
abstract: IntroductionThe burden of migraine on an individual's life is associated with an individual's background. However, limited evidence in Japan exists on the association of age, sex, employment, income, and family caregiving with patient-reported outcomes (PROs) and migraine treatment patterns. This analysis of the ObserVational survey of the Epidemiology, tReatment, and Care Of MigrainE (OVERCOME [Japan]) 2nd study describes the migraine burden and treatment usage of individuals with migraine across these demographic subgroups.MethodsParticipants self-reported demographic and clinical characteristics, and PRO instrument responses, such as Headache Impact Test-6, Migraine Disability Assessment Scale (MIDAS), Migraine-Specific Quality of Life Questionnaire version 2.1, Migraine Interictal Burden Scale-4 (MIBS-4), and Impact of Migraine on Partners and Adolescent Children Scale. They also reported use of over-the-counter and prescription drugs for migraine, and headache-related expenses. Descriptive statistics were reported according to sex, employment status, menstrual-related migraine status and frequency, annual personal and family income, age, and family caregiving status for the elderly.ResultsFemale sex, unemployment, presence of menstrual-related migraine, low personal or family income, and family caregiving for elders appeared to increase migraine burden and impact prescription drug use. Specifically, men tended to have higher triptan (11.7% vs. 8.7%) and preventive medication use (18.3% vs. 11.2%) than women; unemployed women had the highest proportion of MIDAS grade IV (14.1%); women with menstrual-related migraine appeared to have greater MIBS-4 severe burden (36.3% vs. 27.8%) than those without; and family caregivers tended to have higher MIBS-4 severe burden (39.2% vs. 26.0%) and prescription drug use than non-caregivers. Respondent sex further appeared to influence migraine burden and treatment patterns within the employment and income subgroups.ConclusionThese data suggest certain sociodemographic groups may suffer from greater migraine burden and have reduced access to effective treatment and care. We hope this study's results will help healthcare providers and societies identify such populations with migraine and address potential clinical care gaps.

title: Exploring Contraindicated Medications and Corresponding Targeted Genes for Migraine Through Integrated Genetic Approaches.
abstract: ObjectiveTo identify contraindicated medications and corresponding target genes for migraine and its subtypes.MethodUtilizing the Genome-Wide Association Studies (GWAS) for 14 medication-use categories from UK Biobank and GWAS for migraine and its subtypes from FinnGen, our study revealed potential contraindicated drugs for the chronic paroxysmal neurological disorder based on Mendelian randomization (MR). Then we applied the Transcriptome-wide association study (TWAS) within the framework of Omnibus Transcriptome Test using Expression Reference Summary data (OTTERS) and cross-referenced three drug databases to determine the targeted genes of the identified contraindicated medications. Moreover, Summary-data-based Mendelian Randomization (SMR) and INtegration of TWAS And ColocalizaTion (INTACT) were used as sensitivity analyses to further validate the associations and strengthen causal inference. We also performed brain-tissue TWAS across 13 regions to confirm the tissue-specific associations of the hub genes with migraine and its subtypes.ResultsMR analysis revealed that the diuretics and agents that act on the renin-angiotensin system were discovered to be associated with an increased risk of migraine and migraine with aura. By intersecting the results from TWAS and drug databases, 37 and 22 target genes of contraindicated medications were identified for migraine and migraine with aura, respectively. SMR and INTACT confirmed the validity of BLM, C12orf76, GPATCH4, PAM, SERPINC1 for migraine, and ALMS1, GPATCH4, NCF2, SLC12A1, ZKSCAN8P1 for migraine with aura. At the brain-tissue level, we further validated hub gene associations: in migraine, SERPINC1, ZKSCAN8P1, C12orf76, and PAM were significant across brain regions; in migraine with aura, SERPINC1, ALMS1, ZKSCAN8P1, PAM, and NCF2 were significant.ConclusionWe identified the diuretics and agents that act on the renin-angiotensin system as the contraindicated medications for migraine and migraine with aura, and BLM, C12orf76, GPATCH4, PAM, SERPINC were found as the targeted genes of contraindicated drugs for migraine and ALMS1, GPATCH4, NCF2, SLC12A1, ZKSCAN8P1 for migraine with aura, providing new clues for the preventive strategies for migraine and its subtypes.

title: The Impact of Migraine on School Attendance and Psychosocial Functioning in Children and Adolescents: A Cross-sectional Study.
abstract: ObjectiveThis study aimed to evaluate the frequency of school absenteeism and associated clinical, sociodemographic, and psychosocial factors in children, adolescents diagnosed with migraine.MethodsThis cross-sectional, descriptive study included 70 pediatric migraine patients (aged 12-17 years; mean age: 14.8 ± 1.3 years) followed at Necmettin Erbakan University Pediatric Neurology Outpatient Clinic. Participants were diagnosed according to the International Classification of Headache Disorders, 3rd Edition (ICHD-3) criteria. Data were collected via a structured 12-item questionnaire covering demographic characteristics, clinical migraine features, school absenteeism duration, academic impact, parental work loss, and teacher awareness. Statistical analyses included χ2, Mann-Whitney U, and multivariate logistic regression tests.ResultsThe majority of patients were female (62.9%) and in high school (82.9%). Migraine without aura was the predominant subtype (91.4%). The mean school absenteeism over the preceding year was 4.3 ± 2.4 days. Patients with frequent attacks (>1/mo) had significantly longer absenteeism compared with infrequent attackers (5.1 vs 3.3 days; P = .001). Academic decline was reported by 11.4% of patients and was associated with significantly higher absenteeism (7.4 vs 3.9 days; P = .001). Only 22.9% of patients received prophylactic treatment. Parental work loss was universal (100%; mean 2.5 ± 1.1 days). Teacher awareness of migraine diagnosis was absent in all cases (0%).ConclusionMigraine imposes a significant multidimensional burden on children's educational life, with attack frequency being the primary driver of absenteeism. The complete lack of teacher awareness and high rates of parental work loss underscore critical deficiencies in school-health care collaboration. Multidisciplinary strategies integrating optimized prophylaxis, school-based awareness programs, and individualized health plans are urgently needed.

title: Whether Weather Matters with Migraine.
abstract: PURPOSE OF REVIEW: Many patients with migraine report their attacks are triggered by various weather anomalies. Studies have shown mixed results regarding the association of migraine to weather changes. The purpose of the current review is to compile the most up-to-date research studies on how weather may affect migraine. In addition, we explore the association between weather and other inflammatory disease states as well as neurotransmitters. RECENT FINDINGS: Migraine attacks can be related to weather variables such as barometric pressure, humidity, and wind. However, the results of recent studies are inconsistent; weathers' effect on migraine attacks is around 20%. However, very strong weather factors have a more significant effect on migraine attack variables. Many individuals identify weather as a migraine attack trigger, yet we see no causative relationship between weather and migraine patterns. The outcomes of studies indicate mixed results and reflect individual variation in how weather can impact migraine patterns. Similar relationships can be seen with other rheumatologic and pain conditions in general. Overall, the combination of weather plus other factors appears to be a more significant migraine trigger.

title: Association between brain structures and migraine: A bidirectional Mendelian randomization study.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Accumulating evidence of clinical and neuroimaging studies indicated that migraine is related to brain structural alterations. However, it is still not clear whether the associations of brain structural alterations with migraine are likely to be causal, or could be explained by reverse causality confounding. METHODS: We carried on a bidirectional Mendelian randomization analysis in order to identify the causal relationship between brain structures and migraine risk. Summary-level data and independent variants used as instruments came from large genome-wide association studies of total surface area and average thickness of cortex (33,992 participants), gray matter volume (8,428 participants), white matter hyperintensities (50,970 participants), hippocampal volume (33,536 participants), and migraine (102,084 cases and 771,257 controls). RESULTS: We identified suggestive associations of the decreased surface area (OR = 0.85; 95% CI, 0.75-0.96; P = 0.007), and decreased hippocampal volume (OR = 0.74; 95% CI, 0.55-1.00; P = 0.047) with higher migraine risk. We did not find any significant association of gray matter volume, cortical thickness, or white matter hyperintensities with migraine. No evidence supporting the significant association was found in the reverse MR analysis. CONCLUSION: We provided suggestive evidence that surface area and hippocampal volume are causally associated with migraine risk.

title: Comprehensive evaluation of volumetric and microstructural alterations of corpus callosum in migraine patients and subtypes using diffusion tensor imaging (DTI).
abstract: BackgroundWe aimed to evaluate white matter damage, particularly in the corpus callosum, that may contribute to migraine etiology through diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) metrics, while also evaluating the relationship between these metrics, clinical features, and corpus callosum volmetric measurements.MethodsIn this retrospective study, a total of 103 migraine patients (50 with aura, 53 without aura) and 47 healthy controls who had a brain DTI examination were included. The study population was divided into four groups and four DTI metrics obtained from six regions were compared between groups. Corpus callosum volumes were calculated and their relationship with DTI parameters was examined. Age, sex, disease duration, attack frequency, and visual analog score constituted clinical features.ResultsDecreased ADC and RD values in the corpus callosum were observed in the overall migraine group and the migraine with aura subtype, whereas increased FA values were observed in the overall migraine group. Corpus callosum volume was lower in overall migraine group and in its subtypes than in healthy controls. A positive correlation was observed between cingulum ADC values and corpus callosum volume (p = 0.024, r = 0.370). A negative correlation was detected between AD values of the corpus callosum body and corpus callosum volume (p = 0.049, r = -0.335).ConclusionsThe corpus callosum, which is a crucial region in the processing and perception of pain, may indicate loss of white matter integrity as a result of recurrent pain in migraine. This study demonstrates the possible sensitivity of DTI metrics and volumetric measurements in detecting corpus callosum changes in migraine.

Corpus callosum volume was lower in overall migraine group and in its subtypes than in healthy controls. A positive correlation was observed between cingulum ADC values and corpus callosum volume (p = 0.024, r = 0.370). A negative correlation was detected between AD values of the corpus callosum body and corpus callosum volume (p = 0.049, r = -0.335).ConclusionsThe corpus callosum, which is a crucial region in the processing and perception of pain, may indicate loss of white matter integrity as a result of recurrent pain in migraine. This study demonstrates the possible sensitivity of DTI metrics and volumetric measurements in detecting corpus callosum changes in migraine.

title: Circulating Cytokines Mediate the Causal Relationship between Plasma Lipids and Migraine and its Subtypes: A Mediated Mendelian Randomization Study.
abstract: IntroductionMigraine, a primary headache disorder, is the third disabling disease of neurological disorders worldwide. The pathological mechanism underlying migraine remains poorly understood. Lipid metabolism may be related to migraine pathophysiology. We aimed to investigate the causal relationship between plasma lipids and migraine or its subtypes, including migraine with aura (MA) and migraine without aura (MO), and explore whether the circulating cytokines serve as mediators in the pathway from plasma lipids to migraine.MethodsA two-step Mendelian randomization (MR) approach was used to assess the mediating effect. The summary genetic data for 179 lipid species were obtained from were derived from a genome-wide association studies (GWAS) summary dataset encompassing 7,174 individuals. The summary genetic data for 91 circulating cytokines were obtained from genome-wide pQTL mapping data. The summary genetic data of GWAS related to migraine and its subtypes were derived from the FinnGen Release 10 database. The MR Analysis methods included the inversevariance- weighted (IVW), MR-Egger, and weighted median.ResultsThe risk of migraine was reduced mediated by CD5 with phosphatidylinositol (18:1_18:2), sphingomyelin (d34:1), and sphingomyelin (d38:1). The risk of migraine and MA was reduced mediated by CD6 with sphingomyelin (d40:1) and sphingomyelin (d42:2). The risk of migraine and MA was increased mediated by CD6 with phosphatidylethanolamine (O- 16:1_18:2).DiscussionCD5 and CD6 were found to be related to migraine. CD5 and CD6 may affect migraine by immunological dysregulation-induced neuroinflammation. Six plasma lipids are associated with two cytokines, indicating that lipid metabolism participates in neuroinflammation, and T cells may be part of it. Plasma levels of lipids were associated with the risk of migraine. The circulating cytokines may serve as mediators in the pathway from plasma lipids to migraine.ConclusionsCD5 and CD6 appeared to mediate the causal relationship between plasma lipids and migraine or MA, including four kinds of sphingomyelin, one phosphatidylinositol, and one phosphatidylethanolamine.

title: Advance in genetics of migraine.
abstract: PURPOSE OF REVIEW: Migraine is a primary headache disorder and one of the most common and disabling neurological diseases worldwide. Genome-wide association studies have identified ≈40 genetic loci associated with migraine. How these and other genetic findings are used to expand our knowledge on the pathophysiological mechanism of common migraine and rare migraine variants will be discussed. RECENT FINDINGS: The genetic load, based on common polygenic variation, is higher in familial migraine cases than in nonfamilial cases, and higher for migraine with aura and hemiplegic migraine. Migraine shares common genetic variant risks with depression. Specific clinical features of common migraine seem to be determined by genetic factors. A stronger family history of migraine is associated with lower age-at-onset, higher frequency and number of medication days and the migraine with aura subtype. Mild hemiplegic migraine is likely caused by complex polygenic interaction of multiple gene variants and environmental factors, like in common migraine subtypes. Phenotypical features in hemiplegic migraine patients may guide physicians in providing adequate genetic counseling. SUMMARY: Integration of genetic, phenotypic and epigenetic data will help to identify the biological mechanisms by which genetic factors contribute to migraine pathogenesis. Recent studies show the impact of genetics on clinical features and comorbidities in migraine and may guide clinicians to an adequate genetic advice for patients.
